quizzes.q: Which value of n is a counter-example to "n² + n + 41 is prime for every positive integer n"?
quizzes.e: n = 40 gives 1600 + 40 + 41 = 1681 = 41², which is not prime.

quizzes.q: In proof by contradiction, what do you assume at the start?
quizzes.e: Assume the statement is false (that its negation is true), then show this leads to a contradiction, so the original statement must be true.

quizzes.q: To prove √2 is irrational by contradiction, you first assume
quizzes.a: √2 = a/b, with integers a, b sharing no common factor
w: a and b are both even
quizzes.e: Assume √2 is rational in lowest terms, then show a and b must both be even – a contradiction.

quizzes.q: Put the steps proving "the sum of two odd numbers is even" in order
items: Let the odd numbers be 2m + 1 and 2n + 1
m + n + 1 is an integer, so the sum is even
quizzes.e: Write the odd numbers in general form (2m + 1 and 2n + 1, with m and n integers), add, then factor out 2. Since m + n + 1 is an integer, the sum is a multiple of 2, so it is even. Proof by deduction.

quizzes.q: Best method to prove "n³ − n is divisible by 6 for every integer n"
quizzes.e: n³ − n = n(n² − 1) = (n − 1)n(n + 1), the product of three consecutive integers. One of them is even and one is a multiple of 3, so the product is divisible by 2 × 3 = 6. Checking examples is not a proof.

quizzes.q: Which is a counter-example to "all prime numbers are odd"?
quizzes.e: 2 is prime (its only factors are 1 and 2) and it is even, so this single case disproves the statement.

quizzes.q: Which disproves "x² > x for all real x"?
quizzes.e: x = 0.5 gives x² = 0.25, which is less than 0.5. Any x between 0 and 1 (and x = 0 or 1) is a counter-example.

quizzes.q: What is proof by exhaustion?
quizzes.e: Split the problem into a finite number of cases that cover every possibility, then prove the statement is true in each case.

quizzes.q: A general odd number can be written as
quizzes.e: For any integer n, 2n is even, so 2n + 1 is odd. Use different letters (2m + 1, 2n + 1) for two different odd numbers.

quizzes.q: The product of two consecutive integers is always
quizzes.e: Of n and n + 1, one must be even, so n(n + 1) has a factor of 2 and is even.

quizzes.q: Order Euclid's proof that there are infinitely many primes
items: Assume there are finitely many primes p₁, …, pₙ
N is prime or has a prime factor not in the list – contradiction
quizzes.e: Assume a finite list of all primes and form N = (their product) + 1. Dividing N by any prime in the list leaves remainder 1, so N has a prime factor not in the list: a contradiction.

quizzes.q: Order the proof that √2 is irrational
items: Then a² = 2b², so a² and hence a are even
Write a = 2k, giving b² = 2k², so b is even
a and b share factor 2 – contradiction
quizzes.e: Assume √2 = a/b in lowest terms. Squaring gives a² = 2b², so a is even; writing a = 2k shows b is even too. Then a and b share the factor 2, contradicting 'lowest terms'.

quizzes.q: To prove "if n² is even then n is even", it is easiest to prove
quizzes.a: the contrapositive: if n is odd then n² is odd
quizzes.e: Prove the contrapositive: if n is odd, n = 2k + 1, so n² = 4k² + 4k + 1 = 2(2k² + 2k) + 1, which is odd. This is logically equivalent to the original.

quizzes.q: Why does checking n = 1 to 100 not prove a statement for every n?
quizzes.e: Checking examples only covers some cases. There are infinitely many integers, and the statement might fail for a value you have not checked.

quizzes.q: (2n + 1)² − (2n − 1)² simplifies to
quizzes.e: (4n² + 4n + 1) − (4n² − 4n + 1) = 8n. So the difference of the squares of consecutive odd numbers is a multiple of 8.

quizzes.q: "If x² = 9 then x = 3" is
quizzes.e: x = −3 also gives x² = 9, so the statement is false. The correct conclusion is x = 3 or x = −3.

quizzes.q: Find the smallest positive integer n for which n² − n + 11 is not prime.
Which number is irrational?
quizzes.e: √12 = √4 × √3 = 2√3, which is irrational. √16/2 = 2, 0.125 = 1/8 and 22/7 are all rational.

quizzes.q: A proof by deduction must start from
quizzes.e: Deduction starts from known facts, definitions or accepted results, and each logical step follows from the previous one to reach the conclusion.

quizzes.q: Which statement is a valid conclusion of a proof by contradiction?
quizzes.a: The assumption is false, so the original statement is true
quizzes.e: The assumption led to a contradiction, so it must be false. Therefore the original statement is true.

quizzes.q: Order the proof that n³ + 3n² + 2n is divisible by 6
items: Three consecutive integers include a multiple of 2
They also include a multiple of 3
So the product is divisible by 6
quizzes.e: n³ + 3n² + 2n = n(n + 1)(n + 2), three consecutive integers. They include a multiple of 2 and a multiple of 3, and 2 and 3 are coprime, so the product is divisible by 6.

quizzes.q: Order the proof that log₂3 is irrational
items: Assume log₂3 = p/q with positive integers p, q
The left side is even and the right side is odd
quizzes.e: If log₂3 = p/q then 2^(p/q) = 3, so 2^p = 3^q. 2^p is even and 3^q is odd for positive integers, which is impossible: a contradiction.

quizzes.q: To prove there is no greatest even number, assume
quizzes.a: a greatest even number N exists, then consider N + 2
quizzes.e: Assume N is the greatest even number. N + 2 is also even and is greater than N, which contradicts the assumption.

quizzes.q: For integers a and b, if ab is even then
quizzes.a: at least one of a and b is even
quizzes.e: If both a and b were odd, ab would be odd (odd × odd = odd). So if ab is even, at least one of a and b must be even.

quizzes.q: Order the proof that rational + irrational is irrational
items: Assume r + x = q, with r and q rational and x irrational
quizzes.e: Assume r + x = q is rational. Then x = q − r. The difference of two rationals is rational, so x would be rational, contradicting that x is irrational.

quizzes.q: x² − 6x + 10 > 0 for all real x because
quizzes.a: it equals (x − 3)² + 1, which is at least 1
quizzes.e: Complete the square: x² − 6x + 10 = (x − 3)² + 1. A square is never negative, so the expression is at least 1, which is greater than 0.

quizzes.q: For any integer n, n² mod 4 is always
quizzes.e: Even n = 2k gives n² = 4k² (remainder 0). Odd n = 2k + 1 gives n² = 4(k² + k) + 1 (remainder 1). So n² mod 4 is 0 or 1.

quizzes.q: Which disproves "if a > b then a² > b²"?
quizzes.e: a = 1 > b = −2, but a² = 1 and b² = 4, so a² < b². The statement fails when b is negative.

quizzes.q: Proof by exhaustion of a statement about n² mod 3 needs how many cases (n mod 3)?
quizzes.e: Every integer leaves remainder 0, 1 or 2 when divided by 3, so n = 3k, 3k + 1 and 3k + 2 cover every case: 3 cases.

quizzes.q: Prove that the square of an odd number is odd: write (2k + 1)² in the form 2m + 1. What is m?
quizzes.e: (2k + 1)² = 4k² + 4k + 1 = 2(2k² + 2k) + 1, so m = 2k² + 2k, which is an integer.

quizzes.q: Find the remainder when f(x) = x³ − 4x + 5 is divided by (x − 2).
quizzes.e: Remainder theorem: dividing by (x − 2) leaves remainder f(2) = 2³ − 4(2) + 5 = 8 − 8 + 5 = 5.

quizzes.q: f(x) = 2x + 3 and g(x) = x². What is fg(x)?
quizzes.e: fg(x) means apply g first, then f: f(x²) = 2x² + 3.
Cover-up: x = −1 gives A = −4/−2 = 2; x = 1 gives B = 6/2 = 3.

quizzes.q: Describe the transformation mapping y = f(x) onto y = f(x − 3).
quizzes.e: Replacing x with (x − 3) moves the graph 3 units in the positive x-direction: a translation by the vector (3, 0). It is not to the left, despite the minus sign.

quizzes.q: The orange curve is y = f(x + 2). Which transformation maps y = f(x) onto it?
w: Stretch, scale factor 2, in the x-direction
quizzes.e: f(x + a) shifts the graph a units to the left.

quizzes.q: Using the laws of indices for rational exponents, evaluate 27^(2/3).
quizzes.e: 27^(1/3) = 3, then square: 3² = 9. A fractional index m/n means the nth root, raised to the power m.

quizzes.q: Solve the simultaneous equations 2x + y = 7 and x − y = 2 by elimination.
quizzes.e: Adding eliminates y: 3x = 9, so x = 3 and y = 1. Both equations in two variables must be satisfied.

quizzes.q: Find the remainder when f(x) = x³ + 2x² + 3x − 7 is divided by (x + 1).
quizzes.e: Remainder theorem: the remainder is f(−1) = (−1)³ + 2(−1)² + (3)(−1) + (−7) = −9.

quizzes.q: Find the remainder when f(x) = x³ + 1x² + x + 5 is divided by (x − 2).
quizzes.e: Remainder theorem: the remainder is f(2) = (2)³ + 1(2)² + (1)(2) + (5) = 19.

quizzes.q: Find the remainder when f(x) = x³ + 4x² + 6x − 3 is divided by (x + 3).
quizzes.e: Remainder theorem: the remainder is f(−3) = (−3)³ + 4(−3)² + (6)(−3) + (−3) = −12.

quizzes.q: f(x) = 5x − 5 and g(x) = x² + 4. Find fg(2).
quizzes.e: fg(2) means apply g first: g(2) = 4 + 4 = 8. Then f(8) = 5 × 8 − 5 = 35.

quizzes.q: f(x) = 5x + 4 and g(x) = x² + 1. Find fg(2).
quizzes.e: fg(2) means apply g first: g(2) = 4 + 1 = 5. Then f(5) = 5 × 5 + 4 = 29.

quizzes.q: The function f(x) = x², x ∈ ℝ, has no inverse because it is
quizzes.e: f is many-to-one (e.g. f(2) = f(−2) = 4), so an inverse cannot map 4 back to a single value. Restricting the domain to x ≥ 0 makes it one-to-one.

quizzes.q: y = ∣f(x)∣ is obtained from y = f(x) by
quizzes.a: reflecting the parts below the x-axis in the x-axis
quizzes.e: The modulus makes negative outputs positive, so parts of the graph below the x-axis are reflected in the x-axis. Parts above stay the same.

quizzes.q: Evaluate 16^(−3/4) as a decimal (laws of indices, negative rational exponent).
quizzes.e: A negative index means the reciprocal: 16^(3/4) = 2³ = 8, so 16^(−3/4) = 1/8 = 0.125.

quizzes.q: Rationalise the denominator of the surd expression 6/√3.
quizzes.e: Multiply the top and bottom by √3: 6√3/3 = 2√3.

quizzes.q: Rationalise the denominator: 4/(3 − √5) =
quizzes.e: Multiply by the conjugate (3 + √5): 4(3 + √5)/(9 − 5) = 4(3 + √5)/4 = 3 + √5. Manipulating surds uses (a − √b)(a + √b) = a² − b.

quizzes.q: For the quadratic function x² + kx + 9, the discriminant condition for repeated (equal) real roots gives
quizzes.e: b² − 4ac = 0 for repeated roots: k² − 36 = 0, so k = ±6. Real roots need b² − 4ac ≥ 0.

quizzes.q: Completing the square on the quadratic x² − 6x + 11 gives
quizzes.a: (x − 3)² + 2, so the minimum point of its graph is (3, 2)
quizzes.e: Halve −6 to get (x − 3)², which expands to x² − 6x + 9, so add 2. The vertex of the graph is (3, 2).

quizzes.q: Solve the simultaneous equations (one linear, one quadratic) y = x + 1 and y = x² − 1 by substitution.
quizzes.e: Substitute: x² − 1 = x + 1, so x² − x − 2 = 0, (x − 2)(x + 1) = 0. Each x gives y from the linear equation.

quizzes.q: Solve the quadratic inequality x² − 5x + 4 < 0 and write it in set notation.
quizzes.e: The critical values are 1 and 4. The graph is a ∪ shape, below the x-axis between the roots, so 1 < x < 4. Interpreting inequalities graphically helps choose the region.

quizzes.q: Decompose the rational function (3x + 1)/(x − 1)² into partial fractions A/(x − 1) + B/(x − 1)².
quizzes.e: 3x + 1 = A(x − 1) + B. x = 1 gives B = 4; comparing x terms gives A = 3. Repeated (squared) linear factors need both terms.

quizzes.q: A model uses h = 20t − 5t² for the height in m of a ball thrown upwards. Give one limitation of using this function as a model.
quizzes.e: The model ignores air resistance and the ball's size, and it gives negative heights after t = 4 s when the ball has already landed, so it is only valid for 0 ≤ t ≤ 4. A refinement could include air resistance.

quizzes.q: (x − 4) is a factor of x³ + kx² − x − 12. Find k.
quizzes.e: Factor theorem: f(4) = 0, so 64 + 16k − 4 − 12 = 0, giving 16k = −48 and k = −3.

quizzes.q: (x − 1) is a factor of x³ + kx² + 0x − 8. Find k.
quizzes.e: Factor theorem: f(1) = 0, so 1 + 1k + 0 − 8 = 0, giving 1k = 7 and k = 7.

quizzes.q: (x − 1) is a factor of x³ + kx² − 5x − 8. Find k.
quizzes.e: Factor theorem: f(1) = 0, so 1 + 1k − 5 − 8 = 0, giving 1k = 12 and k = 12.
Let y = (x + 4)/5, so x = 5y − 4. Hence f⁻¹(x) = 5x − 4 and f⁻¹(5) = 25 − 4 = 21.

quizzes.q: Solve |3x − 3| = 9 for the positive solution x.
quizzes.e: Take the positive case: 3x − 3 = 9, so 3x = 12 and x = 4. (The negative case gives a negative x.)

quizzes.q: Solve |3x − 6| = 12 for the positive solution x.
quizzes.e: Take the positive case: 3x − 6 = 12, so 3x = 18 and x = 6. (The negative case gives a negative x.)

quizzes.q: y = f(2x) + 3 is obtained from y = f(x) by
quizzes.a: stretch scale factor ½ parallel to x-axis, then translate (0, 3)
w: stretch factor 2 parallel to x-axis, then up 3
stretch factor ½ parallel to y-axis
quizzes.e: f(2x) is a stretch parallel to the x-axis with scale factor ½ (inside changes act on x the opposite way). + 3 is then a translation by the vector (0, 3).

quizzes.q: The graph of y = f⁻¹(x) is a reflection of y = f(x) in which line?
quizzes.e: An inverse swaps x and y, so the graph of y = f⁻¹(x) is the reflection of y = f(x) in the line y = x.

quizzes.q: f(x) = 3/(x − 2). The domain of f⁻¹ is
quizzes.e: The domain of f⁻¹ is the range of f. 3/(x − 2) can take any value except 0, so the domain of f⁻¹ is x ≠ 0.

quizzes.q: Express (−x + 20)/((x − 2)(x + 4)) as A/(x − 2) + B/(x + 4). Find A.
quizzes.e: Multiply through: −x + 20 ≡ A(x + 4) + B(x − 2). Substitute x = 2 so the B term vanishes: 18 = 6A, so A = 3.

quizzes.q: Express (−x + 13)/((x − 4)(x + 5)) as A/(x − 4) + B/(x + 5). Find A.
quizzes.e: Multiply through: −x + 13 ≡ A(x + 5) + B(x − 4). Substitute x = 4 so the B term vanishes: 9 = 9A, so A = 1.

quizzes.q: Express (7x − 9)/((x − 3)(x + 1)) as A/(x − 3) + B/(x + 1). Find A.
quizzes.e: Multiply through: 7x − 9 ≡ A(x + 1) + B(x − 3). Substitute x = 3 so the B term vanishes: 12 = 4A, so A = 3.

quizzes.q: f(x) = 4(x − 1)² + 7 for x ≥ 1. Find f⁻¹(43).
quizzes.e: Minimum 7 at x = 1. Solve 4(x − 1)² + 7 = 43: x − 1 = 3, x = 4.

quizzes.q: f(x) = 3(x − 1)² + 4 for x ≥ 1. Find f⁻¹(31).
quizzes.e: Minimum 4 at x = 1. Solve 3(x − 1)² + 4 = 31: x − 1 = 3, x = 4.
fg(x) = f(4x) = e^(4x) + 5. Setting this equal to 5 + e^4 gives e^(4x) = e^4, so 4x = 4 and x = 1.
fg(x) = f(5x) = e^(5x) + 5. Setting this equal to 5 + e^5 gives e^(5x) = e^5, so 5x = 5 and x = 1.

quizzes.q: Find the gradient of a line perpendicular to 2x + 3y = 6.
quizzes.e: Rearrange: 3y = −2x + 6, so y = −(2/3)x + 2 and the gradient is −2/3. Perpendicular gradients multiply to −1, so the answer is 3/2 = 1.5.

quizzes.q: Find the radius of the circle x² + y² − 6x + 4y − 12 = 0.
quizzes.e: Complete the square: (x − 3)² + (y + 2)² = 12 + 9 + 4 = 25, so r = 5.

quizzes.q: The curve x = t², y = 2t has Cartesian equation
quizzes.e: From y = 2t, t = y/2. Substitute into x = t²: x = y²/4, so y² = 4x.

quizzes.q: A tangent to a circle at P is perpendicular to what?
quizzes.e: The tangent at P is perpendicular to the radius at P, so its gradient is the negative reciprocal of the gradient of the radius.

quizzes.q: Which point lies on y = 3x − 7?
quizzes.e: Substitute each x: for (4, 5), 3(4) − 7 = 5, which matches y. The others fail, e.g. (5, 4) gives 3(5) − 7 = 8, not 4.

quizzes.q: Find the gradient of the line through (1, 4) and (8, -5).
Find the gradient of the line through (2, -2) and (6, 7).
Find the gradient of the line through (1, 1) and (5, -3).
Find the length of the line from (-1, 2) to (5, 6) (3 s.f.).
Find the length of the line from (4, 5) to (-1, -5) (3 s.f.).
The perpendicular bisector of a chord of a circle passes through
quizzes.e: The perpendicular bisector of any chord passes through the centre. Two such bisectors meet at the centre.

quizzes.q: The angle in a semicircle is
quizzes.e: The angle in a semicircle is 90°. So if angle ACB = 90° (gradients multiply to −1), AB is a diameter.

quizzes.q: Find the midpoint x-coordinate of (−3, 4) and (7, −2).
quizzes.e: The midpoint is the mean of the coordinates: x = (−3 + 7)/2 = 2 (and y = (4 − 2)/2 = 1).

quizzes.q: A ball's path is modelled by the parametric equations x = 12t, y = 16t − 5t² (in metres, t in seconds). How far horizontally does it travel before landing (y = 0)?
quizzes.e: y = 0 when t(16 − 5t) = 0, so t = 3.2 s; then x = 12 × 3.2 = 38.4 m. Parametric equations are useful in modelling motion in a variety of contexts.

quizzes.q: Circle x² + y² − 4x − 10y − 7 = 0. Find its radius.
quizzes.e: Complete the square: (x − 2)² + (y − 5)² = 4 + 25 + 7 = 36, so the radius is √36 = 6.

quizzes.q: Circle x² + y² + 8x + 6y − 11 = 0. Find its radius.
quizzes.e: Complete the square: (x + 4)² + (y + 3)² = 16 + 9 + 11 = 36, so the radius is √36 = 6.

quizzes.q: Circle x² + y² − 2x + 0y − 24 = 0. Find its radius.
quizzes.e: Complete the square: (x − 1)² + (y + 0)² = 1 + 0 + 24 = 25, so the radius is √25 = 5.

quizzes.q: Line L passes through (-3, −4) and is perpendicular to y = −½x + 1. Find the y-intercept of L.
quizzes.e: Perpendicular gradients multiply to −1, so L has gradient 2. y = 2x + c through (−3, −4): c = −4 − (2) × (−3) = 2.

quizzes.q: Line L passes through (1, 2) and is perpendicular to y = ½x + 1. Find the y-intercept of L.
quizzes.e: Perpendicular gradients multiply to −1, so L has gradient −2. y = −2x + c through (1, 2): c = 2 − (−2) × (1) = 4.

quizzes.q: Line L passes through (2, 2) and is perpendicular to y = −2x + 1. Find the y-intercept of L.
quizzes.e: Perpendicular gradients multiply to −1, so L has gradient 0.5. y = 0.5x + c through (2, 2): c = 2 − (0.5) × (2) = 1.

quizzes.q: A curve has x = t² + 1, y = 2t³. Find dy/dx when t = 2.
quizzes.e: dy/dt = 6t² and dx/dt = 2t, so dy/dx = 6t² ÷ 2t = 3t. At t = 2, dy/dx = 6.

quizzes.q: To show a line is a tangent to a circle, show the substituted quadratic has
quizzes.e: Substitute the line into the circle. A tangent meets the circle once, so the quadratic has one repeated root: discriminant b² − 4ac = 0.

quizzes.q: How do you convert parametric equations to a Cartesian equation?
quizzes.e: Eliminate the parameter: rearrange one equation for t and substitute it into the other, or use an identity such as cos²t + sin²t = 1.

quizzes.q: x = 3cos t, y = 3sin t describes
quizzes.e: x² + y² = 9(cos²t + sin²t) = 9, a circle of radius 3 centred at the origin.

quizzes.q: The line y = 2x + c is a tangent to y = x² when c =
quizzes.e: x² = 2x + c gives x² − 2x − c = 0. For a tangent, discriminant = 4 + 4c = 0, so c = −1.

quizzes.q: x = t + 1, y = t² has Cartesian equation
quizzes.e: From x = t + 1, t = x − 1. Substitute: y = (x − 1)².

quizzes.q: A circle has centre (5, 2) and passes through (8, 6). The tangent at (8, 6) meets the x-axis at A. Find the x-coordinate of A.
quizzes.e: Radius gradient = 4/3, so the tangent gradient is −3/4. Tangent: y − 6 = −¾(x − 8). At y = 0: x = 8 + 4 × 6/3 = 16.

quizzes.q: A circle has centre (1, 2) and passes through (4, 6). The tangent at (4, 6) meets the x-axis at A. Find the x-coordinate of A.
quizzes.e: Radius gradient = 4/3, so the tangent gradient is −3/4. Tangent: y − 6 = −¾(x − 4). At y = 0: x = 4 + 4 × 6/3 = 12.

quizzes.q: A circle has centre (5, 5) and passes through (8, 9). The tangent at (8, 9) meets the x-axis at A. Find the x-coordinate of A.
quizzes.e: Radius gradient = 4/3, so the tangent gradient is −3/4. Tangent: y − 9 = −¾(x − 8). At y = 0: x = 8 + 4 × 9/3 = 20.

quizzes.q: Find the discriminant of the quadratic in x formed by substituting y = 2x − 2 into x² + y² = 25.
quizzes.e: x² + (2x − 2)² = 25 gives 5x² − 8x − 21 = 0. Discriminant = b² − 4ac = (−8)² − 4 × 5 × (−21) = 484. Positive, so the line crosses the circle twice.

quizzes.q: Find the discriminant of the quadratic in x formed by substituting y = 3x − 1 into x² + y² = 25.
quizzes.e: x² + (3x − 1)² = 25 gives 10x² − 6x − 24 = 0. Discriminant = b² − 4ac = (−6)² − 4 × 10 × (−24) = 996. Positive, so the line crosses the circle twice.

quizzes.q: An arithmetic series has first term 5 and common difference 3. Find the sum of the first 20 terms.
Find the sum to infinity of 12 + 6 + 3 + …
quizzes.e: a = 12 and r = 6/12 = ½. Since the modulus of r is less than 1, S∞ = a/(1 − r) = 12/(1 − ½) = 24.

quizzes.q: The coefficient of x² in (1 + 2x)⁵ is
quizzes.e: The x² term is ⁵C₂ × 1³ × (2x)² = 10 × 4x² = 40x², so the coefficient is 40. Remember to square the 2 as well as the x.

quizzes.q: The binomial expansion of (1 + 3x)⁻¹ is valid for
quizzes.e: (1 + kx)ⁿ for negative or fractional n is valid when the modulus of kx is less than 1. Here 3x must lie between −1 and 1, so −⅓ < x < ⅓.

quizzes.q: uₙ₊₁ = 2uₙ − 1 with u₁ = 3. Find u₄.
Using sigma notation, evaluate the sum of series Σ (from r = 1 to 5) of (2r + 1).
quizzes.e: The terms are 3, 5, 7, 9 and 11, which sum to 35 (an arithmetic series: 5/2 × (3 + 11) = 35).

quizzes.q: Arithmetic sequence: a = 7, d = 5. Find the 18th term.
Arithmetic sequence: a = 2, d = 5. Find the 26th term.
Arithmetic sequence: a = 4, d = 6. Find the 27th term.
Geometric sequence: first term 3, ratio 3. Find the 6th term.
Geometric sequence: first term 2, ratio 3. Find the 6th term.
Σ (from r = 1 to n) of r equals
quizzes.e: 1 + 2 + … + n is an arithmetic series with a = 1, l = n: S = n/2 × (1 + n) = n(n + 1)/2.

quizzes.q: A geometric series converges when the ratio r satisfies
quizzes.e: If −1 < r < 1, rⁿ → 0 as n increases, so the sum approaches a/(1 − r). Otherwise the terms do not shrink and the series diverges.

quizzes.q: uₙ₊₁ = 1/uₙ with u₁ = 2 gives a

quizzes.q: Write 8 sin x + 15 cos x as R sin(x + α). Find R.
quizzes.e: R sin(x + α) = R sin x cos α + R cos x sin α, so R cos α = 8 and R sin α = 15. Square and add: R = √(8² + 15²) = 17.

quizzes.q: Write 5 sin x + 12 cos x as R sin(x + α). Find R.
quizzes.e: R sin(x + α) = R sin x cos α + R cos x sin α, so R cos α = 5 and R sin α = 12. Square and add: R = √(5² + 12²) = 13.

quizzes.q: A closed cylinder has volume 1000 cm³. Find the radius that minimises its surface area (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: h = V/(πr²), so A = 2πr² + 2V/r. dA/dr = 4πr − 2V/r² = 0 gives r³ = V/(2π) = 159.2, so r = 5.42 cm (d²A/dr² > 0, a minimum).

quizzes.q: A closed cylinder has volume 500 cm³. Find the radius that minimises its surface area (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: h = V/(πr²), so A = 2πr² + 2V/r. dA/dr = 4πr − 2V/r² = 0 gives r³ = V/(2π) = 79.58, so r = 4.3 cm (d²A/dr² > 0, a minimum).

quizzes.q: Find dy/dx at (1, 2) for x² + y² + 2xy = 9 (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Differentiate implicitly: 2x + 2y dy/dx + 2(y + x dy/dx) = 0. At (1, 2): 2 + 4 dy/dx + 4 + 2 dy/dx = 0, so dy/dx = −6/6 = −1.

quizzes.q: Evaluate ∫₀² (3x² + 1) dx.
quizzes.e: Integrate: [x³ + x] from 0 to 2 = (8 + 2) − (0 + 0) = 10.

quizzes.q: ∫ (1/x) dx for x > 0 is
quizzes.e: d/dx ln x = 1/x, so ∫ (1/x) dx = ln x + c for x > 0. The power rule fails here because n = −1.

quizzes.q: ∫ cos 2x dx =
quizzes.e: d/dx sin 2x = 2 cos 2x, so to reverse it divide by 2: ∫ cos 2x dx = ½ sin 2x + c.

quizzes.q: Which technique would you use for ∫ x eˣ dx?
quizzes.e: Integration by parts: let u = x (it simplifies when differentiated) and dv/dx = eˣ. Then ∫ x eˣ dx = xeˣ − ∫ eˣ dx = xeˣ − eˣ + c.

quizzes.q: Find the area between y = x² and the x-axis from x = 0 to x = 3.
quizzes.e: Area = ∫₀³ x² dx = [x³/3] from 0 to 3 = 27/3 − 0 = 9 square units.

quizzes.q: Integrate 6x² − 4x + 5 (sums, differences and constant multiples of xⁿ, excluding n = −1).
quizzes.e: Raise each power by one and divide by the new power, then add the constant c.

quizzes.q: Evaluate ∫₁^3 (1/x) dx (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: ∫(1/x) dx = ln x, so the answer is ln 3 − ln 1 = ln 3.

quizzes.q: ∫ sec²x dx =
quizzes.e: d/dx (tan x) = sec²x, so ∫ sec²x dx = tan x + c.

quizzes.q: ∫ e^(5x) dx =
quizzes.e: d/dx e^(5x) = 5e^(5x), so to reverse it divide by 5: ∫ e^(5x) dx = e^(5x)/5 + c.

quizzes.q: Area below the x-axis from integration is
quizzes.e: Where the curve is below the x-axis the integral is negative. For a total area, integrate each part separately and add their sizes.

quizzes.q: Evaluate ∫₀¹ e^(2x) dx (3 s.f.).
Why does the trapezium rule overestimate this integral?
quizzes.a: The curve is convex, so each chord lies above the curve
w: The curve is concave, so each chord lies below it
quizzes.e: For a convex curve (f″ > 0) the tops of the trapezia lie above it.

quizzes.q: Using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, evaluate the definite integral of 3x² from x = 1 to x = 2.
quizzes.e: The integral of 3x² is x³, so [x³] from 1 to 2 = 8 − 1 = 7. Integration is the reverse of differentiation.

quizzes.q: A differential equation model gives a population P = 500e^(0.2t). Interpret the solution in context and state one limitation of it.
quizzes.e: The initial population (t = 0) is 500 and it grows exponentially. A limitation is that it predicts the population grows without limit, which is unrealistic because of limited food, space or other resources.

quizzes.q: Evaluate ∫₀^(π/2) sin(4x) dx (3 s.f.).
Evaluate ∫₀^(π/2) sin(3x) dx (3 s.f.).
Evaluate ∫₀¹ x e^(3x) dx (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: By parts with u = x, dv/dx = e^(3x): ∫ = [x e^(3x)/3] − ∫ e^(3x)/3 dx = [x e^(3x)/3 − e^(3x)/9] from 0 to 1 = 4.57.

quizzes.q: Evaluate ∫₀¹ x e^(x) dx (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: By parts with u = x, dv/dx = e^(x): ∫ = [x e^(x)/1] − ∫ e^(x)/1 dx = [x e^(x)/1 − e^(x)/1] from 0 to 1 = 1.

quizzes.q: Find the area enclosed between y = x(5 − x) and the x-axis (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: The curve meets the x-axis at 0 and 5. Area = ∫₀^5 (5x − x²) dx = [2.5x² − x³/3] = 62.5 − 41.67 = 20.8.

quizzes.q: Find the area enclosed between y = x(2 − x) and the x-axis (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: The curve meets the x-axis at 0 and 2. Area = ∫₀^2 (2x − x²) dx = [1x² − x³/3] = 4 − 2.667 = 1.33.

quizzes.q: ∫ f′(x)/f(x) dx =
quizzes.e: d/dx ln f(x) = f′(x)/f(x), so ∫ f′(x)/f(x) dx = ln(f(x)) + c, taking the modulus of f(x) when it can be negative.

quizzes.q: To integrate sin²x, first use
quizzes.e: Use cos 2x = 1 − 2sin²x, so sin²x = ½(1 − cos 2x). Then ∫ sin²x dx = ½x − ¼ sin 2x + c.

quizzes.q: Evaluate ∫₀^(π/2) sin²x dx (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: sin²x = ½(1 − cos 2x), so the integral is [½x − ¼ sin 2x] from 0 to π/2 = π/4 − 0 = 0.785.

quizzes.q: Integrate using partial fractions linear in the denominator, for x > 1: ∫ 2/((x − 1)(x + 1)) dx =
quizzes.e: 2/((x − 1)(x + 1)) = 1/(x − 1) − 1/(x + 1). Each linear denominator integrates to a ln term.

quizzes.q: Find the area enclosed by y = x² and y = 5x (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: x² = 5x at x = 0 and x = 5. The line is above the curve between them: area = ∫₀^5 (5x − x²) dx = 5³/2 − 5³/3 = 125/6 = 20.8.

quizzes.q: Find the area enclosed by y = x² and y = 4x (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: x² = 4x at x = 0 and x = 4. The line is above the curve between them: area = ∫₀^4 (4x − x²) dx = 4³/2 − 4³/3 = 64/6 = 10.7.

quizzes.q: Use the substitution u = 1 + x² to evaluate ∫₀^3 2x/(1 + x²) dx (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: u = 1 + x² gives du = 2x dx, and the limits become 1 and 10. ∫ du/u = [ln u] from 1 to 10 = ln 10 = 2.3.

quizzes.q: Use the substitution u = 1 + x² to evaluate ∫₀^2 2x/(1 + x²) dx (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: u = 1 + x² gives du = 2x dx, and the limits become 1 and 5. ∫ du/u = [ln u] from 1 to 5 = ln 5 = 1.61.

quizzes.q: dy/dx = y, y = 3 when x = 0. Find y when x = 1 (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Separate: ∫ dy/y = ∫ 1 dx, so ln y = x + c and y = Ae^(x). y = 3 at x = 0 gives A = 3. At x = 1: y = 3e^1 = 8.15.

quizzes.q: dy/dx = 0.5y, y = 3 when x = 0. Find y when x = 1 (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Separate: ∫ dy/y = ∫ 0.5 dx, so ln y = 0.5x + c and y = Ae^(0.5x). y = 3 at x = 0 gives A = 3. At x = 1: y = 3e^0.5 = 4.95.

quizzes.q: Evaluate ∫₁^e ln x dx.
quizzes.e: By parts: [x ln x − x]₁^e = 0 − (−1) = 1.

quizzes.q: f(x) = x³ − 2x − 5. f(2) = −1, f(3) = 16. This shows
quizzes.a: a root lies between 2 and 3 (f is continuous)
quizzes.e: A change of sign of a continuous function implies a root.

quizzes.q: One Newton–Raphson step on f(x) = x² − 5 from x₀ = 2. Find x₁.
When does Newton–Raphson fail?
quizzes.e: If x₀ is at or near a stationary point, f′(x₀) ≈ 0, so dividing by it sends the next estimate far away (or is impossible). It can also fail if it converges to a different root.

quizzes.q: The trapezium rule overestimates the area when the curve is
quizzes.e: For a convex curve (bending upwards) the straight tops of the trapezia lie above the curve, so the rule overestimates. For a concave curve it underestimates.

quizzes.q: xₙ₊₁ = √(xₙ + 2), x₀ = 1. Find x₂ (3 d.p.).
Newton–Raphson for f(x) = x³ − 5 with x₀ = 2.5. Find x₁ (4 s.f.).
Newton–Raphson for f(x) = x³ − 6 with x₀ = 2.5. Find x₁ (4 s.f.).
Newton–Raphson for f(x) = x³ − 8 with x₀ = 2.5. Find x₁ (4 s.f.).
Evaluate f(1.5) for f(x) = x² − 6 to decide the sign (give the value).
Evaluate f(1.5) for f(x) = x² − 3 to decide the sign (give the value).
An iteration xₙ₊₁ = g(xₙ) converges if near the root
quizzes.a: the modulus of g′(x) is less than 1
quizzes.e: The iteration converges if the gradient g′(x) near the root has modulus less than 1 (between −1 and 1). Otherwise it moves away from the root.

quizzes.q: A staircase diagram shows the iteration
quizzes.e: A staircase diagram occurs when 0 < g′(x) < 1 near the root: the iterates approach from one side. A cobweb occurs when g′ is negative.

quizzes.q: Why might a change of sign fail to show a root?
quizzes.e: If the function is not continuous (e.g. it has an asymptote such as 1/x at 0), it can change sign without crossing the x-axis.

quizzes.q: A change of sign may miss roots if
quizzes.a: there are two roots close together in the interval
quizzes.e: With an even number of roots in the interval (e.g. two close together), f has the same sign at both ends, so no change of sign is seen.

quizzes.q: xₙ₊₁ = ∛(xₙ + 7), x₀ = 1. Find x₃ (4 d.p.).
xₙ₊₁ = ∛(xₙ + 8), x₀ = 1. Find x₃ (4 d.p.).

Use the trapezium rule with 4 strips to estimate ∫₀² √(1 + 3x²) dx (3 s.f.).
Use the trapezium rule with 4 strips to estimate ∫₀² √(1 + 1x²) dx (3 s.f.).
Increasing the number of trapezium strips makes the estimate
quizzes.e: More strips means a smaller strip width h, so the chords follow the curve more closely and the estimate is more accurate.

quizzes.q: Why does Newton–Raphson fail if f′(x₀) = 0?
quizzes.e: x₁ = x₀ − f(x₀)/f′(x₀) would divide by zero. Geometrically the tangent is horizontal and never meets the x-axis.

quizzes.q: x³ − 3x + 1 = 0 rearranged as x = (x³ + 1)/3 gives g′ at a root near 0.35 of about
quizzes.e: g(x) = (x³ + 1)/3, so g′(x) = x². Near 0.35, g′ ≈ 0.12, which has modulus less than 1, so the iteration converges.

quizzes.q: To show a root is 1.47 to 2 d.p., evaluate f at
quizzes.e: Any number in [1.465, 1.475) rounds to 1.47. A change of sign between f(1.465) and f(1.475) shows the root is in this interval.

quizzes.q: Upper and lower bounds on an area can be found using
quizzes.a: rectangles above and below the curve
quizzes.e: Rectangles under the curve give a lower bound and rectangles above give an upper bound; the true area lies between them.

quizzes.q: A tank's depth h (m) satisfies h³ + h − 4 = 0. Use the numerical method (iteration) h_(n+1) = (4 − h_n)^(1/3), starting with h₀ = 1.4, until it converges. Give the root to 3 d.p.
quizzes.e: h₁ = 2.6^(1/3) = 1.3751, h₂ = 1.3796, h₃ = 1.3786, ... converging to 1.379 (3 d.p.). Numerical methods solve problems in context when there is no exact method.

quizzes.q: f(x) = x³ + x − 8. Starting at x₀ = 1.5, apply Newton–Raphson twice. Find x₂ (4 d.p.).
quizzes.e: f′(x) = 3x² + 1. x₁ = 1.5 − f(1.5)/f′(1.5) = 1.9032; repeating once more gives x₂ = 1.8360.

quizzes.q: f(x) = x³ + x − 5. Starting at x₀ = 1.5, apply Newton–Raphson twice. Find x₂ (4 d.p.).
quizzes.e: f′(x) = 3x² + 1. x₁ = 1.5 − f(1.5)/f′(1.5) = 1.5161; repeating once more gives x₂ = 1.5160.

quizzes.q: f(x) = x³ + x − 6. Starting at x₀ = 1.5, apply Newton–Raphson twice. Find x₂ (4 d.p.).
quizzes.e: f′(x) = 3x² + 1. x₁ = 1.5 − f(1.5)/f′(1.5) = 1.6452; repeating once more gives x₂ = 1.6344.

quizzes.q: Trapezium rule, 4 strips, for ∫₀¹ e^(−3x²) dx (4 s.f.).
Trapezium rule, 4 strips, for ∫₀¹ e^(−4x²) dx (4 s.f.).
Find the magnitude of 3i + 4j.
quizzes.e: The magnitude of xi + yj is √(x² + y²) = √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5.

quizzes.q: Find the magnitude of 2i − j + 2k.
A(1, 2, 3), B(4, 6, 3). Vector AB is
What does a = kb (k a scalar) tell you about a and b?
quizzes.e: If a = kb, the vectors are parallel (same direction for k > 0, opposite for k < 0), and the magnitude of a is k times that of b.

quizzes.q: Find the distance between (1, 2, 3) and (4, 6, 15).
Use vectors in three dimensions: find the magnitude of 2i − 3j + 6k.
quizzes.e: The magnitude is √(4 + 9 + 36) = √49 = 7. In two dimensions the same idea gives √(x² + y²).

quizzes.e: tan θ = 2/2, so θ = tan⁻¹(1) = 45°.

quizzes.q: Find the angle between 2i + 5j and the positive x-axis (3 s.f.).
A unit vector in the direction of 3i + 4j is
quizzes.e: The magnitude is √(3² + 4²) = 5. Divide by it: (3i + 4j)/5 = 0.6i + 0.8j, which has magnitude 1.

quizzes.q: Position vector of P(2, −1, 5) is
quizzes.e: The position vector of (x, y, z) is xi + yj + zk, so P is 2i − j + 5k.

quizzes.q: If AB = b − a, then BA =
quizzes.e: BA goes the opposite way: BA = a − b = −AB.

quizzes.q: What is a position vector?
quizzes.e: A position vector gives the position of a point relative to the origin O: the vector OP.

quizzes.q: Points A, B, C are collinear if
quizzes.a: AB = k AC for a scalar k
quizzes.e: If AB = k AC, then AB and AC are parallel. They share the point A, so A, B and C lie on one straight line.

quizzes.q: a = 3i + j and b = −i + 2j. Using vector addition and multiplication by scalars, 2a − b =
quizzes.e: 2a = 6i + 2j; subtracting b gives 7i + 0j. Geometrically, 2a − b is the diagonal found by joining 2a and −b tip to tail.

quizzes.q: Forces (3i + 4j) N and (5i − 10j) N act on a particle. Using vectors to solve this problem in context, the magnitude of the resultant force is
quizzes.e: Add the force vectors: 8i − 6j. The magnitude is √(64 + 36) = 10 N.

quizzes.q: a = 2i + 5j and b = 6i + pj are parallel. Find p.
quizzes.e: Parallel vectors are multiples: the i-components give b = 3a, so p = 3 × 5 = 15.

quizzes.q: a = 2i + 2j and b = 6i + pj are parallel. Find p.
quizzes.e: Parallel vectors are multiples: the i-components give b = 3a, so p = 3 × 2 = 6.

quizzes.q: M divides AB in the ratio 1 : 2. OM =
quizzes.e: OM = OA + ⅓AB = a + ⅓(b − a) = ⅔a + ⅓b.

quizzes.q: How do you show that ABCD is a parallelogram using vectors?
quizzes.e: Show AB = DC. Then one pair of opposite sides is equal and parallel, so ABCD is a parallelogram.

quizzes.q: A ship's velocity is (5i + 12j) km/h. Its speed is
quizzes.e: Speed is the magnitude of velocity: √(5² + 12²) = √169 = 13 km/h.

quizzes.q: A = (0, 3, 3), B = (-1, -1, 2). M is the midpoint of AB. Find |OM| (3 s.f.).
A = (-3, 1, 1), B = (3, -2, 6). M is the midpoint of AB. Find |OM| (3 s.f.).
A = (1, -2, 1), B = (-2, 1, 2). M is the midpoint of AB. Find |OM| (3 s.f.).
Triangle with vertices O, A(4, 0, 0) and B(0, 6, 0). Find the area of triangle OAB.
quizzes.e: OA lies along the x-axis and OB along the y-axis, so the angle at O is 90°. Area = ½ × 4 × 6 = 12.

quizzes.q: Triangle with vertices O, A(6, 0, 0) and B(0, 2, 0). Find the area of triangle OAB.
quizzes.e: OA lies along the x-axis and OB along the y-axis, so the angle at O is 90°. Area = ½ × 6 × 2 = 6.

quizzes.q: OABC is a parallelogram with a = 3i + j, c = i + 4j. Find |OB| (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: OB = OA + AB = a + c = 4i + 5j, so its length is √(4² + 5²) = √41 = 6.40.

quizzes.q: A particle moves with velocity (3i − 4j) m/s from position 2i + j. Find its distance from the origin after 2 s (3 s.f.).
Which method selects every kth item after a random start?
quizzes.e: Systematic sampling: pick a random start from the first k items, then take every kth item from the list (k = population ÷ sample size).

quizzes.q: A disadvantage of quota sampling is
quizzes.a: it is not random so may be biased
w: it cannot be used for large populations
quizzes.e: The interviewer chooses who fills each quota.

quizzes.q: What is a sampling frame?
quizzes.e: A sampling frame is a list of all the members of the population that could be sampled, e.g. a school register.

quizzes.q: 300 Y12 and 200 Y13 students. In a stratified sample of 50, how many are Y13?
quizzes.e: Stratified sampling is proportional: Y13 makes up 200/500 of the population, so 200/500 × 50 = 20 students.

quizzes.q: Match each sampling method to its description
quizzes.e: Stratified samples each group in proportion; systematic takes every kth item; quota lets the interviewer fill set groups (not random); opportunity uses whoever is available.

quizzes.q: The whole group you want to study is the
quizzes.e: The population is the whole group of interest. A sample is a selected subset of it.

quizzes.q: Surveying every member of a population is a
quizzes.e: A census measures every member of the population. It is accurate but can be time-consuming and expensive, and it is not practical if testing destroys items.

quizzes.q: Give one advantage of a sample over a census.
quizzes.e: A sample is cheaper and quicker than a census and gives less data to process. It is also essential when testing destroys the items.

quizzes.q: Each item is numbered and chosen with random numbers. This is
quizzes.e: Simple random sampling: every sample of the given size is equally likely. It needs a sampling frame so each item can be numbered.

quizzes.q: Which sampling method is NOT random?
quizzes.e: Opportunity (convenience) sampling uses whoever is available at the time, so it is not random and is likely to be biased.

quizzes.q: A factory has 120 day-shift and 80 night-shift workers. A stratified sample of 30 is taken. How many from night shift?
quizzes.e: Night shift is 80 of the 200 workers, so take 80/200 × 30 = 12 from the night shift (and 18 from the day shift).

quizzes.q: Systematic sample of 20 from a list of 500. What is the interval k?
quizzes.e: k = population size ÷ sample size = 500 ÷ 20 = 25. Choose a random start from 1 to 25, then take every 25th item.

quizzes.q: A disadvantage of opportunity sampling is that it
quizzes.a: is unlikely to represent the population
quizzes.e: The sample is chosen for convenience, so it is likely to be biased and unrepresentative.

quizzes.q: Stratified sampling is useful when
quizzes.a: the population splits into clear groups
quizzes.e: Stratified sampling is used when the population splits into distinct groups (strata). Sampling each group in proportion makes the sample representative.

quizzes.q: What is a sampling unit?
quizzes.e: A sampling unit is a single member (individual or item) of the population that can be selected.

quizzes.q: In the Large Data Set, 'tr' for rainfall means
quizzes.e: 'tr' means trace: less than 0.05 mm of rain. It is usually treated as 0 in calculations.

quizzes.q: Quota sampling is often used in
quizzes.e: Market research interviewers are given quotas (e.g. 20 men aged 18–30) and fill them with people they meet. It is quick but not random.

quizzes.q: Which method gives each member an equal chance and does not divide the population into groups?
quizzes.e: Simple random sampling: every member is equally likely and no division into strata is needed.

quizzes.q: Which data is quantitative?
quizzes.e: Quantitative data are numerical, like daily maximum temperature. Wind direction, cloud type and location are qualitative (categories).

quizzes.q: What is bias in sampling?
quizzes.e: Bias occurs when the sampling method systematically favours some members, so the sample does not represent the population.

quizzes.q: Stratified sample of 40 from 3 groups of sizes 150, 250 and 400. How many from the largest group?
quizzes.e: Total = 150 + 250 + 400 = 800. The largest group gets 400/800 × 40 = 20.

quizzes.q: A student samples the first 50 cars entering a car park to estimate average age of cars in a city. The main problem is
quizzes.e: Cars entering one car park at one time are unlikely to represent all cars in the city, so the sample is biased.

quizzes.q: Why might a systematic sample be biased?
quizzes.e: If the list has a repeating pattern that matches the interval k, the sample may pick the same type of item every time, so it is biased.

quizzes.q: Cluster sampling involves
quizzes.a: randomly choosing whole groups, then sampling within them
quizzes.e: Cluster sampling divides the population into groups (clusters), randomly chooses some whole clusters and samples within them. It is cheaper when the population is spread out.

quizzes.q: Random numbers 07, 23, 91, 23, 45, 62 are used to pick 4 distinct items from a list numbered 01–80. Which number is the 4th item chosen?
quizzes.e: Ignore 91 (out of range) and the repeated 23, so the items are 07, 23, 45 and 62.

quizzes.q: To improve reliability of a sample estimate you should
quizzes.e: Larger random samples vary less from sample to sample, so the estimate is more reliable.

quizzes.q: A survey of a school is done by asking the first 20 students in the canteen. Suggest a better method.
quizzes.e: The canteen sample is opportunity sampling and may be biased. Use a stratified sample by year group, or a simple random sample from the full school register.

quizzes.q: A sampling frame for a school survey could be
quizzes.e: A sampling frame lists every member of the population. The school register lists every student, so it works as a frame.

quizzes.q: Population 2000, sample 5%. What sample size?
A sample should be
quizzes.e: A sample should represent the population so that conclusions from it can be generalised to the whole population.

quizzes.q: Find the mean of 2, 4, 4, 5, 7, 8.
quizzes.e: Mean = total ÷ number of values = (2 + 4 + 4 + 5 + 7 + 8) ÷ 6 = 30 ÷ 6 = 5.

quizzes.q: Outliers lie more than 1.5 × IQR beyond the quartiles. Q₁ = 10, Q₃ = 18. Find the upper limit.
quizzes.e: IQR = Q₃ − Q₁ = 18 − 10 = 8. Upper limit = Q₃ + 1.5 × IQR = 18 + 12 = 30.

quizzes.q: In a histogram, frequency is proportional to
quizzes.e: In a histogram the bar area is proportional to frequency, since frequency density = frequency ÷ class width.

quizzes.q: r = −0.92 indicates
quizzes.e: r close to −1 means a strong negative linear correlation: as one variable increases, the other tends to decrease.

quizzes.q: Why should you avoid extrapolating a regression line?
quizzes.e: The relationship is only known within the range of the data, so predictions outside that range (extrapolation) may be unreliable.

quizzes.q: Σx = 50, Σx² = 300, n = 10. Find the variance.
Which average is most affected by outliers?
quizzes.e: The mean uses every value, so one extreme value shifts it. The median and mode are resistant to outliers.

quizzes.q: Use the box plot to find the interquartile range.
quizzes.e: Read the quartiles from the ends of the box: IQR = Q₃ − Q₁ = 55 − 28 = 27.

quizzes.q: Find the mean of 15, 9, 4, 2, 10, 1 (3 s.f.).
Find the mean of 20, 1, 3, 14, 4, 2 (3 s.f.).
Find the mean of 7, 8, 19, 14, 6, 4 (3 s.f.).
A box plot shows
quizzes.a: min, Q₁, median, Q₃, max and outliers
quizzes.e: A box plot shows the minimum, Q₁, median, Q₃ and maximum, with outliers plotted as separate crosses.

quizzes.q: Positive skew means
quizzes.e: In positive skew the tail is on the right, so a few large values pull the mean above the median.

quizzes.q: Data 3, 7, 8, 12, 15, 21, 30. Find the interquartile range (Q₁ = 7, Q₃ = 21).
quizzes.e: IQR = Q₃ − Q₁ = 21 − 7 = 14. It measures the spread of the middle 50% of the data.

quizzes.q: n = 17, Σx = 92, Σx² = 923. Find the standard deviation (3 s.f.).
n = 13, Σx = 90, Σx² = 714. Find the standard deviation (3 s.f.).

Q₁ = 19, Q₃ = 52. Find the lower outlier boundary (Q₁ − 1.5 × IQR).
Q₁ = 18, Q₃ = 57. Find the lower outlier boundary (Q₁ − 1.5 × IQR).
A class of width 10 has frequency 32. Find its frequency density.
quizzes.e: Frequency density = frequency ÷ class width = 32 ÷ 10 = 3.2.

quizzes.q: A class of width 5 has frequency 25. Find its frequency density.
quizzes.e: Frequency density = frequency ÷ class width = 25 ÷ 5 = 5.

quizzes.q: Adding 5 to every data value changes the standard deviation by
quizzes.e: Adding a constant shifts every value and the mean by 5, but the spread is unchanged, so the standard deviation stays the same.

quizzes.q: Multiplying every value by 3 multiplies the variance by
quizzes.e: Multiplying by 3 multiplies the standard deviation by 3, so the variance (σ²) is multiplied by 3² = 9.

quizzes.q: Explain why correlation does not imply causation.
quizzes.e: Two variables can be correlated because a third factor affects both, or by coincidence. Correlation alone does not show that one causes the other.

quizzes.q: The explanatory variable in y = a + bx is
quizzes.e: x is the explanatory (independent) variable, plotted on the horizontal axis. y is the response variable it is used to predict.

quizzes.q: Which is a cleaning step for the Large Data Set?
quizzes.e: Cleaning means dealing with entries such as 'n/a' (missing data) and 'tr' (trace) before calculating, e.g. removing them or treating tr as 0.

quizzes.q: Coded data y = (x − 70)/5 has mean 2.4 and standard deviation 1.2. Find the standard deviation of x.
quizzes.e: x = 5y + 70. Adding a constant does not change the spread and multiplying by 5 multiplies it by 5, so σx = 5 × 1.2 = 6.

quizzes.q: Coded y = (x − 100)/5 has ȳ = 2.4. Find x̄.
quizzes.e: Rearrange the coding: x = 5y + 100, so x̄ = 5ȳ + 100 = 5 × 2.4 + 100 = 112.

quizzes.q: Grouped data: 10–20 (f = 4), 20–30 (f = 6), 30–50 (f = 10). Estimate the mean using midpoints.
quizzes.e: Midpoints 15, 25 and 40. Σfx = 15 × 4 + 25 × 6 + 40 × 10 = 610 and Σf = 20, so the estimated mean = 610 ÷ 20 = 30.5.

quizzes.q: Same data: estimate the median by interpolation (classes 10–20 f 4, 20–30 f 6, 30–50 f 10).
quizzes.e: n = 20, so the median is the 10th value (n/2). Cumulative frequencies are 4, 10, 20, so the 10th value is at the end of the 20–30 class: median ≈ 30.

quizzes.q: Regression line y = 2.3 + 0.8x for x in [10, 40]. Predict y at x = 25.
quizzes.e: y = 2.3 + 0.8 × 25 = 2.3 + 20 = 22.3. x = 25 is within the data range, so this is interpolation and reasonably reliable.

quizzes.q: P(A) = 0.4, P(B) = 0.5, independent. Find P(A ∩ B).
quizzes.e: For independent events P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B) = 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.2.
Addition rule: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B) = 0.6 + 0.3 − 0.1 = 0.8.

quizzes.q: A and B are mutually exclusive. Then
quizzes.e: Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together, so P(A ∩ B) = 0 and P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B).

quizzes.q: P(A ∩ B) = 0.12, P(B) = 0.4. Find P(A given B).
State the test for independence of A and B.
quizzes.e: A and B are independent if P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B), or equivalently if P(A given B) = P(A).

quizzes.q: Using the tree diagram, find the probability of getting one of each colour.
quizzes.e: One of each colour is red then blue OR blue then red. Multiply along each branch, then add: 0.30 + 0.24 = 0.54.

quizzes.q: A and B are independent with P(A) = 0.2, P(B) = 0.3. Find P(A ∪ B).
A and B are independent with P(A) = 0.4, P(B) = 0.6. Find P(A ∪ B).
A and B are independent with P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.3. Find P(A ∪ B).
A bag has 6 red and 2 blue balls. Two are taken without replacement. Find P(both red) (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: (6/8) × (5/7): one fewer red and one fewer ball for the second pick.

quizzes.q: A bag has 3 red and 4 blue balls. Two are taken without replacement. Find P(both red) (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: (3/7) × (2/6): one fewer red and one fewer ball for the second pick.

quizzes.q: A Venn diagram region outside both A and B represents
quizzes.e: The region outside both circles is 'not A and not B': P(A′ ∩ B′) = 1 − P(A ∪ B).
A either happens or does not, so P(A) + P(A′) = 1 and P(A′) = 1 − P(A).

quizzes.q: What does it mean for events to be independent?
quizzes.e: Events are independent if one happening does not change the probability of the other, so P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B).

quizzes.q: Tree diagram probabilities along a branch are
quizzes.e: Moving along a branch means 'this AND then that', so multiply. Add the results of different complete paths ('OR').

quizzes.q: A card is drawn from 52. Find P(king or heart) (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: 4 kings + 13 hearts − 1 (king of hearts counted twice) = 16 cards. P = 16/52 = 0.308.

quizzes.q: Using the Venn diagram, find P(A given B) (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: P(A given B) = P(A ∩ B) ÷ P(B) = 0.2 ÷ 0.3 = 0.667. Only the B circle counts as the new total.

quizzes.q: P(A) = 0.6, P(A ∩ B) = 0.15. Find P(B given A) (3 s.f.).
P(A) = 0.4, P(A ∩ B) = 0.15. Find P(B given A) (3 s.f.).
P(A) = 0.4, P(A ∩ B) = 0.2. Find P(B given A) (3 s.f.).
P(A) = 0.3, P(B) = 0.5, A and B mutually exclusive. Find P(A ∪ B).
quizzes.e: Mutually exclusive, so P(A ∩ B) = 0 and P(A ∪ B) = 0.3 + 0.5.

quizzes.q: Two fair dice are rolled. Find P(sum = 7).
quizzes.e: There are 36 equally likely outcomes, and 6 give a sum of 7: (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1). P = 6/36 = 1/6.

quizzes.q: If P(A given B) = P(A), then A and B are
quizzes.e: Knowing B has happened does not change the probability of A, which is the definition of independence.

quizzes.q: Events that cannot happen together and cover all outcomes are
quizzes.e: Mutually exclusive means they cannot both happen; exhaustive means together they cover every outcome. Their probabilities add to 1.
Rearrange the addition rule: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∪ B) = 0.4 + 0.5 − 0.7 = 0.2.

quizzes.q: P(A) = 0.5, P(B given A) = 0.4, P(B given A′) = 0.2. Find P(B).
Same events: find P(A given B) (3 s.f.).
Three fair coins are tossed. Find P(at least one head).
quizzes.e: P(no heads) = (½)³ = 0.125, so P(at least one head) = 1 − 0.125 = 0.875.

quizzes.q: A disease affects 5% of people. A test detects it 98% of the time and gives a false positive 10% of the time. Find P(disease given positive) (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: P(positive) = 0.05 × 0.98 + 0.95 × 0.1 = 0.144. P(disease given positive) = 0.049 ÷ 0.144 = 0.34. Most positives are false because the disease is rare.

quizzes.q: A disease affects 5% of people. A test detects it 90% of the time and gives a false positive 10% of the time. Find P(disease given positive) (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: P(positive) = 0.05 × 0.9 + 0.95 × 0.1 = 0.14. P(disease given positive) = 0.045 ÷ 0.14 = 0.321. Most positives are false because the disease is rare.
For X ~ B(n, p) the mean is E(X) = np = 10 × 0.3 = 3.

quizzes.q: For a normal distribution, about 95% of values lie within
quizzes.e: About 68% lie within 1σ, 95% within 2σ (more precisely ±1.96σ) and 99.7% within 3σ of the mean.
A normal distribution is symmetric about its mean, so exactly half the values lie below 50: P(X < 50) = 0.5.

quizzes.q: Give one condition for a binomial model.
quizzes.e: A binomial model needs a fixed number of trials, independent trials, two outcomes (success or failure) and a constant probability of success.
The total probability is 1, so P(Z > 1) = 1 − P(Z < 1) = 1 − 0.8413 = 0.1587.

quizzes.q: A discrete uniform distribution on {1, …, 6} has P(X = 3) =
quizzes.e: In a discrete uniform distribution every outcome is equally likely: 6 outcomes, so each has probability 1/6.

quizzes.q: The normal distribution is
quizzes.e: The normal distribution is continuous, bell-shaped and symmetric about its mean, so mean = median = mode.

quizzes.q: Points of inflection of a normal curve are at
quizzes.e: The normal curve changes from concave to convex one standard deviation from the mean, at x = μ ± σ.

quizzes.q: When can a normal approximate B(n, p)?
quizzes.e: B(n, p) can be approximated by N(np, np(1 − p)) when n is large and p is close to 0.5, so that the distribution is roughly symmetric.

quizzes.q: Continuity correction: P(X ≤ 20) for binomial becomes
quizzes.e: X ≤ 20 includes the whole bar for 20, which stretches to 20.5, so use P(Y < 20.5) for the normal variable Y.

quizzes.q: Var(X) for X ~ B(n, p) is
quizzes.e: For X ~ B(n, p): E(X) = np and Var(X) = np(1 − p).

quizzes.q: Why might a binomial model not suit "number of rainy days in a week"?
quizzes.e: Binomial needs independent trials with a constant probability. Rain on one day makes rain the next day more likely, and the chance varies with the weather pattern.

quizzes.q: X ~ N(30, 25). Find x such that P(X < x) = 0.975 (3 s.f.).
X ~ N(50, σ²) and P(X > 60) = 0.1587. Find σ.
quizzes.e: P(Z > 1) = 0.1587, so 60 is 1 standard deviation above the mean: (60 − 50)/σ = 1, so σ = 10.

quizzes.q: X ~ N(70, σ²) and P(X > 80) = 0.1587. Find σ.
quizzes.e: P(Z > 1) = 0.1587, so 80 is 1 standard deviation above the mean: (80 − 70)/σ = 1, so σ = 10.

quizzes.q: X ~ B(100, 0.4). Using a normal approximation, find the variance of the approximating normal.
quizzes.e: The approximating normal has σ² = np(1 − p) = 100 × 0.4 × 0.6 = 24.

quizzes.q: X ~ B(50, 0.5). Find the mean of the normal approximation.
One-tailed test of H₀: p = 0.3 for an increase. H₁ is
quizzes.e: Testing for an increase, the alternative hypothesis is H₁: p > 0.3 (one-tailed). H₀ always contains the equals sign.

quizzes.q: What is a critical region?
quizzes.e: The critical region is the set of values of the test statistic that would lead you to reject H₀. Its boundary is the critical value.

quizzes.q: p-value 0.03 at the 5% level. You
quizzes.e: The p-value 0.03 is less than the significance level 0.05, so the result is significant: reject H₀. This never proves either hypothesis.

quizzes.q: A two-tailed test at 10% puts in each tail
quizzes.e: In a two-tailed test the significance level is split equally between the tails: 10% ÷ 2 = 5% in each.

quizzes.q: Testing a correlation coefficient, what is H₀?
quizzes.e: H₀: ρ = 0 (no correlation in the population), against H₁: ρ > 0, ρ < 0 or ρ ≠ 0.

quizzes.q: The null hypothesis is the
quizzes.a: assumption we test against, assumed true
quizzes.e: H₀ is the assumption tested, taken to be true unless there is enough evidence against it. It is written with '='.

quizzes.q: A 5% significance level means
quizzes.a: 5% chance of wrongly rejecting a true H₀
quizzes.e: The significance level is the probability of rejecting H₀ when it is actually true. At 5%, this happens with probability 0.05.

quizzes.q: A test statistic in the critical region leads you to
quizzes.e: A value in the critical region is significant, so reject H₀ in favour of H₁.

quizzes.q: What is the acceptance region?
quizzes.e: The acceptance region is the set of values of the test statistic for which H₀ is not rejected (everything outside the critical region).

quizzes.q: H₁: p ≠ 0.5 is a
quizzes.e: H₁: p ≠ 0.5 looks for a change in either direction, so it is a two-tailed test.

quizzes.q: Conclusions must be written
quizzes.e: Write the conclusion in context and without certainty, e.g. 'There is evidence at the 5% level that the coin is biased.'

quizzes.q: The p-value is
quizzes.a: the probability of a result at least this extreme if H₀ is true
quizzes.e: The p-value is the probability of getting a result at least as extreme as the one observed, assuming H₀ is true. Reject H₀ if it is less than the significance level.

quizzes.q: Why should you not say "H₀ is accepted"?
quizzes.e: Not rejecting H₀ only means there is not enough evidence against it. It does not prove H₀ is true.

quizzes.q: Testing for correlation uses the
quizzes.e: Calculate the product moment correlation coefficient r and compare it with the critical value for the sample size and significance level.

quizzes.q: A one-tailed test for a decrease in p at 5% puts
quizzes.e: Testing for a decrease, H₁: p < p₀, so all 5% goes in the lower tail.

quizzes.q: Testing a normal mean uses the distribution of
quizzes.e: If X ~ N(μ, σ²), the sample mean of n values satisfies x̄ ~ N(μ, σ²/n). Use z = (x̄ − μ)/(σ/√n).

quizzes.q: PMCC critical value 0.5494, sample r = 0.61, one-tailed H₁: ρ > 0. Conclusion?
quizzes.a: Reject H₀: evidence of positive correlation
quizzes.e: r = 0.61 > 0.5494, so it is in the critical region. Reject H₀: there is evidence of positive correlation in the population.

quizzes.q: H₀: p = 0.3, H₁: p < 0.3, n = 10. Observed X = 1. Find the p-value P(X ≤ 1) (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Under H₀, X ~ B(10, 0.3). p-value = P(X ≤ 1) = 0.149. Compare it with the significance level: reject H₀ if it is smaller.

quizzes.q: H₀: p = 0.3, H₁: p < 0.3, n = 17. Observed X = 0. Find the p-value P(X ≤ 0) (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Under H₀, X ~ B(17, 0.3). p-value = P(X ≤ 0) = 0.00233. Compare it with the significance level: reject H₀ if it is smaller.

quizzes.q: H₀: p = 0.3, H₁: p < 0.3, n = 11. Observed X = 0. Find the p-value P(X ≤ 0) (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Under H₀, X ~ B(11, 0.3). p-value = P(X ≤ 0) = 0.0198. Compare it with the significance level: reject H₀ if it is smaller.

quizzes.q: Increasing the sample size in a test generally
quizzes.a: makes it easier to detect a real effect
quizzes.e: A larger n makes σ/√n smaller, so a real difference is more likely to be significant. α is fixed by the test.

quizzes.q: A test of H₀: μ = 50 against H₁: μ > 50 uses n = 25 from N(μ, 10²). Find the z-value for x̄ = 53.5.
For the test above at 5% (critical z = 1.645), find the smallest x̄ that leads to rejecting H₀ (3 s.f.).
H₀: p = 0.5, n = 10, H₁: p > 0.5. Observed X = 9. Find P(X ≥ 9) (4 d.p.).
X ~ B(23, 0.5) under H₀. H₁: p > 0.5 at 5%. Find the smallest c with P(X ≥ c) ≤ 0.05 (critical value).
quizzes.e: P(X ≥ 16) = 1 − P(X ≤ 15) = 0.0466, which is at most 0.05, but P(X ≥ 15) = 0.1050 is greater than 0.05. So c = 16.

quizzes.q: X ~ B(17, 0.3) under H₀. H₁: p > 0.3 at 5%. Find the smallest c with P(X ≥ c) ≤ 0.05 (critical value).
quizzes.e: P(X ≥ 9) = 1 − P(X ≤ 8) = 0.0403, which is at most 0.05, but P(X ≥ 8) = 0.1046 is greater than 0.05. So c = 9.

quizzes.q: For X ~ B(20, 0.4), the critical region is X ≥ 13. Find the actual significance level (4 d.p.).
quizzes.e: Actual significance level = P(X ≥ 13) = 1 − P(X ≤ 12).

quizzes.q: For X ~ B(19, 0.4), the critical region is X ≥ 12. Find the actual significance level (4 d.p.).
quizzes.e: Actual significance level = P(X ≥ 12) = 1 − P(X ≤ 11).

quizzes.q: Sample mean of 36 values from N(μ, 13²) is x̄. Find the standard error of x̄ (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Standard error = σ/√n = 13 ÷ √36 = 13 ÷ 6 = 2.17.

quizzes.q: Sample mean of 16 values from N(μ, 7²) is x̄. Find the standard error of x̄ (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Standard error = σ/√n = 7 ÷ √16 = 7 ÷ 4 = 1.75.

quizzes.q: The newton in SI base units is
quizzes.e: F = ma, so 1 N = 1 kg × 1 m s⁻² = 1 kg m s⁻².

quizzes.q: Convert 72 km/h to m/s.
quizzes.e: 72 km/h = 72 000 m ÷ 3600 s = 20 m/s. A shortcut is to divide by 3.6.

quizzes.q: A 'light' string in a model means
quizzes.e: 'Light' means the mass is negligible, so the tension is the same throughout the string. 'Inextensible' means it cannot stretch.

quizzes.q: What does modelling an object as a particle mean?
quizzes.e: As a particle, the object's size is negligible: its mass acts at a single point, so rotation and air resistance from its shape are ignored.

quizzes.q: Weight of a 5 kg mass (g = 9.8).
Which is a vector quantity?
quizzes.e: A vector has magnitude and direction. Velocity is a vector; speed, mass and time are scalars.

quizzes.q: The unit of acceleration is
quizzes.e: Acceleration is the change of velocity per second: (m s⁻¹) ÷ s = m s⁻².

quizzes.q: What is the difference between mass and weight?
quizzes.e: Mass is the amount of matter in kg and does not change. Weight is the gravitational force on it, W = mg, in newtons.

quizzes.q: Convert 126 km/h to m/s.
1 N is the force giving
quizzes.a: 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m s⁻²
w: 1 g an acceleration of 1 m s⁻²
1 kg a speed of 1 m s⁻¹
quizzes.e: From F = ma: 1 N gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m s⁻².

quizzes.q: An 'inextensible' string means
quizzes.a: it does not stretch, so connected particles share acceleration
quizzes.e: An inextensible string does not stretch, so particles connected by it move with the same speed and acceleration.

quizzes.q: A 'smooth' surface means
quizzes.e: 'Smooth' means friction is negligible and is ignored in the model.

quizzes.q: A 'rigid' body means
quizzes.e: A rigid body does not bend or change shape under forces, as with rods and beams.

quizzes.q: A 'uniform' rod means
quizzes.a: its mass is evenly distributed (weight at its midpoint)
quizzes.e: Uniform means the mass is evenly spread, so the centre of mass (and the weight) is at the midpoint.

quizzes.q: Convert 0.25 km to cm.

Find the weight of 300 g on the Moon (g = 1.6).
Convert a density of 2.7 g/cm³ to kg/m³.
quizzes.e: 1 g/cm³ = 0.001 kg ÷ 10⁻⁶ m³ = 1000 kg/m³, so 2.7 g/cm³ = 2700 kg/m³.

quizzes.q: Convert 500 cm² to m².
Modelling a ball as a particle ignores
quizzes.a: air resistance effects of size and spin
quizzes.e: As a particle the ball has no size, so effects that depend on its size and spin, such as air resistance, are ignored.

quizzes.q: Give one limitation of taking g = 9.8 m s⁻².
quizzes.e: g varies slightly with location (latitude) and height above sea level, so 9.8 m s⁻² is an approximation.

A model treats a lift as a particle. A refinement would be
quizzes.a: including air resistance or the lift's dimensions
quizzes.e: A refinement makes the model more realistic, e.g. including air resistance or the lift's dimensions.

quizzes.q: A cyclist travels 4.5 km in 15 minutes. Find the average speed in m/s.
quizzes.e: 4.5 km = 4500 m and 15 minutes = 900 s. Average speed = 4500 ÷ 900 = 5 m/s.

quizzes.q: A car travels at a constant 72 km/h. How far does it go in 45 s?

The area under a velocity–time graph is

quizzes.e: With no air resistance, no horizontal force acts, so the horizontal acceleration is zero and the horizontal velocity is constant. Only gravity acts, vertically.

quizzes.e: Vertical component = U sin θ = 20 sin 30° = 20 × 0.5 = 10 m/s.

quizzes.q: The gradient of a velocity–time graph is
quizzes.e: Gradient = change in velocity ÷ time = acceleration (dv/dt).

quizzes.q: u = 9 m/s, a = 5 m s⁻², t = 8 s. Find the displacement.

quizzes.e: The SUVAT equations are derived assuming constant acceleration. For variable acceleration use calculus.

quizzes.q: For variable acceleration a(t), velocity is found by
quizzes.a: integrating a with respect to t
quizzes.e: v = ∫ a dt, with the constant found from the initial velocity. Integrating v gives displacement.

quizzes.q: What is the vertical velocity of a projectile at its highest point?
quizzes.e: At the highest point the projectile stops rising and starts falling, so its vertical velocity is zero. It still moves horizontally.

quizzes.q: Displacement differs from distance because displacement
quizzes.e: Displacement is a vector: the straight-line distance in a stated direction from the start. Distance is a scalar.

quizzes.q: A train accelerates from rest at 0.5 m s⁻² for 40 s. Find the distance.
