A stone is thrown down at 11 m/s from a height of 16 m. Find its speed on hitting the ground (g = 9.8, 3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Taking down as positive: v² = u² + 2as = 11² + 2 × 9.8 × 16 = 434.6, so v = 20.8 m/s.

quizzes.q: A stone is thrown down at 14 m/s from a height of 32 m. Find its speed on hitting the ground (g = 9.8, 3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Taking down as positive: v² = u² + 2as = 14² + 2 × 9.8 × 32 = 823.2, so v = 28.7 m/s.

quizzes.q: A stone is thrown down at 10 m/s from a height of 8 m. Find its speed on hitting the ground (g = 9.8, 3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Taking down as positive: v² = u² + 2as = 10² + 2 × 9.8 × 8 = 256.8, so v = 16 m/s.

quizzes.q: v = 2t² + 2t m/s. Find the displacement from t = 0 to t = 3.
v = 3t² + 2t m/s. Find the displacement from t = 0 to t = 3.
quizzes.e: s = ∫₀³ (3t² + 2t) dt = [1t³ + t²]₀³ = 27 + 9 = 36 m.

quizzes.q: A projectile's path (no air resistance) is a
quizzes.e: x = (U cos θ)t and y = (U sin θ)t − ½gt². Eliminating t gives y as a quadratic in x: a parabola.

quizzes.q: Two balls thrown horizontally and dropped from the same height land
quizzes.e: Both start with zero vertical velocity and have the same vertical acceleration g, so they land at the same time. Horizontal motion does not affect vertical motion.

quizzes.q: To find the time of flight of a projectile, which direction's motion do you use?
quizzes.e: Use the vertical motion: for level ground, set the vertical displacement s = 0 and solve for t.

quizzes.q: A car decelerates uniformly from 25 m/s to rest in 50 m. Find the time taken.
Particle: s = t³ − 6t² + 9t. Find the time (other than t = 1) when it is momentarily at rest.
quizzes.e: v = ds/dt = 3t² − 12t + 9 = 3(t − 1)(t − 3). v = 0 at t = 1 and t = 3, so the other time is t = 3 s.

quizzes.q: For s = t³ − 6t² + 9t, find the total distance travelled from t = 0 to t = 3.
quizzes.e: s(0) = 0, s(1) = 1 − 6 + 9 = 4, s(3) = 27 − 54 + 27 = 0. It moves 4 m forward then 4 m back: total 8 m.

quizzes.q: A projectile is launched at 17 m/s at 60° above horizontal level ground. Find its range (g = 9.8, 3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Vertical: 0 = (17 sin 60°)t − 4.9t², so t = 3 s. Horizontal: range = 17 cos 60° × 3 = 25.5 m.

quizzes.q: A projectile is launched at 28 m/s at 45° above horizontal level ground. Find its range (g = 9.8, 3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Vertical: 0 = (28 sin 45°)t − 4.9t², so t = 4.04 s. Horizontal: range = 28 cos 45° × 4.04 = 80 m.

quizzes.q: A projectile is launched at 29 m/s at 60° above horizontal level ground. Find its range (g = 9.8, 3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Vertical: 0 = (29 sin 60°)t − 4.9t², so t = 5.13 s. Horizontal: range = 29 cos 60° × 5.13 = 74.3 m.

quizzes.q: Launched at 15 m/s at 45°. Find its maximum height (g = 9.8, 3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: At the top the vertical velocity is 0: 0 = (15 sin 45°)² − 2 × 9.8 × h, so h = 112.5 ÷ 19.6 = 5.74 m.

quizzes.q: Launched at 25 m/s at 30°. Find its maximum height (g = 9.8, 3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: At the top the vertical velocity is 0: 0 = (25 sin 30°)² − 2 × 9.8 × h, so h = 156.2 ÷ 19.6 = 7.97 m.

quizzes.q: A resultant force of 12 N acts on 3 kg. Find the acceleration.
quizzes.e: F = ma, so a = F/m = 12/3 = 4 m s⁻².

quizzes.q: 2 kg block, rough horizontal surface, μ = 0.4. Limiting friction (g = 9.8)?
quizzes.e: On a horizontal surface R = mg = 2 × 9.8 = 19.6 N. Limiting friction F = μR = 0.4 × 19.6 = 7.84 N.

quizzes.q: A particle in equilibrium has
quizzes.e: Equilibrium means zero resultant force, so the particle is at rest or moving at constant velocity. Forces can still act.

quizzes.q: 3 kg and 1 kg hang over a smooth pulley. Find the acceleration (g = 9.8).
quizzes.e: Treat the system as one: resultant force = (3 − 1)g = 19.6 N acting on 4 kg, so a = 19.6/4 = 4.9 m s⁻².

quizzes.q: State Newton's third law.
quizzes.e: If body A exerts a force on body B, then B exerts a force on A that is equal in size, opposite in direction and of the same type.

quizzes.q: Component of weight down a slope at angle θ
quizzes.e: Resolve the weight parallel to the slope: mg sin θ down the slope; mg cos θ is the component perpendicular to it.

quizzes.q: Newton's first law says an object with no resultant force
quizzes.a: stays at rest or moves at constant velocity
quizzes.e: With no resultant force an object stays at rest or keeps moving at constant velocity.

quizzes.q: The normal reaction on a block on a horizontal floor (no other vertical forces) equals
quizzes.e: Vertically the block is in equilibrium, so R − mg = 0 and R = mg (its weight).

quizzes.q: A 3 kg block on a smooth slope at 40°. Find its acceleration (g = 9.8, 3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: The only force along the smooth slope is mg sin θ, so a = g sin θ = 9.8 × sin 40° = 6.3 m s⁻² (the mass cancels).

quizzes.q: A 3 kg block on a smooth slope at 20°. Find its acceleration (g = 9.8, 3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: The only force along the smooth slope is mg sin θ, so a = g sin θ = 9.8 × sin 20° = 3.35 m s⁻² (the mass cancels).

quizzes.q: Friction on a block at rest (not limiting) is
quizzes.a: at most μR, just enough to prevent motion
quizzes.e: Friction only grows as large as needed to prevent motion, up to the maximum μR, so F ≤ μR.

quizzes.q: On a smooth pulley, the tension in the string is
quizzes.e: A light string over a smooth pulley has the same tension on both sides.

quizzes.q: What does 'limiting equilibrium' mean?
quizzes.e: In limiting equilibrium the object is on the point of moving, so friction has its maximum value F = μR.

quizzes.q: The force exerted on a pulley by the string is
quizzes.a: the resultant of the tensions on both sides
quizzes.e: The string pulls the pulley along both sections, so the force on the pulley is the vector sum of the two tensions.

quizzes.q: A lift accelerating upwards makes the reaction on a passenger
quizzes.e: R − mg = ma with a upwards, so R = m(g + a), which is greater than mg.

quizzes.q: Resolving forces means
quizzes.e: Resolving splits each force into perpendicular components (usually horizontal and vertical, or along and perpendicular to a slope).

quizzes.q: A 3 kg mass hangs from a string in a lift accelerating down at 2 m s⁻². Find the tension (g = 9.8).
quizzes.e: Taking down as positive: mg − T = ma, so T = m(g − a) = 3 × (9.8 − 2) = 23.4 N.

quizzes.q: A 6 kg box is pulled horizontally by 51 N on a rough floor, μ = 0.1. Find its acceleration (g = 9.8, 3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: R = mg = 58.8 N, so friction = 0.1 × 58.8 = 5.88 N. F − friction = ma: a = (51 − 5.88) ÷ 6 = 7.52 m s⁻².

quizzes.q: A 8 kg box is pulled horizontally by 56 N on a rough floor, μ = 0.1. Find its acceleration (g = 9.8, 3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: R = mg = 78.4 N, so friction = 0.1 × 78.4 = 7.84 N. F − friction = ma: a = (56 − 7.84) ÷ 8 = 6.02 m s⁻².

quizzes.q: A 2 kg box is pulled horizontally by 42 N on a rough floor, μ = 0.3. Find its acceleration (g = 9.8, 3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: R = mg = 19.6 N, so friction = 0.3 × 19.6 = 5.88 N. F − friction = ma: a = (42 − 5.88) ÷ 2 = 18.1 m s⁻².

quizzes.q: A block on a rough slope at angle θ is about to slide. Then μ =
quizzes.e: Limiting: friction μR = mg sin θ with R = mg cos θ, so μmg cos θ = mg sin θ and μ = tan θ.

quizzes.q: In a connected-particle problem, why do both particles have the same acceleration?
quizzes.e: The string is taut and inextensible, so the particles move together with the same acceleration.

quizzes.q: A towbar between a car and trailer is modelled as
quizzes.a: a light rigid rod (tension or thrust)
quizzes.e: A towbar is a light rigid rod: unlike a string it can push (thrust) as well as pull (tension).

quizzes.q: Forces (3i + 4j) N and (5i − 2j) N act on a 2 kg particle. Find the magnitude of its acceleration (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Resultant = 8i + 2j N, so a = (4i + j) m s⁻². Magnitude = √(4² + 1²) = √17 = 4.12 m s⁻².

quizzes.q: A 5 kg block is at rest on a rough horizontal floor. A 20 N force at 30° above horizontal just moves it. Find μ (3 s.f., g = 9.8).
quizzes.e: Vertically: R = 49 − 20 sin 30° = 39 N. Horizontally (limiting): 20 cos 30° = 17.32 = μ × 39, so μ = 0.444.

quizzes.q: A car of mass 1000 kg tows a 500 kg trailer with resistances 200 N and 100 N. Driving force 1800 N. Find the tension in the towbar.
quizzes.e: Whole system: 1800 − 300 = 1500a, so a = 1 m s⁻². Trailer: T − 100 = 500 × 1, so T = 600 N.

quizzes.q: A has mass 3 kg, B has mass 2 kg and the table is smooth (F = 0). Find the acceleration (g = 9.8).
quizzes.e: Only B's weight drives the system: 2 × 9.8 = 19.6 N on a total mass of 5 kg, so a = 19.6 ÷ 5 = 3.92 m s⁻².

quizzes.q: A 4 kg block on a rough table (μ = 0.3) is joined by a light string over a smooth pulley to a hanging 3 kg mass. Find the acceleration (g = 9.8, 3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Hanging mass: 3g − T = 3a. Block: T − 0.3 × 4g = 4a. Add: 29.4 − 11.76 = 7a, so a = 2.52 m s⁻².

quizzes.q: A 6 kg block on a rough table (μ = 0.2) is joined by a light string over a smooth pulley to a hanging 4 kg mass. Find the acceleration (g = 9.8, 3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Hanging mass: 4g − T = 4a. Block: T − 0.2 × 6g = 6a. Add: 39.2 − 11.76 = 10a, so a = 2.74 m s⁻².

quizzes.q: A 6 kg block on a rough table (μ = 0.2) is joined by a light string over a smooth pulley to a hanging 5 kg mass. Find the acceleration (g = 9.8, 3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Hanging mass: 5g − T = 5a. Block: T − 0.2 × 6g = 6a. Add: 49 − 11.76 = 11a, so a = 3.39 m s⁻².

quizzes.q: A 5 kg block slides down a rough 25° slope, μ = 0.2. Find its acceleration (g = 9.8, 3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: R = mg cos θ, so friction = μmg cos θ. mg sin θ − μmg cos θ = ma, so a = 9.8(sin 25° − 0.2 cos 25°) = 2.37 m s⁻².

quizzes.q: A 6 kg block slides down a rough 30° slope, μ = 0.3. Find its acceleration (g = 9.8, 3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: R = mg cos θ, so friction = μmg cos θ. mg sin θ − μmg cos θ = ma, so a = 9.8(sin 30° − 0.3 cos 30°) = 2.35 m s⁻².

quizzes.q: A 4 N force acts perpendicular, 0.5 m from a pivot. Moment?
quizzes.e: Moment = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot = 4 × 0.5 = 2 N m.

quizzes.q: A rigid body in equilibrium has
quizzes.a: zero resultant force and zero resultant moment
quizzes.e: A rigid body is in equilibrium only if the resultant force is zero and the resultant moment about any point is zero.

quizzes.q: A uniform 2 m rod of weight 30 N rests on supports at its ends. Reaction at each end?
quizzes.e: The rod is uniform, so its weight acts at the midpoint, equidistant from both supports. By symmetry each reaction is 30 ÷ 2 = 15 N.

quizzes.q: Where does the weight of a uniform rod act?
quizzes.e: For a uniform rod the centre of mass is at its midpoint, so the weight acts there.

quizzes.q: Plank pivoted at centre. A 50 N child sits 1.2 m left. How far right must a 60 N child sit?
quizzes.e: Moments about the pivot: 50 × 1.2 = 60 × d, so d = 60/60 = 1.0 m.

quizzes.q: The unit of a moment is
quizzes.e: Moment = force × perpendicular distance, so the unit is the newton metre (N m).

quizzes.q: The moment of a force about a point is
quizzes.e: Moment = force × perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force.

quizzes.q: A rod resting on two supports is about to tip about one support. What is the reaction at the other support?
quizzes.e: When the rod is about to tip about one support, it is just losing contact with the other, so that reaction is zero.

quizzes.q: A uniform rod of length 4 m has its centre of mass at
quizzes.e: A uniform rod's centre of mass is at its midpoint: 2 m from either end.

quizzes.q: Taking moments about a point where an unknown force acts
quizzes.a: eliminates that force from the equation
quizzes.e: That force has zero distance from the point, so its moment is zero and it does not appear in the equation.

quizzes.q: A see-saw balances with 300 N at 2 m one side. A 400 N child sits on the other side at
quizzes.e: Moments about the pivot: 300 × 2 = 400 × d, so d = 600 ÷ 400 = 1.5 m.

quizzes.q: For a ladder against a smooth wall, the wall's reaction is
quizzes.e: A smooth wall has no friction, so its reaction is perpendicular to the wall, i.e. horizontal.

quizzes.q: A non-uniform rod's weight acts at
quizzes.a: its centre of mass, not necessarily the middle
quizzes.e: The weight acts at the centre of mass, which is not necessarily the midpoint for a non-uniform rod. Find it using moments.

quizzes.q: What two equations do you use for a body in equilibrium under several forces?
quizzes.e: Resolve forces (resultant zero in two perpendicular directions) and take moments about a point (resultant moment zero).

quizzes.q: Clockwise moment 24 N m, anticlockwise 18 N m. The resultant moment is
quizzes.e: Resultant moment = 24 − 18 = 6 N m in the direction of the larger moment, clockwise.

quizzes.q: Moving a load further from the pivot
quizzes.e: Moment = force × distance, so a greater distance gives a greater moment.

quizzes.q: A rod on two supports: as a load moves toward support A, the reaction at A
quizzes.e: Taking moments about B, the load's moment about B grows as it moves away from B towards A, so the reaction at A increases.

quizzes.q: A uniform 5 m beam of weight 111 N rests on supports at each end. A 83 N load is 3 m from the left end. Find the reaction at the right support (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Moments about the left end: R × 5 = 111 × 2.5 + 83 × 3 = 526.5, so R = 105 N.

quizzes.q: A uniform 7 m beam of weight 107 N rests on supports at each end. A 72 N load is 6 m from the left end. Find the reaction at the right support (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Moments about the left end: R × 7 = 107 × 3.5 + 72 × 6 = 806.5, so R = 115 N.

quizzes.q: A uniform 6 m beam of weight 193 N rests on supports at each end. A 55 N load is 5 m from the left end. Find the reaction at the right support (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Moments about the left end: R × 6 = 193 × 3 + 55 × 5 = 854, so R = 142 N.

quizzes.q: A non-uniform 6 m rod balances on a pivot 2 m from end A. Its centre of mass is
quizzes.e: A rod balances on a single pivot only if its weight acts through the pivot, so the centre of mass is 2 m from A.

quizzes.q: Why is a ladder more likely to slip as a person climbs higher?
quizzes.e: The higher the person, the larger their moment about the base. The wall must push harder to balance it, so more friction is needed at the floor.

quizzes.q: A uniform 5 m plank of weight 200 N rests on supports 1 m from each end. How far beyond a support can a 400 N man walk before it tips?
quizzes.e: The weight acts at the centre, 1.5 m from each support. On the point of tipping about a support, the other reaction is 0: 400d = 200 × 1.5, so d = 0.75 m.

quizzes.q: A non-uniform 4 m rod of weight 60 N is supported at its ends; reactions are 20 N and 40 N. How far is the centre of mass from the 20 N end?
quizzes.e: Moments about the 20 N end: 60x = 40 × 4 = 160, so x = 160 ÷ 60 = 2.67 m.

quizzes.q: A uniform 3 m rod of weight 50 N is hinged to a wall and held horizontal by a string at its free end making 30° with the rod. Find the tension.
quizzes.e: Moments about the hinge: the vertical component of tension T sin 30° acts 3 m away and the weight 1.5 m away. 3T sin 30° = 50 × 1.5, so 1.5T = 75 and T = 50 N.

quizzes.q: A uniform 5 m ladder of weight 86 N rests against a smooth wall at 60° to rough ground and is about to slip. Find the friction at the ground (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Moments about the base: F = S, S × L sin 60° = W × (L/2) cos 60°.

quizzes.q: A uniform 4 m ladder of weight 177 N rests against a smooth wall at 60° to rough ground and is about to slip. Find the friction at the ground (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Moments about the base: F = S, S × L sin 60° = W × (L/2) cos 60°.

quizzes.q: A uniform 8 m ladder of weight 162 N rests against a smooth wall at 60° to rough ground and is about to slip. Find the friction at the ground (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Moments about the base: F = S, S × L sin 60° = W × (L/2) cos 60°.

quizzes.q: A uniform 5 m rod of weight 60 N is held horizontal by a vertical string at one end and a pivot at the other. Find the tension (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Moments about the pivot: T × 5 = 60 × 2.5 (weight at the midpoint), so T = 60 ÷ 2 = 30 N.

quizzes.q: A uniform 5 m rod of weight 78 N is held horizontal by a vertical string at one end and a pivot at the other. Find the tension (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Moments about the pivot: T × 5 = 78 × 2.5 (weight at the midpoint), so T = 78 ÷ 2 = 39 N.

sections.name: Module 1: Development of practical skills in physics

quizzes.q: Which instrument has a resolution of 0.01 mm?
quizzes.e: A micrometer screw gauge reads to 0.01 mm; a vernier caliper reads to 0.1 mm (or 0.02 mm) and a metre rule to 1 mm.

quizzes.q: What is a systematic error?
quizzes.e: An error that shifts every reading by the same amount, e.g. a zero error.

quizzes.q: Repeating readings and averaging reduces
quizzes.e: Random errors scatter readings both above and below the true value, so averaging repeats reduces their effect. Systematic errors shift every reading the same way, so averaging does not remove them.

quizzes.q: What does it mean for measurements to be precise?
quizzes.e: Precise measurements are close to each other (a small spread), whether or not they are close to the true value.

quizzes.q: Order the steps to find g with a falling ball and two light gates
items: Measure the distance between the gates
Release the ball from rest above the gates
Record the speed at each gate
Use v² = u² + 2as to find g
quizzes.e: Measure the separation s, release the ball from rest so it falls through both gates, and record its speeds u and v. Then g = (v² − u²) ÷ 2s. Repeat and average.

quizzes.q: Parallax error is reduced by
quizzes.a: reading the scale at eye level, perpendicular to it
quizzes.e: Parallax error happens when the eye is not level with the reading. Reading the scale at eye level, with the line of sight perpendicular to the scale, removes it.

quizzes.q: Which is a control variable when finding the resistivity of a wire?
quizzes.e: Resistivity changes with temperature, so the temperature of the wire must be kept constant. Length is the independent variable and resistance is measured.

quizzes.q: Which is the correct way to use a micrometer to measure the diameter of a wire?
quizzes.a: check the zero error, close the jaws gently using the ratchet, and take readings at several points along the wire
w: squeeze the jaws as tight as possible
take one reading only at the end of the wire
use the metre rule scale on the side
quizzes.e: Using apparatus correctly means checking for zero error, not crushing the sample, and repeating readings at different positions and orientations.

quizzes.q: Which table heading presents data in the appropriate format?
quizzes.e: The convention is quantity / unit, and all values in the column are then pure numbers given to the same number of decimal places.

quizzes.q: A voltage is calculated from V = IR using I = 0.25 A (2 s.f.) and R = 4.70 Ω (3 s.f.). The appropriate number of significant figures for the answer is
quizzes.e: Give the answer to the same number of significant figures as the least precise data: 1.2 V (2 s.f.).

quizzes.q: When selecting the axes for a graph to test whether y is proportional to x,
quizzes.a: plot y on the vertical axis and x on the horizontal axis, with appropriate scales, quantities and units, and check for a straight line through the origin
w: plot x and y on the same axis
label the axes with units only
use a logarithmic scale on one axis only
quizzes.e: Selection and labelling of axes means choosing which variable goes on each axis and giving each a scale, quantity and unit.

quizzes.q: One reading in a set of repeats is far from the others. This reading is
quizzes.a: an anomaly, which should be checked, repeated and left out of the mean
w: a systematic error that affects every reading
quizzes.e: Identification of anomalies is part of analysing experimental measurements; an anomalous result is usually caused by a mistake in that single reading.

quizzes.q: Which is a correct investigative approach to practical work?
quizzes.a: change one independent variable, measure the dependent variable, and control all other variables
w: change several variables at once to save time
only record results that fit your prediction
measure the dependent variable once only
quizzes.e: Scientific method: test a hypothesis by changing one variable at a time and controlling the rest.

quizzes.q: Before using a radioactive source or a high-voltage supply, you should
quizzes.a: follow the written instructions and the risk assessment so that you use the equipment and materials safely and correctly
w: start straight away and read the instructions afterwards
remove any safety guards to see better
only follow instructions you agree with
quizzes.e: Practical endorsement skills include following written instructions and using equipment safely.

quizzes.q: Which is the best way to keep appropriate records of experimental activities?
quizzes.a: record raw readings, units, date and any changes to the method straight into a lab book
w: write results on scrap paper and copy the good ones later
record readings from memory at the end
quizzes.e: Records must be complete and made at the time, so the experiment could be repeated and checked.

quizzes.q: When using ionising radiation from a radioactive source with a Geiger–Müller tube detector, the first measurement should be
quizzes.a: the background count rate with no source present
w: the count rate with the source touching the tube
the count rate with lead in the way
quizzes.e: The background count must be subtracted from every reading. Sources are handled with tongs and kept away from the body.

quizzes.q: Repeat readings: 2.57, 2.57, 2.03, 2.05 s. Find the mean (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Mean = (2.57 + 2.57 + 2.03 + 2.05) ÷ 4 = 2.3 s. Include every reading unless one is clearly anomalous.

quizzes.q: Repeat readings: 2.5, 2.44, 2.4, 2.18 s. Find the mean (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Mean = (2.5 + 2.44 + 2.4 + 2.18) ÷ 4 = 2.38 s. Include every reading unless one is clearly anomalous.

quizzes.q: Repeat readings: 2.36, 2.36, 2.35, 2.1 s. Find the mean (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Mean = (2.36 + 2.36 + 2.35 + 2.1) ÷ 4 = 2.29 s. Include every reading unless one is clearly anomalous.

quizzes.q: A best-fit line passes through (2, 8) and (10, 17). Find its gradient (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Gradient = Δy ÷ Δx = (17 − 8) ÷ (10 − 2) = 1.12. Use points far apart on the line, not data points off it.

quizzes.q: A best-fit line passes through (3, 4) and (7, 19). Find its gradient (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Gradient = Δy ÷ Δx = (19 − 4) ÷ (7 − 3) = 3.75. Use points far apart on the line, not data points off it.

quizzes.q: A best-fit line passes through (1, 4) and (8, 17). Find its gradient (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Gradient = Δy ÷ Δx = (17 − 4) ÷ (8 − 1) = 1.86. Use points far apart on the line, not data points off it.

quizzes.q: A zero error is an example of a
quizzes.e: A zero error shifts every reading by the same amount in the same direction, so it is a systematic error; averaging does not remove it.

quizzes.q: The independent variable is the one you
quizzes.e: The independent variable is the one you change deliberately; the dependent variable is measured, and it is usually plotted on the y-axis against the independent variable on the x-axis.

quizzes.q: Why should you measure the time for 10 oscillations rather than 1?
quizzes.e: Your reaction time adds the same absolute uncertainty to each timing. Over 10 oscillations this is a much smaller fraction of the total time, so the percentage uncertainty in the period is 10 times smaller.

quizzes.q: A reading is 2.35 V on a voltmeter with resolution 0.01 V. Its uncertainty is usually taken as
quizzes.e: For a digital meter, the uncertainty is usually taken as ± the resolution, the smallest change the instrument can show (here 0.01 V).

quizzes.q: An anomalous result should be
quizzes.a: identified, then repeated or excluded from the mean
quizzes.e: Check an anomalous reading for a mistake. Repeat it if you can; otherwise leave it out of the mean and the line of best fit, and say why.

quizzes.q: A graph of T² against L for a pendulum is
quizzes.a: a straight line through the origin
quizzes.e: From T = 2π√(L/g), T² = (4π²/g)L. This has the form y = mx, so T² against L is a straight line through the origin.

quizzes.q: You must design an experiment to find how the period of a pendulum depends on its length. Which experimental design is best?
quizzes.a: vary the length over a wide range, time 10 swings for each length and repeat, keeping the mass and amplitude fixed
w: time one swing for a single length
change the length and the mass at the same time
use only two lengths so the graph is quick to draw
quizzes.e: A good design changes only the independent variable, uses a wide range with several values, controls other variables and reduces timing uncertainty by timing many swings.

quizzes.q: A student plans to measure g by timing a dropped ball with a hand-held stopwatch over 0.5 m. Evaluate whether this method is appropriate to meet the expected outcome of an accurate value of g.
quizzes.e: The fall takes only about 0.3 s, so the human reaction time (about 0.2 s) gives a huge percentage uncertainty. The method is not appropriate; light gates or a longer drop would be needed.

quizzes.q: After plotting results, how should you process and interpret the data to reach a valid conclusion?
quizzes.e: Describe the trend or relationship shown by the graph (using the gradient or intercept if needed), and check that the data support it within the uncertainties and that other variables were controlled, so the conclusion is valid.

quizzes.q: A student measures five times for a trolley: 1.23 s, 1.25 s, 1.22 s, 1.24 s and 1.26 s. Find the mean time in seconds (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Add the readings and divide by 5: 6.20 ÷ 5 = 1.24 s. Analysis of quantitative data uses simple mathematical skills such as means, ranges and gradients.

quizzes.q: When plotting a graph from experimental results, you should
quizzes.a: choose scales so the points cover more than half the grid, label each axis with quantity and unit, and draw a line of best fit
w: join each point to the next with straight lines
start both axes at zero even if all points are bunched in a corner
use scales such as 3 squares per unit
quizzes.e: Suitable graphs use a sensible scale (1, 2 or 5 per division), labelled axes with units and a best-fit line or curve so the gradient and intercept can be interpreted.

quizzes.q: How should you evaluate the results of an experiment before drawing conclusions?
quizzes.e: Compare the result with an accepted value (percentage difference), consider the uncertainties and the spread of repeats, and look for anomalies before deciding whether the conclusion is justified.

quizzes.q: Suggest one way to refine the experimental design when timing a falling object with a stopwatch.
quizzes.e: Use light gates connected to a data logger (or video analysis) instead of a hand-held stopwatch, removing reaction time; or increase the drop height. Refining a design means suggesting improvements to the procedure and apparatus.

quizzes.q: A student uses a spreadsheet to process data and an online journal for research. Correct practice is to
quizzes.a: use the software to calculate and plot data, report findings clearly, and cite each source of information used
w: copy text from websites without a reference
present data without units if a computer plotted it
quizzes.e: Research skills use online and offline sources (websites, textbooks, printed scientific sources); every source must be correctly cited in a reference list.

quizzes.q: To check a circuit built from a circuit diagram using a DC power supply, cells and components, you should
quizzes.a: check each component matches the diagram, the ammeter is in series, the voltmeter in parallel and the polarity of the meters and diode is correct
w: connect the voltmeter in series with the component
set the supply to its maximum before switching on
quizzes.e: Correctly constructing and checking circuits includes the right placement and polarity of meters and components before switching on.

quizzes.q: To measure the speed of sound, a signal generator drives a loudspeaker and a microphone is moved away until the oscilloscope traces are back in phase. The distance moved between consecutive in-phase positions is
quizzes.e: Generating and measuring waves with a microphone and loudspeaker: then v = fλ with f from the signal generator.

quizzes.q: Which practical technique uses a laser to investigate interference and diffraction of light?
quizzes.a: shining a laser through a double slit or diffraction grating onto a screen and measuring the fringe spacing
w: shining a laser through a convex lens to measure focal length
reflecting a laser off a mirror
using a laser to heat a metal block
quizzes.e: A laser gives coherent monochromatic light, so fringes are bright and well defined; λ = ax/D or d sin θ = nλ.

quizzes.q: Readings 2.26, 2.24, 2.43, 2.6 s. Find the absolute uncertainty as half the range.
quizzes.e: Range = 2.6 − 2.24 = 0.36 s. Uncertainty = half the range = 0.18 s.

quizzes.q: Readings 2.57, 2.33, 2.27, 2.16 s. Find the absolute uncertainty as half the range.
quizzes.e: Range = 2.57 − 2.16 = 0.41 s. Uncertainty = half the range = 0.205 s.

quizzes.q: Readings 2.02, 2.02, 2.28, 2.19 s. Find the absolute uncertainty as half the range.
quizzes.e: Range = 2.28 − 2.02 = 0.26 s. Uncertainty = half the range = 0.13 s.

quizzes.q: A micrometer reads 0.59 mm ± 0.01 mm. Find the percentage uncertainty in the cross-sectional area (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: % uncertainty in d = 0.01 ÷ 0.59 × 100 = 1.69%. A = πd²/4 ∝ d², so double it: 3.39%.

quizzes.q: A micrometer reads 0.58 mm ± 0.01 mm. Find the percentage uncertainty in the cross-sectional area (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: % uncertainty in d = 0.01 ÷ 0.58 × 100 = 1.72%. A = πd²/4 ∝ d², so double it: 3.45%.

quizzes.q: A micrometer reads 0.26 mm ± 0.01 mm. Find the percentage uncertainty in the cross-sectional area (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: % uncertainty in d = 0.01 ÷ 0.26 × 100 = 3.85%. A = πd²/4 ∝ d², so double it: 7.69%.

quizzes.q: To find g from a T² against L graph, use
quizzes.e: The gradient of T² against L is 4π²/g, so g = 4π² ÷ gradient.

quizzes.q: Why plot ln y against x for y = Ae^(kx)?
quizzes.e: Taking logs: ln y = ln A + kx, which has the form y = c + mx. A graph of ln y against x is a straight line with gradient k and intercept ln A.

quizzes.q: Which reduces random error in timing a falling ball?
quizzes.a: using light gates connected to a data logger
w: using a ruler with finer markings
quizzes.e: Light gates connected to a data logger start and stop the timing automatically, removing the human reaction time and its random variation.

quizzes.q: How would you check a micrometer for zero error?
quizzes.e: Close the jaws fully (using the ratchet) and check that the reading is zero. Any reading is the zero error, which is subtracted from later readings.

quizzes.q: For P = I²R, I has 2% uncertainty and R 1%. Percentage uncertainty in P is
quizzes.e: P = I²R, so % uncertainty in P = 2 × % in I + % in R = 2 × 2% + 1% = 5%.

quizzes.q: Data-logging is preferred when
quizzes.a: readings change quickly or over a long time
quizzes.e: A data logger can take many readings per second, or readings over a long time, without human error. It is best when values change quickly or slowly over a long period.

quizzes.q: Best-fit gradient 2.41, worst-fit gradient 2.6. Find the percentage uncertainty in the gradient (3 s.f.).
Best-fit gradient 5.0, worst-fit gradient 5.47. Find the percentage uncertainty in the gradient (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: % uncertainty = (worst − best) ÷ best × 100 = (5.47 − 5.0) ÷ 5.0 × 100 = 9.4%.

quizzes.q: Best-fit gradient 2.55, worst-fit gradient 2.83. Find the percentage uncertainty in the gradient (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: % uncertainty = (worst − best) ÷ best × 100 = (2.83 − 2.55) ÷ 2.55 × 100 = 11%.

The SI base unit of current is the
quizzes.e: The seven SI base quantities include current, with base unit the ampere (A). The coulomb, volt and ohm are derived units.

quizzes.q: The joule in SI base units is
quizzes.e: J = N m, and N = kg m s⁻², so J = kg m s⁻² × m = kg m² s⁻².

quizzes.q: Convert 2.5 kWh to joules (give the number × 10⁶ J).
Match each quantity to its SI unit
quizzes.e: Charge is in coulombs (C), energy in joules (J), power in watts (W = J s⁻¹) and resistance in ohms (Ω = V A⁻¹).

quizzes.q: The prefix 'pico' means
quizzes.e: pico (p) = 10⁻¹², nano = 10⁻⁹, femto = 10⁻¹⁵, micro = 10⁻⁶.

quizzes.q: Which is NOT an SI base unit?
quizzes.e: The newton is a derived unit (1 N = 1 kg m s⁻²). The kelvin, mole and second are SI base units.

quizzes.q: The prefix 'giga' means
quizzes.e: giga (G) = 10⁹; mega = 10⁶, tera = 10¹², kilo = 10³.

quizzes.q: Mass, length, time, current, temperature and amount are
quizzes.e: The seven SI base quantities are mass, length, time, current, temperature, amount of substance and luminous intensity.

quizzes.q: A physical quantity is written as
quizzes.a: a numerical value multiplied by a unit, e.g. 9.81 m s⁻²
quizzes.e: Every physical quantity has a numerical value and a unit; a number without a unit is meaningless.

quizzes.q: The correct way to label a graph axis or table column for time measured in seconds is
quizzes.e: The convention is quantity / unit for both graph axes and table columns.

quizzes.q: Write 8 kA in amps (give the number in standard form; enter e.g. 3e-6).
quizzes.e: kilo (k) means × 1000, so 8 kA = 8000 A.

quizzes.e: kilo (k) means × 1000, so 5 kA = 5000 A.

quizzes.q: Write 6 kA in amps (give the number in standard form; enter e.g. 3e-6).
quizzes.e: kilo (k) means × 1000, so 6 kA = 6000 A.

quizzes.q: Write 7 kA in amps (give the number in standard form; enter e.g. 3e-6).
quizzes.e: kilo (k) means × 1000, so 7 kA = 7000 A.

quizzes.q: Estimate: KE of a 60 kg runner at 7 m/s.
quizzes.e: KE = ½mv² = ½ × 60 × 7² = 1470 J.

quizzes.q: Estimate: KE of a 67 kg runner at 6 m/s.
quizzes.e: KE = ½mv² = ½ × 67 × 6² = 1206 J.

quizzes.q: Estimate: KE of a 69 kg runner at 5 m/s.
The unit of power in base units is
quizzes.e: W = J s⁻¹ = (kg m² s⁻²) s⁻¹ = kg m² s⁻³.

quizzes.q: The coulomb in base units is
quizzes.e: From Q = It, 1 C = 1 A × 1 s = 1 A s.

quizzes.q: The volt in base units is
quizzes.e: V = W/Q = J ÷ (A s) = kg m² s⁻² ÷ (A s) = kg m² s⁻³ A⁻¹.

quizzes.q: What is a derived unit?
quizzes.e: A derived unit is made by combining base units by multiplying or dividing, e.g. 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻².

quizzes.q: An order-of-magnitude estimate of the mass of an adult is
quizzes.e: An adult's mass is about 70 kg, which is closest to 10² kg as an order of magnitude.

quizzes.q: An estimate of the wavelength of visible light is
quizzes.e: Visible light has wavelengths of about 400–700 nm, so 5 × 10⁻⁷ m (500 nm) is a good estimate.

quizzes.q: Make an estimate of the physical quantity: the mass of an adult person is about
quizzes.e: Making estimates of physical quantities: typical values include an adult mass of 50–100 kg, a door height of 2 m and walking speed of 1.5 m s⁻¹.

quizzes.q: A 900 W heater runs for 4 hours. Find the energy in MJ (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Convert time to seconds: 4 × 3600 = 14400 s. E = Pt = 900 × 14400 = 1.3 × 10⁷ J = 13 MJ.

quizzes.q: A 900 W heater runs for 5 hours. Find the energy in MJ (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Convert time to seconds: 5 × 3600 = 18000 s. E = Pt = 900 × 18000 = 1.62 × 10⁷ J = 16.2 MJ.

quizzes.q: A 500 W heater runs for 4 hours. Find the energy in MJ (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Convert time to seconds: 4 × 3600 = 14400 s. E = Pt = 500 × 14400 = 7.2 × 10⁶ J = 7.2 MJ.

quizzes.q: Which equation is homogeneous?
quizzes.e: An equation is homogeneous if every term has the same base units. In v² = u² + 2as, each term is in m² s⁻².

quizzes.q: The Young modulus in base units is
quizzes.e: E = stress ÷ strain, and strain has no units, so E has the units of stress, Pa = N m⁻² = kg m s⁻² ÷ m² = kg m⁻¹ s⁻².

quizzes.q: Can a homogeneous equation still be wrong? Explain.
quizzes.e: Yes. Checking units cannot detect a missing or wrong dimensionless constant, such as ½ or 2π, so a homogeneous equation can still be wrong.

quizzes.q: Estimate the energy (J) used by a 2 kW kettle boiling for 3 minutes.
The unit of the Planck constant h in base units is
quizzes.e: From E = hf, h = E ÷ f, with units J ÷ s⁻¹ = J s = kg m² s⁻² × s = kg m² s⁻¹.

quizzes.e: k = F ÷ v² = 40 ÷ 4² = 2.5. Units: N ÷ (m s⁻¹)² = kg m s⁻² × s² m⁻² = kg m⁻¹.

quizzes.q: Drag F = kv². F = 30 N at 3 m/s. Find k and give its value (3 s.f.) — units kg m⁻¹.
quizzes.e: k = F ÷ v² = 30 ÷ 3² = 3.33. Units: N ÷ (m s⁻¹)² = kg m s⁻² × s² m⁻² = kg m⁻¹.

quizzes.q: Length = 50.0 ± 0.5 cm. Percentage uncertainty?
quizzes.e: Percentage uncertainty = absolute uncertainty ÷ value × 100 = 0.5 ÷ 50.0 × 100 = 1%.

quizzes.q: A = 2.0 ± 2%, B = 3.0 ± 3%. Percentage uncertainty in A × B?
quizzes.e: When quantities are multiplied or divided, add their percentage uncertainties: 2% + 3% = 5%.

quizzes.q: Percentage uncertainty in r is 2%. Percentage uncertainty in r³?
quizzes.e: For a power, multiply the percentage uncertainty by the power: 3 × 2% = 6%.

quizzes.q: An accurate measurement is
quizzes.e: Accuracy is how close a measurement is to the true value. Precision is about the spread of repeated readings.

quizzes.q: Worst-fit lines through error bars let you find
quizzes.e: Draw the best-fit and worst acceptable lines through the error bars. The uncertainty in the gradient is the difference between the best and worst gradients.

quizzes.q: Precision describes
quizzes.a: how close repeated readings are to each other
quizzes.e: Precision describes how close repeated readings are to each other (a small spread). It says nothing about the true value.

quizzes.q: 29 ± 2 cm. Percentage uncertainty (3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: % uncertainty = absolute ÷ value × 100 = 2 ÷ 29 × 100 = 6.9%.

quizzes.q: 21 ± 1 cm. Percentage uncertainty (3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: % uncertainty = absolute ÷ value × 100 = 1 ÷ 21 × 100 = 4.76%.

quizzes.q: 33 ± 1 cm. Percentage uncertainty (3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: % uncertainty = absolute ÷ value × 100 = 1 ÷ 33 × 100 = 3.03%.

quizzes.q: 26 ± 2 cm. Percentage uncertainty (3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: % uncertainty = absolute ÷ value × 100 = 2 ÷ 26 × 100 = 7.69%.

quizzes.q: When adding two quantities, you combine their
quizzes.e: When adding or subtracting quantities, add their absolute uncertainties.

quizzes.q: When multiplying quantities, you combine their
quizzes.e: When multiplying or dividing quantities, add their percentage (or fractional) uncertainties.

quizzes.q: What is a random error?
quizzes.e: A random error causes unpredictable variation in readings, so they scatter about the mean value.

quizzes.q: To reduce the effect of random error, you should
quizzes.e: Repeating readings and taking the mean reduces the effect of random errors, because the scatter above and below the true value tends to cancel.

quizzes.q: A result is accurate if
quizzes.a: it is close to the true value
quizzes.e: An accurate result is close to the true (accepted) value. A precise result has a small spread.

quizzes.q: The percentage difference between an experimental 9.6 and accepted 9.81 is about
Length 5% uncertain, width 2% uncertain. Percentage uncertainty in area?
quizzes.e: Area = length × width, so add the percentage uncertainties: 5% + 2% = 7%.

quizzes.q: Length 1% uncertain, width 5% uncertain. Percentage uncertainty in area?
quizzes.e: Area = length × width, so add the percentage uncertainties: 1% + 5% = 6%.

quizzes.q: Length 2% uncertain, width 3% uncertain. Percentage uncertainty in area?
quizzes.e: Area = length × width, so add the percentage uncertainties: 2% + 3% = 5%.

A gradient is 4.0 with ±5%. y-intercept irrelevant. The quantity k = 1/gradient has uncertainty
quizzes.e: For k = 1/gradient, the power is −1, so the percentage uncertainty is 1 × 5% = 5%.

quizzes.q: How do you find the uncertainty in a gradient from a graph?
quizzes.e: Draw the line of best fit and the worst acceptable line (steepest or shallowest) through all the error bars. The uncertainty is the difference between their gradients.

quizzes.q: If error bars of all points cross a straight line through the origin, then
quizzes.e: If a straight line through the origin passes through every error bar, the data are consistent with direct proportionality within the uncertainties.

quizzes.q: The diameter of a wire is best measured with a
quizzes.a: micrometer at several places and averaged
quizzes.e: A wire may not be uniform, so measure its diameter with a micrometer at several places and orientations along it and take the mean.
