Two perpendicular forces of 6 N and 8 N. Magnitude of the resultant?
quizzes.e: The forces are perpendicular, so use Pythagoras: √(6² + 8²) = √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10 N.

quizzes.q: A 20 N force at 30° to the horizontal. Horizontal component (3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: Horizontal component = F cos θ = 20 × cos 30° = 20 × 0.866 = 17.3 N.

quizzes.q: Which is a vector?
quizzes.e: Displacement has magnitude and direction, so it is a vector. Speed, mass and energy are scalars.

quizzes.q: What two things describe a vector?
quizzes.e: A vector has both magnitude (size) and direction, e.g. velocity, force and displacement.

quizzes.q: Weight component perpendicular to a slope at angle θ
quizzes.e: The angle between the weight and the normal to the slope is θ, so the component perpendicular to the slope is mg cos θ (and mg sin θ acts down the slope).

quizzes.q: Which is a scalar?
quizzes.e: Kinetic energy has magnitude only, so it is a scalar. Momentum, weight and acceleration all have direction.

quizzes.q: Displacement 3 km east then 4 km north gives a resultant displacement of
quizzes.e: The displacements are perpendicular: √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5 km (north-east of the start).

quizzes.q: Which list contains only vector quantities?
quizzes.e: A vector quantity has magnitude and direction (velocity, force, displacement); a scalar quantity has magnitude only (speed, mass, energy, distance).

quizzes.q: A 59 N force acts at 50° above horizontal. Find the vertical component (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Vertical component = F sin θ = 59 × sin 50° = 45.2 N.

quizzes.q: A 15 N force acts at 30° above horizontal. Find the vertical component (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Vertical component = F sin θ = 15 × sin 30° = 7.5 N.

quizzes.q: A 29 N force acts at 20° above horizontal. Find the vertical component (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Vertical component = F sin θ = 29 × sin 20° = 9.92 N.

quizzes.q: A 10 N force acts at 35° above horizontal. Find the vertical component (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Vertical component = F sin θ = 10 × sin 35° = 5.74 N.

quizzes.q: Three coplanar forces in equilibrium form
quizzes.e: In equilibrium the vector sum is zero, so drawing the three forces tip to tail gives a closed triangle.

quizzes.q: The resultant of 5 N and 12 N can range from
quizzes.e: The resultant is largest when the forces act in the same direction (5 + 12 = 17 N) and smallest when opposite (12 − 5 = 7 N).

quizzes.q: What does it mean to resolve a vector?
quizzes.e: Resolving a vector means splitting it into two perpendicular components, e.g. F cos θ and F sin θ, whose combined effect is the same as the vector.

quizzes.q: A plane flies north at 200 m/s in a 50 m/s east wind. Its ground velocity direction is
quizzes.e: Adding the velocities tip to tail gives a resultant pointing east of north, at tan⁻¹(50/200) ≈ 14° from north, with speed √(200² + 50²) ≈ 206 m s⁻¹.

quizzes.q: Subtracting vector B from A is the same as
quizzes.e: Vector subtraction A − B is the same as A + (−B), where −B has the same magnitude as B but the opposite direction.

quizzes.q: Perpendicular forces 6 N and 12 N. Find the angle of the resultant to the 6 N force (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: tan θ = 12 ÷ 6, so θ = tan⁻¹(2) = 63.4° to the 6 N force.

quizzes.q: Perpendicular forces 13 N and 18 N. Find the angle of the resultant to the 13 N force (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: tan θ = 18 ÷ 13, so θ = tan⁻¹(1.38) = 54.2° to the 13 N force.

quizzes.q: Perpendicular forces 3 N and 12 N. Find the angle of the resultant to the 3 N force (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: tan θ = 12 ÷ 3, so θ = tan⁻¹(4) = 76° to the 3 N force.

quizzes.q: Perpendicular forces 17 N and 20 N. Find the angle of the resultant to the 17 N force (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: tan θ = 20 ÷ 17, so θ = tan⁻¹(1.18) = 49.6° to the 17 N force.

quizzes.q: A boat heads across a river at 6 m/s; the current is 1 m/s. Find the resultant speed (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: The velocities are perpendicular: v = √(6² + 1²) = √37 = 6.08 m s⁻¹.

quizzes.q: A boat heads across a river at 4 m/s; the current is 4 m/s. Find the resultant speed (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: The velocities are perpendicular: v = √(4² + 4²) = √32 = 5.66 m s⁻¹.

quizzes.q: A boat heads across a river at 6 m/s; the current is 2 m/s. Find the resultant speed (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: The velocities are perpendicular: v = √(6² + 2²) = √40 = 6.32 m s⁻¹.

quizzes.q: An object is in equilibrium on a slope. The resultant of friction and normal reaction is
quizzes.a: equal and opposite to its weight
quizzes.e: Three forces act (weight, friction, normal reaction). For equilibrium, the resultant of friction and the normal reaction must be equal and opposite to the weight.

quizzes.q: A lamp hangs from two strings at equal angles. Why does tension rise as the strings get more horizontal?
quizzes.e: The weight is fixed, so the total vertical component of the tensions must stay equal to it. As the strings get more horizontal, sin θ gets smaller, so the tension must increase.

quizzes.q: A 20 N lamp hangs from two strings each at 30° to the horizontal. Find the tension in each.
quizzes.e: Vertically: 2T sin 30° = 20 N, so T = 20 ÷ (2 × 0.5) = 20 N.

quizzes.q: Change in velocity from 10 m/s east to 10 m/s north. Magnitude (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Δv = v − u. The two velocities are perpendicular and equal in size, so the size of Δv is √(10² + 10²) = 14.1 m s⁻¹ (pointing north-west).

quizzes.q: For a body on a frictionless slope, the normal reaction is
quizzes.e: On a frictionless slope there is no acceleration perpendicular to the slope, so the normal reaction equals the perpendicular component of the weight, mg cos θ.

quizzes.q: Two forces 25 N and 40 N act at 60° to each other. Find the resultant magnitude (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: R² = F₁² + F₂² + 2F₁F₂ cos θ = 25² + 40² + 2 × 25 × 40 × cos 60°, so R = 56.8 N.

quizzes.q: Two forces 12 N and 31 N act at 120° to each other. Find the resultant magnitude (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: R² = F₁² + F₂² + 2F₁F₂ cos θ = 12² + 31² + 2 × 12 × 31 × cos 120°, so R = 27.1 N.

quizzes.q: Two forces 20 N and 36 N act at 60° to each other. Find the resultant magnitude (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: R² = F₁² + F₂² + 2F₁F₂ cos θ = 20² + 36² + 2 × 20 × 36 × cos 60°, so R = 49.2 N.

quizzes.q: Two forces 10 N and 24 N act at 60° to each other. Find the resultant magnitude (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: R² = F₁² + F₂² + 2F₁F₂ cos θ = 10² + 24² + 2 × 10 × 24 × cos 60°, so R = 30.3 N.

quizzes.q: A 10 kg mass rests on a slope at 40°. Find the friction needed to stop it sliding (3 s.f., g = 9.81).
quizzes.e: Friction must balance the weight component down the slope: F = mg sin θ = 10 × 9.81 × sin 40° = 63.1 N.

quizzes.q: A 8 kg mass rests on a slope at 30°. Find the friction needed to stop it sliding (3 s.f., g = 9.81).
quizzes.e: Friction must balance the weight component down the slope: F = mg sin θ = 8 × 9.81 × sin 30° = 39.2 N.

quizzes.q: A 10 kg mass rests on a slope at 30°. Find the friction needed to stop it sliding (3 s.f., g = 9.81).
quizzes.e: Friction must balance the weight component down the slope: F = mg sin θ = 10 × 9.81 × sin 30° = 49 N.

quizzes.q: A car at 15 m/s decelerates at 3 m s⁻². Braking distance?
quizzes.e: Use v² = u² + 2as with v = 0, u = 15 and a = −3: 0 = 225 − 6s, so s = 37.5 m.

quizzes.q: The gradient of a displacement–time graph is
quizzes.e: The gradient of a displacement–time graph is Δs/Δt, which is the velocity.

quizzes.q: A stone is thrown horizontally from a 20 m cliff. Time to land (g = 9.81, 3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: Vertically, u = 0 and s = ½gt², so t = √(2s/g) = √(2 × 20 ÷ 9.81) = 2.02 s.

quizzes.q: Define thinking distance.
quizzes.e: Thinking distance is the distance travelled during the driver's reaction time, at constant speed, before the brakes are applied: speed × reaction time.

quizzes.q: The stone above is thrown at 12 m/s. Horizontal distance (3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: The horizontal velocity stays constant: distance = 12 × 2.02 = 24.2 m.

quizzes.q: The area under a speed–time graph is
quizzes.e: The area under a speed–time graph is the distance travelled; for a velocity–time graph it is the displacement.

quizzes.q: Use the graph to find the acceleration during the first 4 s.
quizzes.e: Acceleration is the gradient of the v–t graph: a = Δv ÷ Δt = 10 m s⁻¹ ÷ 4 s = 2.5 m s⁻².

quizzes.q: u = 2 m/s, a = 3 m s⁻², t = 4 s. Find v.
u = 4 m/s, a = 5 m s⁻², t = 5 s. Find v.
u = 10 m/s, a = 1 m s⁻², t = 7 s. Find v.
u = 8 m/s, a = 2 m s⁻², t = 7 s. Find v.
An object in free fall (no air resistance) has
quizzes.e: In free fall the only force is weight, so the acceleration is constant at g ≈ 9.81 m s⁻² downwards.

quizzes.q: Braking distance increases with
quizzes.e: From v² = u² + 2as with v = 0, braking distance s = u² ÷ 2a, so it is proportional to the speed squared.

quizzes.q: Give two factors that increase thinking distance.
quizzes.e: Thinking distance = speed × reaction time. Higher speed, tiredness, alcohol or drugs, and distractions (such as phones) all increase it.

quizzes.q: In projectile motion, the horizontal velocity
quizzes.e: With no air resistance there is no horizontal force, so the horizontal velocity of a projectile stays constant.

quizzes.q: An object thrown up returns to the thrower's hand with
quizzes.a: the same speed it was thrown with
quizzes.e: With no air resistance the motion is symmetrical: the object loses kinetic energy going up and regains the same amount coming down, so it returns at the same speed.

quizzes.q: Use the velocity–time graph to find the total displacement in the 10 s.
Which technique would best investigate the motion and collisions of objects on an air track?
quizzes.a: two light gates connected to a data logger measure the speeds of the gliders before and after the collision
w: a metre rule and a stopwatch read by eye
quizzes.e: Techniques and procedures include gliders, light gates, ticker timers and video analysis. Air tracks reduce friction so momentum can be checked.

quizzes.q: A car at 16 m/s: reaction time 0.6 s, deceleration 5 m s⁻². Find the stopping distance (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Thinking distance = 16 × 0.6 = 9.6 m. Braking distance = v² ÷ 2a = 16² ÷ 10 = 25.6 m. Total = 35.2 m.

quizzes.q: A car at 20 m/s: reaction time 0.6 s, deceleration 7 m s⁻². Find the stopping distance (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Thinking distance = 20 × 0.6 = 12 m. Braking distance = v² ÷ 2a = 20² ÷ 14 = 28.6 m. Total = 40.6 m.

quizzes.q: A car at 22 m/s: reaction time 0.8 s, deceleration 4 m s⁻². Find the stopping distance (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Thinking distance = 22 × 0.8 = 17.6 m. Braking distance = v² ÷ 2a = 22² ÷ 8 = 60.5 m. Total = 78.1 m.

quizzes.q: A car at 22 m/s: reaction time 0.6 s, deceleration 7 m s⁻². Find the stopping distance (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Thinking distance = 22 × 0.6 = 13.2 m. Braking distance = v² ÷ 2a = 22² ÷ 14 = 34.6 m. Total = 47.8 m.

quizzes.q: An object is dropped from 9 m. Find the time to fall (3 s.f., g = 9.81).
An object is dropped from 21 m. Find the time to fall (3 s.f., g = 9.81).
An object is dropped from 10 m. Find the time to fall (3 s.f., g = 9.81).
The maximum range on level ground (no drag) is at a launch angle of
quizzes.e: Range R = u² sin 2θ ÷ g, which is largest when sin 2θ = 1, i.e. 2θ = 90° and θ = 45°.

quizzes.q: How can you find g using a light gate and a falling card of known length?
quizzes.e: Drop the card through two light gates a known distance s apart. Each gate gives a speed (card length ÷ time). Then g = (v² − u²) ÷ 2s.

quizzes.q: A car accelerates from 12 m/s to 30 m/s over 210 m. Find the acceleration (3 s.f.).
A ball is thrown up at 20 m/s. Find the max height (g = 9.81, 3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: At the top v = 0: 0 = u² − 2gh, so h = u² ÷ 2g = 400 ÷ (2 × 9.81) = 20.4 m.

quizzes.q: An s–t graph that curves upward with increasing gradient shows
quizzes.e: The gradient of an s–t graph is the velocity. An increasing gradient means increasing velocity, so the object is accelerating.

quizzes.q: A ball is kicked at 28 m/s at 40° on level ground. Find its range (3 s.f., g = 9.81).
quizzes.e: Vertical: t = 2U sin θ ÷ g = 3.67 s. Horizontal: range = U cos θ × t = 21.4 × 3.67 = 78.7 m.

quizzes.q: A ball is kicked at 29 m/s at 50° on level ground. Find its range (3 s.f., g = 9.81).
quizzes.e: Vertical: t = 2U sin θ ÷ g = 4.53 s. Horizontal: range = U cos θ × t = 18.6 × 4.53 = 84.4 m.

quizzes.q: A ball is kicked at 18 m/s at 60° on level ground. Find its range (3 s.f., g = 9.81).
quizzes.e: Vertical: t = 2U sin θ ÷ g = 3.18 s. Horizontal: range = U cos θ × t = 9 × 3.18 = 28.6 m.

quizzes.q: A ball is kicked at 18 m/s at 30° on level ground. Find its range (3 s.f., g = 9.81).
quizzes.e: Vertical: t = 2U sin θ ÷ g = 1.83 s. Horizontal: range = U cos θ × t = 15.6 × 1.83 = 28.6 m.

quizzes.q: A stone is thrown vertically up at 7 m/s from a 11 m cliff top. Find the time to hit the ground below (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Take up as positive: −11 = 7t − 4.905t². Solve 4.905t² − 7t − 11 = 0 and take the positive root: t = 2.37 s.

quizzes.q: A stone is thrown vertically up at 11 m/s from a 23 m cliff top. Find the time to hit the ground below (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Take up as positive: −23 = 11t − 4.905t². Solve 4.905t² − 11t − 23 = 0 and take the positive root: t = 3.56 s.

quizzes.q: A stone is thrown vertically up at 7 m/s from a 13 m cliff top. Find the time to hit the ground below (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Take up as positive: −13 = 7t − 4.905t². Solve 4.905t² − 7t − 13 = 0 and take the positive root: t = 2.49 s.

quizzes.q: Terminal velocity is reached when
quizzes.e: At terminal velocity the drag equals the weight, so the resultant force is zero and the acceleration is zero.

quizzes.q: Density of a 0.50 kg object of volume 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ m³?
Pressure due to 10 m of water (ρ = 1000, g = 9.81)?
State the principle of moments.
quizzes.e: For an object in equilibrium, the sum of the clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments about that point.

quizzes.q: Upthrust on a submerged object equals
quizzes.e: Archimedes' principle: the upthrust on an object in a fluid equals the weight of the fluid it displaces.

quizzes.q: Drag on an object generally increases with
quizzes.e: Drag increases with speed (roughly with v² at high speeds), as well as with cross-sectional area.

quizzes.q: F₁ = 6.0 N acts at d₁ = 0.40 m. The beam balances with d₂ = 0.30 m. Find F₂.
quizzes.e: Principle of moments: F₁d₁ = F₂d₂, so 6.0 × 0.40 = F₂ × 0.30 and F₂ = 2.4 ÷ 0.30 = 8.0 N.

quizzes.q: The newton, the unit of force, is equal to
quizzes.e: From F = ma, 1 N gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m s⁻².

quizzes.q: Resultant force 21 N on 18 kg. Acceleration (3 s.f.)?
Resultant force 23 N on 9 kg. Acceleration (3 s.f.)?
Resultant force 12 N on 5 kg. Acceleration (3 s.f.)?
Find the pressure due to the fluid at 7 m depth in a fluid of density 1000 kg m⁻³ (3 s.f., kPa).
quizzes.e: p = hρg = 7 × 1000 × 9.81 = 68700 Pa = 68.7 kPa (pressure due to the fluid only).

quizzes.q: Find the pressure due to the fluid at 5 m depth in a fluid of density 1000 kg m⁻³ (3 s.f., kPa).
quizzes.e: p = hρg = 5 × 1000 × 9.81 = 49000 Pa = 49 kPa (pressure due to the fluid only).

quizzes.q: Find the pressure due to the fluid at 2 m depth in a fluid of density 800 kg m⁻³ (3 s.f., kPa).
quizzes.e: p = hρg = 2 × 800 × 9.81 = 15700 Pa = 15.7 kPa (pressure due to the fluid only).

quizzes.q: A skydiver opens the parachute. Immediately after, the skydiver
quizzes.e: Opening the parachute suddenly increases the drag so that it is greater than the weight. The resultant force is upwards, so the skydiver decelerates.

quizzes.q: The centre of gravity is
quizzes.a: the point where the weight appears to act
quizzes.e: The centre of gravity is the point where the whole weight of an object appears to act. For a uniform, symmetrical object it is at the geometric centre.

quizzes.q: State the condition for an object to be in equilibrium.
quizzes.e: An object is in equilibrium when the resultant force on it is zero and the resultant moment about any point is zero.

quizzes.q: An object floats when
quizzes.e: A floating object is in equilibrium, so the upthrust (weight of fluid displaced) equals its weight.

quizzes.q: Torque of a couple equals
quizzes.e: The torque of a couple = one of the forces × the perpendicular distance between the lines of action of the two forces. A couple causes rotation but no translation.

quizzes.q: The block (2.0 kg) rests on the slope at θ = 30°. Find the friction force acting on it (g = 9.81, 3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: At rest the forces along the slope balance, so friction = mg sin θ = 2.0 × 9.81 × sin 30° = 9.81 N, acting up the slope.

quizzes.q: A constant force of 6.0 N acts on a 2.0 kg puck at rest on frictionless ice. How far does it move in 4.0 s (one-dimensional motion under constant force)? Answer in m.
quizzes.e: a = F/m = 3.0 m s⁻², so s = ½at² = ½ × 3.0 × 16 = 24 m.

quizzes.q: A ball is thrown horizontally. Its two-dimensional motion under the constant force of gravity has
quizzes.a: constant horizontal velocity and constant downward acceleration
quizzes.e: With only weight acting (a constant force), the acceleration is g downwards and the horizontal component of velocity does not change.

quizzes.q: A 60 kg diver stands on a 0.020 m² area. Find the pressure on the solid board in kPa (2 s.f.). (g = 9.81 N kg⁻¹)
quizzes.e: p = F/A = 60 × 9.81 ÷ 0.020 = 29 400 Pa = 29 kPa. p = F/A applies to solids, liquids and gases.

quizzes.q: Find the upthrust on a fully submerged object of volume 2.17 × 10⁻³ m³ in fluid of density 1030 kg m⁻³ (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Upthrust = weight of fluid displaced = Vρg = 0.00217 × 1030 × 9.81 = 21.9 N.

quizzes.q: Find the upthrust on a fully submerged object of volume 1.27 × 10⁻³ m³ in fluid of density 1030 kg m⁻³ (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Upthrust = weight of fluid displaced = Vρg = 0.00127 × 1030 × 9.81 = 12.8 N.

quizzes.q: Find the upthrust on a fully submerged object of volume 1.03 × 10⁻³ m³ in fluid of density 1000 kg m⁻³ (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Upthrust = weight of fluid displaced = Vρg = 0.00103 × 1000 × 9.81 = 10.1 N.

quizzes.q: Find the upthrust on a fully submerged object of volume 2.32 × 10⁻³ m³ in fluid of density 1030 kg m⁻³ (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Upthrust = weight of fluid displaced = Vρg = 0.00232 × 1030 × 9.81 = 23.4 N.

quizzes.q: A 37 N force acts at 60° to a spanner of length 0.51 m. Find the moment about the nut (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Perpendicular distance = d sin θ = 0.51 × sin 60° = 0.442 m. Moment = 37 × 0.442 = 16.3 N m.

quizzes.q: A 47 N force acts at 45° to a spanner of length 0.23 m. Find the moment about the nut (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Perpendicular distance = d sin θ = 0.23 × sin 45° = 0.163 m. Moment = 47 × 0.163 = 7.64 N m.

quizzes.q: A 43 N force acts at 30° to a spanner of length 0.55 m. Find the moment about the nut (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Perpendicular distance = d sin θ = 0.55 × sin 30° = 0.275 m. Moment = 43 × 0.275 = 11.8 N m.

quizzes.q: Why does a car with a lower centre of mass topple less easily?
quizzes.a: its weight's line of action stays within the base for larger tilts
quizzes.e: A car topples when the line of action of its weight passes outside its base. With a lower centre of mass, it can be tilted further before this happens.

quizzes.q: Explain why a falling object reaches terminal velocity.
quizzes.e: As the speed increases, drag increases while the weight stays the same. The resultant force falls until drag equals weight; then the acceleration is zero and the speed is constant.

quizzes.q: A 2.0 cm³ cube of density 7800 kg m⁻³ in water. Find its apparent weight (mN, 3 s.f., g = 9.81).
Pressure in a fluid depends on
quizzes.e: Pressure in a fluid is p = hρg: it depends only on depth, the density of the fluid and g, not on the shape of the container.

quizzes.q: A free-body diagram should show
quizzes.a: all forces acting on one object
quizzes.e: A free-body diagram shows all the forces acting on one object only, drawn as arrows from the object.

quizzes.q: A couple of two 26 N forces 0.42 m apart. Find the torque.
quizzes.e: Torque of a couple = one force × perpendicular separation = 26 × 0.42 = 10.9 N m.

quizzes.q: A couple of two 16 N forces 0.11 m apart. Find the torque.
quizzes.e: Torque of a couple = one force × perpendicular separation = 16 × 0.11 = 1.76 N m.

quizzes.q: A couple of two 8 N forces 0.34 m apart. Find the torque.
quizzes.e: Torque of a couple = one force × perpendicular separation = 8 × 0.34 = 2.72 N m.

quizzes.q: A uniform 1.0 m ruler of weight 3 N is pivoted at 0.40 m. What weight at the 0.15 m mark balances it? (3 s.f.)
quizzes.e: The weight acts at the centre (0.50 m), 0.10 m right of the pivot: moment = 3 × 0.10 = 0.3 N m. The unknown weight is 0.25 m left: W = 0.3 ÷ 0.25 = 1.2 N.

quizzes.q: A uniform 1.0 m ruler of weight 3 N is pivoted at 0.40 m. What weight at the 0.30 m mark balances it? (3 s.f.)
quizzes.e: The weight acts at the centre (0.50 m), 0.10 m right of the pivot: moment = 3 × 0.10 = 0.3 N m. The unknown weight is 0.10 m left: W = 0.3 ÷ 0.10 = 3 N.

quizzes.q: A uniform 1.0 m ruler of weight 4 N is pivoted at 0.40 m. What weight at the 0.05 m mark balances it? (3 s.f.)
quizzes.e: The weight acts at the centre (0.50 m), 0.10 m right of the pivot: moment = 4 × 0.10 = 0.4 N m. The unknown weight is 0.35 m left: W = 0.4 ÷ 0.35 = 1.14 N.

quizzes.q: 50 N moves an object 4 m at 60° to the force. Work done?
2 kg falls 5 m from rest. Final speed (g = 9.81, 3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: Ep lost = Ek gained: mgh = ½mv², so v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 9.81 × 5) = 9.90 m s⁻¹. The mass cancels.

quizzes.q: A motor lifts 100 N through 3 m in 6 s. Power?
Efficiency =
quizzes.e: Efficiency = useful output energy (or power) ÷ total input energy (or power). Multiply by 100 for a percentage.

quizzes.q: State the principle of conservation of energy.
quizzes.e: Energy cannot be created or destroyed; it can only be transferred from one form to another. The total energy of a closed system stays constant.

quizzes.q: Work done is zero when the force is
quizzes.e: W = Fx cos θ. If the force is perpendicular to the displacement, θ = 90° and cos 90° = 0, so no work is done.

quizzes.q: The watt is equal to
quizzes.e: 1 watt is 1 joule per second: power is the rate of energy transfer.

quizzes.q: Find the kinetic energy of an object of mass 1200 kg moving at 15 m s⁻¹, in kJ (3 s.f.).
A motor does 3600 J of work in 1.5 minutes. Its power in watts?
quizzes.e: P = W/t = 3600 J ÷ 90 s = 40 W. The unit watt is one joule per second.

quizzes.q: KE of 1 kg at 14 m/s?
quizzes.e: KE = ½mv² = ½ × 1 × 14² = 98 J.

quizzes.q: KE of 8 kg at 2 m/s?
quizzes.e: KE = ½mv² = ½ × 8 × 2² = 16 J.

quizzes.q: KE of 7 kg at 12 m/s?
quizzes.e: KE = ½mv² = ½ × 7 × 12² = 504 J.

quizzes.q: GPE gained by 8 kg raised 16 m (3 s.f., g = 9.81)?
GPE gained by 4 kg raised 20 m (3 s.f., g = 9.81)?
GPE gained by 10 kg raised 4 m (3 s.f., g = 9.81)?
A pendulum at the top of its swing has
quizzes.e: At the top of the swing the pendulum is momentarily at rest, so it has zero KE and maximum gravitational potential energy.

quizzes.q: Define work done.
quizzes.e: Work done = force × distance moved in the direction of the force, W = Fx cos θ.

quizzes.q: A ball dropped from twice the height hits the ground with
quizzes.e: v = √(2gh). Doubling h multiplies v by √2.

quizzes.q: Energy wasted in a motor is mostly
quizzes.e: Most wasted energy in a motor is transferred as thermal energy, by friction in the bearings and by the resistance of the coils.

quizzes.q: P = Fv applies when
quizzes.a: a constant force moves an object at constant velocity
quizzes.e: P = Fv gives the power needed for a force F to move an object at speed v, e.g. the driving force on a vehicle moving at constant velocity.

quizzes.q: A pulley system lifts 50 N through 2.0 m when 25 N is pulled through 5.0 m. The efficiency of this mechanical system as a percentage?
quizzes.e: Useful output = 50 × 2.0 = 100 J; input = 25 × 5.0 = 125 J; efficiency = 100/125 = 80%.

quizzes.q: A car’s engine delivers 10 kW at a steady 24 m/s. Find the driving force (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: At steady speed P = Fv, so F = P ÷ v = 10000 ÷ 24 = 417 N.

quizzes.q: A car’s engine delivers 11 kW at a steady 26 m/s. Find the driving force (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: At steady speed P = Fv, so F = P ÷ v = 11000 ÷ 26 = 423 N.

quizzes.q: A car’s engine delivers 29 kW at a steady 38 m/s. Find the driving force (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: At steady speed P = Fv, so F = P ÷ v = 29000 ÷ 38 = 763 N.

quizzes.q: A car’s engine delivers 14 kW at a steady 22 m/s. Find the driving force (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: At steady speed P = Fv, so F = P ÷ v = 14000 ÷ 22 = 636 N.

quizzes.q: A car's top speed is reached when
quizzes.e: At top speed the car is not accelerating, so the driving force equals the total resistive forces; the engine's power is then P = Fv.

quizzes.q: Why is the KE of a car more than doubled when speed doubles?
quizzes.e: KE = ½mv². Doubling v multiplies KE by 2² = 4, so it quadruples.

quizzes.q: A 60 kg person climbs 3.0 m of stairs in 4.0 s. Find their power (3 s.f., g = 9.81).
A ball bounces to 80% of its height each time. Energy lost per bounce is
quizzes.e: GPE = mgh, so reaching 80% of the height means 80% of the energy is kept and 20% of the GPE is lost each bounce (as heat and sound).

quizzes.q: A motor of efficiency 60% lifts 243 kg through 20 m in 16 s. Find its input power (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Useful power = mgh ÷ t = 243 × 9.81 × 20 ÷ 16 = 2980 W. Input = useful ÷ efficiency = 2980 ÷ 0.6 = 4970 W.

quizzes.q: A motor of efficiency 80% lifts 196 kg through 16 m in 22 s. Find its input power (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Useful power = mgh ÷ t = 196 × 9.81 × 16 ÷ 22 = 1400 W. Input = useful ÷ efficiency = 1400 ÷ 0.8 = 1750 W.

quizzes.q: A motor of efficiency 70% lifts 168 kg through 9 m in 34 s. Find its input power (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Useful power = mgh ÷ t = 168 × 9.81 × 9 ÷ 34 = 436 W. Input = useful ÷ efficiency = 436 ÷ 0.7 = 623 W.

quizzes.q: A motor of efficiency 60% lifts 151 kg through 8 m in 18 s. Find its input power (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Useful power = mgh ÷ t = 151 × 9.81 × 8 ÷ 18 = 658 W. Input = useful ÷ efficiency = 658 ÷ 0.6 = 1100 W.

quizzes.q: A 47 kg skier descends 7 m from rest and reaches 7 m/s. Find the energy dissipated (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: GPE lost = 47 × 9.81 × 7 = 3230 J. KE gained = ½ × 47 × 7² = 1150 J. Dissipated = 2080 J.

quizzes.q: A 61 kg skier descends 17 m from rest and reaches 4 m/s. Find the energy dissipated (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: GPE lost = 61 × 9.81 × 17 = 10200 J. KE gained = ½ × 61 × 4² = 488 J. Dissipated = 9680 J.

quizzes.q: A 46 kg skier descends 5 m from rest and reaches 7 m/s. Find the energy dissipated (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: GPE lost = 46 × 9.81 × 5 = 2260 J. KE gained = ½ × 46 × 7² = 1130 J. Dissipated = 1130 J.

quizzes.q: A spring (k = 200 N/m) is stretched 0.05 m. Elastic potential energy?
quizzes.e: Elastic potential energy = ½kx² = ½ × 200 × 0.05² = 0.25 J.

quizzes.q: 40 N on a wire of area 2.0 × 10⁻⁷ m². Stress (give × 10⁸ Pa)?
Young modulus =
quizzes.e: Young modulus E = stress ÷ strain = σ/ε. It is the gradient of the linear part of a stress–strain graph.

quizzes.q: What is plastic deformation?
quizzes.e: In plastic deformation the material does not return to its original shape when the load is removed; it is permanently deformed.

quizzes.q: Two identical springs (k) in series have combined stiffness
quizzes.e: For springs in series, 1/k_total = 1/k + 1/k = 2/k, so k_total = k/2. The combination stretches twice as far.

quizzes.q: Hooke's law states that extension is
quizzes.a: proportional to force (up to the limit of proportionality)
quizzes.e: Hooke's law: the extension is directly proportional to the applied force, F = kx, up to the limit of proportionality.

quizzes.q: Elastic deformation means the material
quizzes.a: returns to its original shape when unloaded
quizzes.e: Elastic deformation is reversible: the material returns to its original shape and size when the load is removed.

quizzes.q: A force that shortens a spring causes
quizzes.e: Tensile forces stretch and produce extension; compressive forces squash and produce compression.

quizzes.q: A spring (k = 72 N/m) has a 17 N load. Extension (cm, 3 s.f.)?
A spring (k = 198 N/m) has a 17 N load. Extension (cm, 3 s.f.)?
A spring (k = 284 N/m) has a 13 N load. Extension (cm, 3 s.f.)?
A 2.67 m wire extends by 1.2 mm. Find the strain (3 s.f., × 10⁻³).
A 1.46 m wire extends by 1.7 mm. Find the strain (3 s.f., × 10⁻³).
A 1.52 m wire extends by 1.6 mm. Find the strain (3 s.f., × 10⁻³).
The area under a force–extension graph is
quizzes.a: work done (elastic energy stored if elastic)
quizzes.e: The area under a force–extension graph is the work done. For elastic deformation it equals the elastic potential energy stored, ½Fx for a straight line.

quizzes.q: What is the ultimate tensile strength?
quizzes.e: The ultimate tensile strength is the maximum stress a material can withstand when it is stretched before it breaks.

quizzes.q: A brittle material
quizzes.a: breaks with little or no plastic deformation
quizzes.e: A brittle material (e.g. glass, cast iron) breaks with little or no plastic deformation.

quizzes.q: A ductile material
quizzes.a: can be drawn into wires (large plastic deformation)
quizzes.e: A ductile material (e.g. copper) can undergo large plastic deformation, so it can be drawn into wires.

quizzes.q: Rubber's loading and unloading curves differ. The area between them is
quizzes.e: The area between the loading and unloading curves is the energy dissipated as heat in each cycle (hysteresis).

quizzes.q: A wire of diameter 0.8 mm carries 56 N. Find the stress (3 s.f., give × 10⁸ Pa).
A wire of diameter 1.0 mm carries 88 N. Find the stress (3 s.f., give × 10⁸ Pa).
A wire of diameter 1.0 mm carries 154 N. Find the stress (3 s.f., give × 10⁸ Pa).
A wire of diameter 1.0 mm carries 127 N. Find the stress (3 s.f., give × 10⁸ Pa).
Springs of 65 N/m and 62 N/m in parallel. Combined k?
quizzes.e: Springs in parallel: k = k₁ + k₂ = 65 + 62 = 127 N m⁻¹.

quizzes.q: Springs of 76 N/m and 63 N/m in parallel. Combined k?
quizzes.e: Springs in parallel: k = k₁ + k₂ = 76 + 63 = 139 N m⁻¹.

quizzes.q: Two wires, same material and length; B has twice A's diameter. Under the same load B extends
quizzes.e: Twice the diameter gives 4 times the cross-sectional area, so the stress is ¼ and (for the same E) the strain and extension are ¼ as much.

quizzes.q: Why do you measure a wire's diameter at several points?
quizzes.e: A wire may not have a uniform diameter. Measuring at several points (and in different directions) and averaging gives a better value of the area and reduces random error.

quizzes.q: A 2.0 m wire of area 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m² stretches 1.0 mm under 100 N. Find E (× 10¹¹ Pa).
quizzes.e: Stress = 100 ÷ 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ = 1.0 × 10⁸ Pa; strain = 0.0010 ÷ 2.0 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴. E = stress ÷ strain = 2.0 × 10¹¹ Pa.

quizzes.q: Up to the limit of proportionality, the gradient of a stress–strain graph is
quizzes.e: The gradient of the straight part of a stress–strain graph is the Young modulus, E = σ/ε.

quizzes.q: A wire: length 2.6 m, diameter 1.0 mm, load 71 N, extension 2.1 mm. Find the Young modulus (3 s.f., × 10¹¹ Pa).
A wire: length 1.8 m, diameter 0.8 mm, load 68 N, extension 2.0 mm. Find the Young modulus (3 s.f., × 10¹¹ Pa).
A wire: length 2.7 m, diameter 0.5 mm, load 156 N, extension 2.8 mm. Find the Young modulus (3 s.f., × 10¹¹ Pa).
A wire: length 3.0 m, diameter 0.5 mm, load 59 N, extension 1.7 mm. Find the Young modulus (3 s.f., × 10¹¹ Pa).
Springs of 41 N/m and 48 N/m in series carry 6.0 N. Find the total elastic energy stored (3 s.f.).
Springs of 31 N/m and 53 N/m in series carry 6.0 N. Find the total elastic energy stored (3 s.f.).
Springs of 38 N/m and 27 N/m in series carry 6.0 N. Find the total elastic energy stored (3 s.f.).

topics.title: 3.5 Newton’s laws of motion and momentum

quizzes.q: A 2 kg trolley at 3 m/s sticks to a stationary 1 kg trolley. Common speed?
quizzes.e: Momentum before = 2 × 3 = 6 kg m s⁻¹. After, the 3 kg pair moves together: 3v = 6, so v = 2 m s⁻¹.

quizzes.q: Impulse from 40 N for 0.25 s?
quizzes.e: Impulse = FΔt = 40 × 0.25 = 10 N s (= change in momentum).

quizzes.q: In a perfectly elastic collision
quizzes.e: In a perfectly elastic collision the total kinetic energy is conserved. Momentum is conserved in every collision.

quizzes.q: State Newton's second law in terms of momentum.
quizzes.e: Newton's second law: the net force on an object is equal to its rate of change of momentum, F = Δp/Δt.

quizzes.q: Area under a force–time graph is
quizzes.e: The area under a force–time graph is FΔt, the impulse, which equals the change in momentum.

quizzes.q: The unit of momentum is
quizzes.e: Momentum p = mv, so its unit is kg × m s⁻¹ = kg m s⁻¹ (equivalent to N s).

quizzes.q: Momentum is
quizzes.e: Momentum p = mv has direction (the same as the velocity), so it is a vector.

quizzes.q: Which statement about the collision shown is true?
quizzes.a: Momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not
w: Both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved
Kinetic energy is conserved but momentum is not
quizzes.e: Momentum is always conserved; KE falls from 9 J to 6 J, so it is inelastic.

quizzes.q: Match each of Newton's three laws of motion to its statement.
pairs: an object stays at rest or moves at constant velocity unless a resultant force acts
the resultant force equals the rate of change of momentum
if A exerts a force on B then B exerts an equal and opposite force on A
quizzes.e: Newton's three laws: inertia, F = Δp/Δt, and equal and opposite pairs acting on different bodies.

quizzes.q: A 2 kg trolley at 6 m/s sticks to a stationary 4 kg trolley. Common velocity (3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: Momentum before = 2 × 6 = 12 kg m s⁻¹. After, mass 6 kg moves together: v = 12 ÷ 6 = 2 m s⁻¹.

quizzes.q: A 1 kg trolley at 4 m/s sticks to a stationary 5 kg trolley. Common velocity (3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: Momentum before = 1 × 4 = 4 kg m s⁻¹. After, mass 6 kg moves together: v = 4 ÷ 6 = 0.667 m s⁻¹.

quizzes.q: A 2 kg trolley at 7 m/s sticks to a stationary 5 kg trolley. Common velocity (3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: Momentum before = 2 × 7 = 14 kg m s⁻¹. After, mass 7 kg moves together: v = 14 ÷ 7 = 2 m s⁻¹.

quizzes.q: Crumple zones reduce injury by
quizzes.a: increasing the collision time, reducing force
quizzes.e: The change in momentum is fixed, but a crumple zone increases the collision time. Since F = Δp/Δt, the force on the passengers is smaller.

quizzes.q: State the principle of conservation of momentum.
quizzes.e: The total momentum of a system remains constant provided no external resultant force acts on it.

quizzes.q: An inelastic collision
quizzes.a: conserves momentum but not kinetic energy
quizzes.e: In an inelastic collision total momentum is conserved, but some kinetic energy is transferred to heat, sound and deformation.

quizzes.q: In an explosion from rest, the total momentum afterwards is
quizzes.e: Before the explosion the total momentum is zero, and momentum is conserved, so afterwards it is still zero: the pieces move off with equal and opposite momenta.

quizzes.q: For the collision shown, how much kinetic energy is lost?
quizzes.e: KE before = ½ × 2 × 3² = 9 J; KE after = ½ × 3 × 2² = 6 J. KE lost = 9 − 6 = 3 J, transferred to heat and sound.

quizzes.q: A 2.0 kg trolley at 3.0 m s⁻¹ collides with and sticks to a stationary 1.0 kg trolley. Find their speed after the collision in one dimension (m s⁻¹).
quizzes.e: Momentum is conserved in the interaction of bodies: 2.0 × 3.0 = 3.0 × v, so v = 2.0 m s⁻¹.

quizzes.q: A 0.17 kg ball hits a wall at 10 m/s and rebounds at 19 m/s, contact 0.1 s. Find the average force (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: The velocity reverses, so Δp = m(u + v) = 0.17 × (10 + 19) = 4.93 kg m s⁻¹. F = Δp ÷ t = 4.93 ÷ 0.1 = 49.3 N.

quizzes.q: A 0.16 kg ball hits a wall at 16 m/s and rebounds at 9 m/s, contact 0.05 s. Find the average force (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: The velocity reverses, so Δp = m(u + v) = 0.16 × (16 + 9) = 4 kg m s⁻¹. F = Δp ÷ t = 4 ÷ 0.05 = 80 N.

quizzes.q: A 0.37 kg ball hits a wall at 17 m/s and rebounds at 10 m/s, contact 0.05 s. Find the average force (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: The velocity reverses, so Δp = m(u + v) = 0.37 × (17 + 10) = 9.99 kg m s⁻¹. F = Δp ÷ t = 9.99 ÷ 0.05 = 200 N.

quizzes.q: A 0.07 kg ball hits a wall at 13 m/s and rebounds at 17 m/s, contact 0.03 s. Find the average force (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: The velocity reverses, so Δp = m(u + v) = 0.07 × (13 + 17) = 2.1 kg m s⁻¹. F = Δp ÷ t = 2.1 ÷ 0.03 = 70 N.

quizzes.q: A 7 kg gun fires a 0.047 kg bullet at 441 m/s. Recoil speed (3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: Total momentum is zero before and after: Mv_gun = mv_bullet, so v = 0.047 × 441 ÷ 7 = 2.96 m s⁻¹.

quizzes.q: A 4 kg gun fires a 0.048 kg bullet at 369 m/s. Recoil speed (3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: Total momentum is zero before and after: Mv_gun = mv_bullet, so v = 0.048 × 369 ÷ 4 = 4.43 m s⁻¹.

quizzes.q: A 7 kg gun fires a 0.04 kg bullet at 241 m/s. Recoil speed (3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: Total momentum is zero before and after: Mv_gun = mv_bullet, so v = 0.04 × 241 ÷ 7 = 1.38 m s⁻¹.

quizzes.q: A rocket accelerates in space because
quizzes.a: it pushes exhaust gas backward, which pushes it forward
quizzes.e: The rocket pushes the exhaust gases backwards, and by Newton's third law the gases push the rocket forwards. Momentum is conserved: the gas gains backward momentum and the rocket forward.

quizzes.q: A ball hits a wall and bounces back at the same speed. Why is its momentum change not zero?
quizzes.e: Momentum is a vector. Its direction reverses, so Δp = mv − (−mv) = 2mv, not zero.

quizzes.q: A 0.15 kg ball at 20 m/s is caught in 0.05 s. Find the average force.
A 1200 kg car at 15 m/s hits a stationary 800 kg car; they move together. Find their speed.
quizzes.e: Momentum before = 1200 × 15 = 18 000 kg m s⁻¹. After, (1200 + 800)v = 18 000, so v = 9 m s⁻¹.

quizzes.q: Newton's third law pairs act on
quizzes.a: different objects and are the same type of force
quizzes.e: A Newton's third law pair acts on two different objects, is of the same type, and is equal in size and opposite in direction (e.g. Earth pulls Moon, Moon pulls Earth).

quizzes.q: 3 kg at 7 m/s collides head-on with 5 kg moving at 2 m/s the other way; they stick. Find the KE lost (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Momentum: 3 × 7 − 5 × 2 = 8v, so v = 1.38 m s⁻¹. KE before = 83.5 J; after = 7.56 J. Lost = 75.9 J.

quizzes.q: 5 kg at 8 m/s collides head-on with 4 kg moving at 1 m/s the other way; they stick. Find the KE lost (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Momentum: 5 × 8 − 4 × 1 = 9v, so v = 4 m s⁻¹. KE before = 162 J; after = 72 J. Lost = 90 J.

quizzes.q: 4 kg at 6 m/s collides head-on with 5 kg moving at 4 m/s the other way; they stick. Find the KE lost (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Momentum: 4 × 6 − 5 × 4 = 9v, so v = 0.444 m s⁻¹. KE before = 112 J; after = 0.889 J. Lost = 111 J.

quizzes.q: 3 kg at 3 m/s collides head-on with 1 kg moving at 4 m/s the other way; they stick. Find the KE lost (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Momentum: 3 × 3 − 1 × 4 = 4v, so v = 1.25 m s⁻¹. KE before = 21.5 J; after = 3.12 J. Lost = 18.4 J.

quizzes.q: Water (ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³) leaves a hose of area 0.009 m² at 17 m/s and stops on a wall. Find the force (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Mass per second = ρAv = 1000 × 0.009 × 17 = 153 kg s⁻¹. F = rate of change of momentum = 153 × 17 = 2600 N.

quizzes.q: Water (ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³) leaves a hose of area 0.009 m² at 8 m/s and stops on a wall. Find the force (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Mass per second = ρAv = 1000 × 0.009 × 8 = 72 kg s⁻¹. F = rate of change of momentum = 72 × 8 = 576 N.

quizzes.q: Water (ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³) leaves a hose of area 0.005 m² at 11 m/s and stops on a wall. Find the force (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Mass per second = ρAv = 1000 × 0.005 × 11 = 55 kg s⁻¹. F = rate of change of momentum = 55 × 11 = 605 N.

quizzes.q: 2.0 A flows for 30 s. Charge?
How many electrons in 1.6 C (give × 10¹⁹)?
quizzes.e: Number of electrons = Q ÷ e = 1.6 ÷ 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1.0 × 10¹⁹.

quizzes.q: Kirchhoff's first law follows from conservation of
quizzes.e: Kirchhoff's first law (current in = current out at a junction) follows from conservation of charge.

quizzes.q: What are the charge carriers in an electrolyte?
quizzes.e: In an electrolyte the charge carriers are positive and negative ions. In metals they are free electrons.

quizzes.q: I = nAve, n = 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³, A = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m², I = 1.0 A. v (give × 10⁻⁵ m/s, 3 s.f.)?
Conventional current flows
quizzes.e: Conventional current flows from + to − around the circuit outside the cell. Electrons actually flow from − to +.

quizzes.q: The elementary charge is
quizzes.e: The elementary charge e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, the size of the charge on a proton or an electron.

quizzes.q: The coulomb, the unit of charge, is
quizzes.a: the charge passing a point when a current of 1 A flows for 1 s
quizzes.e: From Q = It, 1 C = 1 A s.

quizzes.q: 1.4 A for 206 s. Charge (3 s.f.)?
2.5 A for 151 s. Charge (3 s.f.)?
0.1 A for 454 s. Charge (3 s.f.)?
2.5 A for 535 s. Charge (3 s.f.)?
Charge is quantised, meaning it comes in
quizzes.e: Charge is quantised: any charge is a whole-number multiple of the elementary charge, Q = ±ne.

quizzes.q: Why are insulators poor conductors?
quizzes.e: Insulators have very few free (delocalised) charge carriers, so the number density n is tiny and almost no current flows.

quizzes.q: A semiconductor has a number density of charge carriers that
quizzes.a: is between that of metals and insulators
quizzes.e: A semiconductor's number density of charge carriers is much less than a metal's but more than an insulator's, and it increases with temperature.

quizzes.q: In I = nAve, if the wire narrows, the drift velocity
quizzes.e: I = nAve. With the same I and n, a smaller A means a larger drift velocity v.

quizzes.q: How many electrons pass a point per second for 3.0 A? (give × 10¹⁸, 3 s.f.)
quizzes.e: Each electron carries 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, so electrons per second = I ÷ e = 3.0 ÷ (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 1.88 × 10¹⁹.

quizzes.q: How many electrons pass a point per second for 2.6 A? (give × 10¹⁸, 3 s.f.)
quizzes.e: Each electron carries 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, so electrons per second = I ÷ e = 2.6 ÷ (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 1.63 × 10¹⁹.

quizzes.q: How many electrons pass a point per second for 1.4 A? (give × 10¹⁸, 3 s.f.)
quizzes.e: Each electron carries 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, so electrons per second = I ÷ e = 1.4 ÷ (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 8.75 × 10¹⁸.

quizzes.q: How many electrons pass a point per second for 4.9 A? (give × 10¹⁸, 3 s.f.)
quizzes.e: Each electron carries 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, so electrons per second = I ÷ e = 4.9 ÷ (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 3.06 × 10¹⁹.

quizzes.q: 138 C passes in 31 s. Current (3 s.f.)?
17 C passes in 7 s. Current (3 s.f.)?
167 C passes in 50 s. Current (3 s.f.)?
Drift velocity in a metal wire is typically
w: close to the speed of light
quizzes.e: Drift velocities are typically less than 1 mm s⁻¹ because the number density of free electrons in a metal is so large.

quizzes.q: Why does a lamp light almost instantly when switched on despite slow drift velocity?
quizzes.e: The wire is already full of free electrons. When the switch closes, the electric field travels round the circuit at nearly the speed of light, so electrons everywhere start drifting at once.

quizzes.q: A 0.5 mm² copper wire (n = 8.5 × 10²⁸) carries 2.0 A. Drift velocity (× 10⁻⁴ m/s, 3 s.f.).
In an electrolyte, current is due to
quizzes.a: positive and negative ions moving in opposite directions
quizzes.e: In an electrolyte the charge carriers are ions: positive ions move one way and negative ions the other, and both contribute to the current.

quizzes.q: Charge of 3.0 × 10⁴ C flows in 2 hours. Average current (3 s.f.)?
Wire diameter 1.0 mm, n = 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³, I = 0.5 A. Mean drift velocity (mm/s, 3 s.f.)?
Wire diameter 1.5 mm, n = 6.0 × 10²⁸ m⁻³, I = 2.6 A. Mean drift velocity (mm/s, 3 s.f.)?
Wire diameter 1.5 mm, n = 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³, I = 1.7 A. Mean drift velocity (mm/s, 3 s.f.)?
Wire diameter 1.0 mm, n = 6.0 × 10²⁸ m⁻³, I = 1.2 A. Mean drift velocity (mm/s, 3 s.f.)?
At a junction 0.8 A and 1.6 A flow in; one wire carries 0.3 A out. Find the current in the other outgoing wire.
quizzes.e: Kirchhoff’s first law: current in = current out. 0.8 + 1.6 = 0.3 + I, so I = 2.1 A.

quizzes.q: At a junction 1.9 A and 2.0 A flow in; one wire carries 0.3 A out. Find the current in the other outgoing wire.
quizzes.e: Kirchhoff’s first law: current in = current out. 1.9 + 2.0 = 0.3 + I, so I = 3.6 A.

quizzes.q: At a junction 0.7 A and 1.3 A flow in; one wire carries 0.3 A out. Find the current in the other outgoing wire.
quizzes.e: Kirchhoff’s first law: current in = current out. 0.7 + 1.3 = 0.3 + I, so I = 1.7 A.

quizzes.q: A 12 V supply drives 0.5 A. Power?
ρ = 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m, L = 2.0 m, A = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m². Resistance?
As current through a filament lamp increases, its resistance
quizzes.e: More current makes the filament hotter. The metal ions vibrate more, so electrons collide with them more often and the resistance increases.

quizzes.q: Define potential difference.
quizzes.e: Potential difference is the energy transferred from electrical to other forms per unit charge: V = W/Q, and 1 V = 1 J C⁻¹.

quizzes.q: As temperature rises, an NTC thermistor's resistance
quizzes.e: Heating the semiconductor releases more charge carriers (higher n), so the current increases and the resistance decreases.

quizzes.q: The ohm is
quizzes.e: R = V/I, so 1 Ω = 1 V A⁻¹.

quizzes.q: Match each circuit symbol description to its component.
pairs: rectangle with a diagonal arrow through it
rectangle with a bent line through it
quizzes.e: Circuit symbols are used to draw circuit diagrams, e.g. a diode's arrow shows the direction of conventional current it allows.

quizzes.q: In a circuit diagram using standard symbols, a voltmeter is drawn
quizzes.e: Ammeters go in series, voltmeters in parallel.

quizzes.q: Ohm's law states that, for a metallic conductor at constant temperature,
quizzes.a: the current is directly proportional to the potential difference
w: the power is proportional to the current
the current is inversely proportional to the p.d.
quizzes.e: Ohm's law holds only if physical conditions such as temperature stay constant, giving a straight line through the origin on an I–V graph.

quizzes.q: Power dissipated in 8 Ω with 6 V across it (3 s.f.)?
Power dissipated in 65 Ω with 7 V across it (3 s.f.)?
Power dissipated in 61 Ω with 14 V across it (3 s.f.)?
An ohmic conductor at constant temperature has an I–V graph that is
quizzes.a: a straight line through the origin
quizzes.e: An ohmic conductor obeys Ohm's law: at constant temperature I ∝ V, so the I–V graph is a straight line through the origin.

quizzes.q: A diode conducts when
quizzes.a: forward biased above its threshold pd
quizzes.e: A diode conducts (very low resistance) only when forward biased with a p.d. above its threshold, about 0.6 V for silicon. Reverse biased, it has very high resistance.

quizzes.q: Why does a filament lamp's resistance increase with current?
quizzes.e: A larger current heats the filament, so the metal ions vibrate more. Electrons collide with them more often, so the resistance increases.

quizzes.q: Resistivity depends on
quizzes.e: Resistivity is a property of the material and its temperature. Resistance also depends on the length and area (R = ρL/A), but resistivity does not.

quizzes.q: EMF differs from pd because emf is
quizzes.a: energy transferred to charge by the source per coulomb
w: energy transferred from charge to components
quizzes.e: E.m.f. is the energy transferred to each coulomb of charge by the source; p.d. is the energy transferred from each coulomb to a component.

quizzes.q: When investigating the electrical characteristics of a filament lamp, you should
quizzes.a: use a variable power supply or potential divider, measure V and I over a range including reversed polarity, and plot an I–V graph
w: measure one pair of readings only
quizzes.e: Techniques for investigating I–V characteristics use a potential divider to vary the p.d. from zero, with readings in both directions.

quizzes.q: Wire: ρ = 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m, L = 0.5 m, diameter 0.5 mm. Resistance (3 s.f.)?
Wire: ρ = 4.9 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m, L = 2.9 m, diameter 0.3 mm. Resistance (3 s.f.)?
Wire: ρ = 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m, L = 1.8 m, diameter 0.3 mm. Resistance (3 s.f.)?
Wire: ρ = 1.1 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m, L = 1.6 m, diameter 0.5 mm. Resistance (3 s.f.)?
A 1500 W appliance runs 4 h. At 24p per kWh, find the cost (p).
quizzes.e: Energy = 1.5 kW × 4 h = 6 kWh. Cost = 6 × 24 = 144p.

quizzes.q: A 800 W appliance runs 3 h. At 22p per kWh, find the cost (p).
quizzes.e: Energy = 0.8 kW × 3 h = 2.4 kWh. Cost = 2.4 × 22 = 52.8p.

quizzes.q: A 1500 W appliance runs 3 h. At 29p per kWh, find the cost (p).
quizzes.e: Energy = 1.5 kW × 3 h = 4.5 kWh. Cost = 4.5 × 29 = 130.5p.

quizzes.q: Superconductors have zero resistivity
quizzes.e: A superconductor has zero resistivity below its critical temperature, so a current can flow with no energy loss. They are used in MRI magnets and particle accelerators.

quizzes.q: Why does an NTC thermistor's resistance fall as temperature rises?
quizzes.e: In an NTC thermistor, heating releases more free charge carriers (n increases), so for the same p.d. the current is larger and the resistance falls.

quizzes.q: A 2.0 kW kettle on 230 V. Find the current (3 s.f.).
Energy transferred when 5.0 C passes through 12 V.
An LED emits light when
quizzes.e: When forward biased and conducting, electrons cross the junction and drop to a lower energy level, emitting photons.

quizzes.q: A 12 V, 40 W lamp is run at 6 V (assume constant R). Find its power (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: R = V² ÷ P = 12² ÷ 40 = 3.6 Ω. At the new pd, P = V² ÷ R = 10 W (halving V quarters P).

quizzes.q: A 230 V, 40 W lamp is run at 115 V (assume constant R). Find its power (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: R = V² ÷ P = 230² ÷ 40 = 1320 Ω. At the new pd, P = V² ÷ R = 10 W (halving V quarters P).

quizzes.q: A wire of resistance 8 Ω is stretched to twice its length (same volume). New resistance?
quizzes.e: Same volume, so doubling L halves A. R = ρL/A becomes ρ(2L)/(A/2) = 4R: 4 × 8 = 32 Ω.

quizzes.q: A wire of resistance 14 Ω is stretched to twice its length (same volume). New resistance?
quizzes.e: Same volume, so doubling L halves A. R = ρL/A becomes ρ(2L)/(A/2) = 4R: 4 × 14 = 56 Ω.

quizzes.q: Power dissipated in 39 Ω with 23 V across it (3 s.f.)?
6 Ω and 3 Ω in parallel. Total resistance?
quizzes.e: 1/R = 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/6 + 2/6 = 3/6, so R = 2 Ω. Parallel resistance is always less than the smallest resistor.

quizzes.q: 12 V across 2 kΩ and 4 kΩ in series. pd across 4 kΩ?
quizzes.e: The p.d. divides in the ratio of the resistances: V = 12 × 4 ÷ (2 + 4) = 8 V.

quizzes.q: EMF 9 V, internal resistance 1 Ω, external 2 Ω. Terminal pd?
quizzes.e: I = ε ÷ (R + r) = 9 ÷ (2 + 1) = 3 A. Terminal p.d. V = IR = 3 × 2 = 6 V (3 V are "lost" in the internal resistance).

quizzes.q: Kirchhoff's second law follows from conservation of
quizzes.e: Kirchhoff's second law (sum of e.m.f.s = sum of p.d.s around any loop) follows from conservation of energy.

quizzes.q: What are 'lost volts'?
quizzes.e: Lost volts are the energy per coulomb transferred in the internal resistance of the source: Ir = ε − V.

quizzes.q: In a series circuit the current is
quizzes.e: A series circuit has only one path, so the same current passes through every component.

quizzes.q: In parallel branches the pd is
quizzes.e: Each parallel branch connects across the same two points, so the p.d. across each branch is the same.

quizzes.q: In the parallel circuit, R₁ = R₂ = 10 Ω. What is the total resistance?
quizzes.e: For resistors in parallel, 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ = 1/10 + 1/10 = 1/5, so R = 5 Ω. Two equal resistors in parallel give half of one.

quizzes.q: 18 Ω, 6 Ω and 18 Ω in series. Total?
quizzes.e: In series R = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ = 18 + 6 + 18.

quizzes.q: 4 Ω, 11 Ω and 3 Ω in series. Total?
quizzes.e: In series R = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ = 4 + 11 + 3.

quizzes.q: 9 Ω, 16 Ω and 19 Ω in series. Total?
quizzes.e: In series R = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ = 9 + 16 + 19.

quizzes.q: Adding another resistor in parallel makes the total resistance
quizzes.e: Each extra parallel path lets more current flow for the same p.d., so the total resistance falls (1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + …).

quizzes.q: What does a potential divider do?
quizzes.e: A potential divider uses two (or more) resistors in series to split the supply p.d. into a chosen fraction: V_out = V_in × R₂ ÷ (R₁ + R₂).

quizzes.q: A voltmeter ideally has
quizzes.e: An ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance, so it draws no current and does not change the circuit it measures.

quizzes.q: An ammeter ideally has
quizzes.e: An ideal ammeter has zero resistance, so it does not reduce the current it measures.

quizzes.q: As load resistance falls, terminal pd of a real cell
quizzes.e: Lower load resistance means a larger current, so the lost volts Ir increase and the terminal p.d. (ε − Ir) falls.

quizzes.q: The light on the LDR gets brighter. What happens to V_out?

quizzes.q: The Sun will end its life as a
quizzes.e: The Sun is a low-mass star. After its red giant phase it will lose its outer layers and leave a white dwarf.

quizzes.e: Undeflected particles have equal electric and magnetic forces: EQ = BQv, so v = E/B. Q cancels, so any charge with that speed passes.

quizzes.e: A proton is uud: charge +⅔ + ⅔ − ⅓ = +1. A neutron is udd.

quizzes.e: 15 days is 3 half-lives, so the fraction left is (½)³ = 0.125.

quizzes.q: What did alpha scattering show?
quizzes.e: Most alpha particles went straight through, so the atom is mostly empty space. A few were deflected through large angles by a tiny, dense, positive nucleus.

quizzes.q: Match each particle to its class
quizzes.e: Protons are baryons (3 quarks), pions are mesons (quark–antiquark), electrons are leptons (fundamental) and photons are exchange (gauge) bosons.

quizzes.q: In β⁻ decay, a down quark becomes
quizzes.e: In β⁻ decay a down quark changes into an up quark, so a neutron becomes a proton: n → p + e⁻ + ν̄ₑ.

quizzes.q: An alpha particle is
quizzes.e: An alpha particle is a helium nucleus: 2 protons and 2 neutrons, with charge +2e.

quizzes.q: The most penetrating radiation is
quizzes.e: Gamma rays are the most penetrating; they are only reduced by several cm of lead. Alpha is stopped by paper and beta by a few mm of aluminium.

quizzes.q: Radioactive decay is described as spontaneous and random because
quizzes.a: it is not affected by external conditions, and it is impossible to predict which nucleus will decay next
w: every nucleus decays at the same time
it only happens when a detector is near
quizzes.e: Each nucleus has a constant probability λ of decaying per second; you can only predict the behaviour of a large number.

quizzes.q: Half-life 24 days. Fraction left after 48 days?
quizzes.e: 48 days = 2 half-lives, so the fraction left = (½)^2 = 0.25.

quizzes.q: Half-life 29 days. Fraction left after 116 days?
quizzes.e: 116 days = 4 half-lives, so the fraction left = (½)^4 = 0.0625.

quizzes.q: Half-life 4 days. Fraction left after 16 days?
quizzes.e: 16 days = 4 half-lives, so the fraction left = (½)^4 = 0.0625.

quizzes.q: The strong nuclear force is
quizzes.a: attractive up to ~3 fm and repulsive below ~0.5 fm
quizzes.e: The strong nuclear force acts between nucleons. It is attractive up to about 3 fm and repulsive below about 0.5 fm, which stops the nucleus collapsing.

quizzes.q: What is meant by isotopes?
quizzes.e: Isotopes of an element have the same number of protons (proton number) but different numbers of neutrons (nucleon number).

quizzes.q: In β⁺ decay a proton becomes
quizzes.a: a neutron, a positron and a neutrino
quizzes.e: In β⁺ decay a proton changes into a neutron, emitting a positron and an electron neutrino: p → n + e⁺ + νₑ (an up quark becomes a down quark).

quizzes.q: Nuclear fission releases energy because
quizzes.a: products have higher binding energy per nucleon
quizzes.e: Fission products have a higher binding energy per nucleon than the heavy nucleus, so the total mass falls and the mass defect is released as energy (E = mc²).

quizzes.q: Which particle is a baryon?
quizzes.e: A baryon is made of three quarks. The neutron (udd) is a baryon; the pion is a meson; electrons and neutrinos are leptons.

quizzes.a: a down quark (−⅓e) becomes an up quark (+⅔e)
w: an up quark (+⅔e) becomes a down quark (−⅓e)
a strange quark (−⅓e) becomes an up quark
quizzes.e: In beta-plus (β⁺) decay the opposite happens: an up quark becomes a down quark, and a positron and neutrino are emitted. Charge is conserved in both.

quizzes.q: In the absorption experiment, the count rate from a source drops to background with a few mm of aluminium but not with paper. The source emits
quizzes.e: Alpha is stopped by paper, beta by a few millimetres of aluminium, and gamma is only reduced by thick lead.

quizzes.e: N = 8.0 × 10¹⁰ × e^(−1.0) = 2.94 × 10¹⁰, which is 2.9 × 10¹⁰ to 2 s.f. The activity A = λN follows the same exponential decay.

quizzes.q: In a simulation of radioactive decay using dice, 600 dice are thrown and every six is removed. On average, the fraction removed each throw is
quizzes.a: 1/6, like the decay constant per unit time
quizzes.e: Each die has the same chance of "decaying" each throw, so the number left falls exponentially, modelling N = N₀e^(−λt).

quizzes.q: In a spreadsheet model of radioactive decay with a time step Δt, each new row calculates
quizzes.e: The graphical and spreadsheet modelling of ΔN/Δt = −λN uses small iterative steps; smaller Δt gives a closer match to the exponential.

quizzes.q: In radioactive dating (carbon-dating), a sample has 25% of the original carbon-14 activity. The half-life of carbon-14 is 5700 years. How old is it, in years?
quizzes.e: 25% = (½)², so two half-lives have passed: 2 × 5700 = 11 400 years.

quizzes.q: A gamma photon produces an electron and a positron near a nucleus. This is an example of
quizzes.a: pair production (creation of a particle–antiparticle pair)
quizzes.e: In pair production energy becomes mass; in annihilation, a particle and its antiparticle meet and their mass becomes two photons.

quizzes.q: Describe one environmental impact of nuclear waste.
quizzes.e: High-level waste stays radioactive for thousands of years, so it must be stored safely and securely; leaks could contaminate the environment and harm living things.

quizzes.e: Control rods (e.g. boron) absorb neutrons, so moving them in or out controls the rate of fission and keeps the chain reaction steady.

quizzes.e: Air reflects almost all ultrasound because its acoustic impedance is very different from skin. The gel removes the air and has an impedance similar to skin, so most ultrasound enters the body.

quizzes.q: PET scanners detect
quizzes.a: pairs of gamma photons from annihilation
quizzes.e: A positron from the tracer annihilates with an electron, producing two gamma photons that travel in opposite directions. Detecting both locates the source.

quizzes.q: Technetium-99m is a good tracer because it
quizzes.a: emits only gamma and has a ~6 h half-life
quizzes.e: Tc-99m emits only gamma rays (which escape the body and are easy to detect) and has a half-life of about 6 hours: long enough for the scan, short enough to keep the dose low.

quizzes.q: X-rays are produced when

quizzes.e: In an X-ray tube, electrons accelerated through a high p.d. hit a metal target (tungsten) and decelerate rapidly, emitting X-ray photons.

quizzes.e: Pair production makes an electron and a positron, each of rest energy 0.51 MeV, so the photon needs at least 2 × 0.51 = 1.02 MeV.

quizzes.q: What is a CAT scan?
quizzes.e: In a CAT scan, a thin fan-shaped X-ray beam from a rotating tube passes through the patient to a ring of detectors. A computer builds a 3D image from many slices.

quizzes.q: A gamma camera uses a collimator to
quizzes.a: only allow gamma rays parallel to the tubes through
quizzes.e: The collimator is a lead plate with long parallel holes. Only gamma rays travelling along the tubes reach the crystal, which gives a sharp image.

quizzes.q: The piezoelectric effect is used in ultrasound to
quizzes.e: An alternating p.d. makes a piezoelectric crystal vibrate, producing ultrasound; returning ultrasound makes the crystal vibrate and produce a p.d., so it also detects it.

quizzes.q: Doppler ultrasound measures
quizzes.e: Doppler ultrasound measures the frequency shift of ultrasound reflected from moving blood cells, giving the speed of blood flow.

quizzes.q: Half-value thickness for μ = 0.22 cm⁻¹ (cm, 3 s.f.)?

The Compton effect involves
quizzes.a: a photon scattering off an electron, losing energy
quizzes.e: In the Compton effect (about 0.5–5 MeV) an X-ray photon scatters off an electron, giving it some energy, so the scattered photon has a longer wavelength.

quizzes.q: Why does PET need a cyclotron nearby?
quizzes.e: PET tracers such as fluorine-18 have short half-lives (about 110 minutes), so they must be made in a nearby cyclotron and used quickly.

quizzes.e: Fe is [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s². When it forms an ion the 4s electrons are lost first, so Fe²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁶, i.e. 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁶.

quizzes.q: Why does first ionisation energy decrease down a group?
quizzes.e: More shielding and larger radius, so weaker attraction to the outer electron.

quizzes.q: Order the stages of time-of-flight mass spectrometry
quizzes.e: Ions are made (electrospray or electron impact), accelerated by an electric field to the same kinetic energy, drift through the flight tube (lighter ions faster), then hit the detector.

quizzes.q: Why is first IE lower for Al than Mg?
quizzes.a: Al's outer electron is in a higher-energy 3p sub-level
quizzes.e: Al's outer electron is in the 3p sub-level, which is higher in energy than 3s and partly shielded by the 3s electrons, so it is easier to remove despite the extra proton.

quizzes.q: How many neutrons in ^32S?
quizzes.e: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 32 − 16 = 16.

quizzes.q: How many neutrons in ^80Br?

quizzes.q: How many neutrons in ^64Cu?

quizzes.q: How many electrons in a Al3+ ion?
quizzes.e: Al has 13 protons, so 13 electrons as an atom. A charge of +3 means losing 3: 13 − (+3) = 10.

quizzes.q: How many electrons in a K+ ion?
quizzes.e: K has 19 protons, so 19 electrons as an atom. A charge of +1 means losing 1: 19 − (+1) = 18.

quizzes.q: How many electrons in a Br− ion?
quizzes.e: Br has 35 protons, so 35 electrons as an atom. A charge of −1 means gaining 1: 35 − (−1) = 36.

quizzes.q: In TOF mass spectrometry, ions are formed by electrospray by
quizzes.e: In electrospray ionisation the sample is dissolved in a volatile solvent and sprayed through a charged needle; each molecule gains a proton, giving MH⁺ ions.

quizzes.q: In electron impact ionisation, the sample
quizzes.a: is bombarded with high-energy electrons, knocking out an electron
quizzes.e: Electron impact: high-energy electrons from an electron gun knock an electron off each atom or molecule, giving X⁺ ions (used for low-Mr samples).

quizzes.q: What causes the peak at m/z = 72?
quizzes.e: Chlorine has isotopes ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl. Cl₂⁺ peaks appear at 70 (³⁵Cl³⁵Cl), 72 (³⁵Cl³⁷Cl) and 74 (³⁷Cl³⁷Cl). 35 + 37 = 72.

quizzes.q: Rutherford's gold-foil experiment changed the model of the atom because a few alpha particles were deflected through large angles. This showed that
quizzes.a: the atom has a tiny, dense, positive nucleus
w: electrons sit in fixed energy levels
the atom is a positive sphere with electrons embedded in it
quizzes.e: Most of the atom is empty space, but the mass and positive charge are concentrated in a tiny nucleus. This replaced the "plum pudding" model.

quizzes.q: Put these models of the atom in the order they were proposed, earliest first.
quizzes.e: Each model replaced the last when new experimental evidence (the electron, alpha scattering, line spectra) could not be explained by the old one.

quizzes.q: Why is the second IE of an element always larger than the first?
quizzes.e: After the first electron is lost, the next is removed from a positive ion. The same number of protons attracts fewer electrons, so they are held more strongly.

quizzes.q: First IE of oxygen is lower than nitrogen because
quizzes.a: O's 2p has a paired electron, which repels
quizzes.e: N is 2p³ with one electron in each 2p orbital. O is 2p⁴, so one 2p orbital holds a pair; the repulsion between the paired electrons makes one easier to remove.

quizzes.q: TOF mass spec: ions of m/z 24 (charge +1) have KE 4.5 × 10⁻¹⁶ J and drift 1.5 m. Time of flight (µs, 3 s.f.)?

quizzes.q: TOF mass spec: ions of m/z 24 (charge +1) have KE 1.9 × 10⁻¹⁶ J and drift 1.0 m. Time of flight (µs, 3 s.f.)?

quizzes.e: A standard solution has an accurately known concentration. It is made by dissolving a known mass of solid and making it up to the mark in a volumetric flask.

quizzes.e: Balance C first (3CO₂), then H (4H₂O), then O: 6 + 4 = 10 O atoms, so 5O₂.

quizzes.e: pV = nRT uses SI units: p in Pa, V in m³ and T in K. Convert dm³ to m³ by dividing by 1000 (and cm³ by 10⁶).

quizzes.q: Why might the actual yield be less than the theoretical yield?
quizzes.e: The reaction may be incomplete or reversible, side reactions may form other products, and some product is lost during separation and purification.
