quizzes.q: Shape of NH₃
quizzes.e: N has 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair. The lone pair repels more strongly, giving a trigonal pyramidal shape (about 107°).

quizzes.q: Bond angle in H₂O?
quizzes.e: Four electron pairs give a tetrahedral basis of 109.5°. Each of the two lone pairs reduces the angle by about 2.5°, giving 104.5°.

quizzes.q: Match each molecule to its shape
quizzes.e: Count the electron pairs around the central atom: 4 bonding (tetrahedral), 3 (trigonal planar), 2 double bonds (linear), 6 (octahedral). None have lone pairs.

quizzes.q: Which has a giant covalent structure?
quizzes.e: SiO₂ is macromolecular: each Si is covalently bonded to 4 O atoms in a giant lattice. CO₂ and I₂ are simple molecules; NaCl is ionic.

quizzes.q: Strongest intermolecular force between H₂O molecules?
quizzes.e: Water has O–H bonds and lone pairs on O, so hydrogen bonds form between molecules. These are stronger than the other intermolecular forces.

quizzes.q: Ionic bonding is
quizzes.a: electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions
quizzes.e: Ionic bonding is the strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions in a lattice, e.g. Na⁺ and Cl⁻ in NaCl.

quizzes.q: A dative covalent bond forms when
quizzes.a: one atom provides both electrons of the shared pair
quizzes.e: In a dative (co-ordinate) bond one atom donates both electrons of the shared pair, e.g. NH₃ donates its lone pair to H⁺ to form NH₄⁺.

quizzes.q: Electronegativity is
quizzes.a: the power of an atom to attract the pair of electrons in a covalent bond
quizzes.e: Electronegativity is the power of an atom to attract the pair of electrons in a covalent bond. It increases across a period and up a group; fluorine is the highest.

quizzes.q: Using its position in the Periodic Table, predict the charge on an ion of sulfur (Group 16).
quizzes.e: Sulfur has 6 outer electrons and gains 2 to fill its outer shell, so it forms S²⁻. Group 16 elements form 2− ions.

quizzes.q: Shape of H₂O?
quizzes.e: Count the electron pairs around the central atom (bonding and lone pairs). They repel to get as far apart as possible, which sets the shape.

quizzes.q: Shape of NH₄⁺?
quizzes.e: Count the electron pairs around the central atom (bonding and lone pairs). They repel to get as far apart as possible, which sets the shape.

quizzes.q: Shape of PH₃?
quizzes.e: Count the electron pairs around the central atom (bonding and lone pairs). They repel to get as far apart as possible, which sets the shape.

quizzes.q: Shape of CH₄?
quizzes.e: Count the electron pairs around the central atom (bonding and lone pairs). They repel to get as far apart as possible, which sets the shape.

quizzes.q: Why does graphite conduct electricity?
quizzes.e: Each carbon bonds covalently to 3 others in flat layers. The fourth outer electron from each carbon is delocalised between the layers and can move, carrying charge.

quizzes.q: Diamond has a high melting point because
quizzes.a: many strong covalent bonds must be broken
w: it has van der Waals forces
quizzes.e: Diamond is giant covalent: every carbon is bonded to four others, so many strong covalent bonds must be broken to melt it.

quizzes.q: Ice is less dense than water because
quizzes.a: hydrogen bonds hold molecules in an open lattice
quizzes.e: In ice each H₂O forms hydrogen bonds to four others in an open tetrahedral lattice, so the molecules are further apart than in liquid water.

quizzes.q: A molecule with polar bonds can be non-polar if
quizzes.a: it is symmetrical so the dipoles cancel
quizzes.e: If the molecule is symmetrical, the bond dipoles act in opposite directions and cancel, e.g. linear CO₂ and tetrahedral CCl₄ are non-polar.

quizzes.q: NH₄⁺ has 4 bonding pairs and no lone pairs. Using the diagram, what is its bond angle?
quizzes.e: Four bonding pairs, no lone pairs: tetrahedral like CH₄, 109.5°.

quizzes.q: Magnesium has a high melting point because it has
quizzes.a: a giant metallic lattice of Mg²⁺ ions and delocalised electrons
w: simple molecules held by van der Waals forces
an ionic lattice of Mg²⁺ and Mg²⁻ ions
quizzes.e: Strong electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons needs a lot of energy to overcome. Mg gives two electrons per atom to the sea.

quizzes.q: Shape of PCl₅?
quizzes.e: Count the bonding and lone pairs around the central atom. Electron pairs repel as far apart as possible, and lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs.

quizzes.q: Shape of SiCl₄?
quizzes.e: Count the bonding and lone pairs around the central atom. Electron pairs repel as far apart as possible, and lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs.

quizzes.q: Shape of BF₃?
quizzes.e: Count the bonding and lone pairs around the central atom. Electron pairs repel as far apart as possible, and lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs.

quizzes.q: Shape of XeF₄?
quizzes.e: Count the bonding and lone pairs around the central atom. Electron pairs repel as far apart as possible, and lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs.

quizzes.q: Why does the boiling point of the alkanes increase with chain length?
quizzes.e: Longer chains have more electrons and a larger surface area of contact, so the induced dipole–dipole (van der Waals) forces are stronger and need more energy to overcome.

quizzes.q: H₂O has a higher boiling point than H₂S because
quizzes.e: O is much more electronegative than S, so H₂O forms hydrogen bonds between molecules. H₂S has only weaker permanent dipole and van der Waals forces.

quizzes.q: Metals are malleable because
quizzes.a: layers of positive ions can slide over each other
quizzes.e: In a metal the layers of positive ions can slide over each other while the delocalised electrons still hold them together, so the metal is malleable.

quizzes.q: Ionic compounds conduct when molten because
quizzes.e: When molten (or dissolved) the ions are free to move and carry charge. In the solid the ions are fixed in the lattice, so it does not conduct.

quizzes.q: Bond angle in BF₃?
quizzes.e: Start from the shape set by the total number of electron pairs. Each lone pair repels more strongly and reduces the bond angle by about 2.5°.

quizzes.q: Bond angle in BeCl₂?
quizzes.e: Start from the shape set by the total number of electron pairs. Each lone pair repels more strongly and reduces the bond angle by about 2.5°.

quizzes.q: Bond angle in AlCl₄⁻?
quizzes.e: Start from the shape set by the total number of electron pairs. Each lone pair repels more strongly and reduces the bond angle by about 2.5°.

quizzes.q: Bond angle in NH₃?
quizzes.e: Start from the shape set by the total number of electron pairs. Each lone pair repels more strongly and reduces the bond angle by about 2.5°.

quizzes.q: Bond angle in SiCl₄?
quizzes.e: Start from the shape set by the total number of electron pairs. Each lone pair repels more strongly and reduces the bond angle by about 2.5°.

quizzes.q: Bond angle in CH₄?
quizzes.e: Start from the shape set by the total number of electron pairs. Each lone pair repels more strongly and reduces the bond angle by about 2.5°.

quizzes.q: q = mcΔT for 50 g water, ΔT = 6.0 K, c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹?
quizzes.e: q = mcΔT = 50 × 4.18 × 6.0 = 1254 J (1.25 kJ). Use the mass of the water, not the reactants.

quizzes.q: Standard enthalpy of formation forms
quizzes.a: 1 mol of a compound from its elements in standard states
quizzes.e: ΔfH° is the enthalpy change when 1 mol of a compound forms from its elements in their standard states under standard conditions (100 kPa and a stated temperature, usually 298 K).

quizzes.q: Why are mean bond enthalpies less accurate?
quizzes.e: Mean bond enthalpies are averages of the same bond over many different compounds, so they are not exact for the bond in any particular molecule.

quizzes.q: ΔfH: CO₂ −394, H₂O(l) −286, CH₄ −75 kJ mol⁻¹. ΔcH of CH₄?
quizzes.e: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. ΔcH = ΣΔfH(products) − ΣΔfH(reactants) = (−394 + 2 × −286) − (−75) = −891 kJ mol⁻¹. O₂ has ΔfH = 0.

quizzes.q: An exothermic reaction has ΔH that is
quizzes.e: In an exothermic reaction energy is released to the surroundings, so the products have less enthalpy than the reactants and ΔH is negative.

quizzes.q: Standard conditions are
quizzes.a: 100 kPa and a stated temperature (usually 298 K)
quizzes.e: Standard conditions are 100 kPa and a stated temperature, usually 298 K, with solutions at 1 mol dm⁻³ and substances in their standard states.

quizzes.q: Define enthalpy change of combustion.
quizzes.e: ΔcH° is the enthalpy change when 1 mole of a substance is completely burned in oxygen, with all reactants and products in their standard states under standard conditions.

quizzes.q: 40 g of water rises by 3.7 K (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹). Find q in J (3 s.f.).
73 g of water rises by 12.3 K (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹). Find q in J (3 s.f.).
30 g of water rises by 6.9 K (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹). Find q in J (3 s.f.).
Hess's law states that the enthalpy change
quizzes.a: is independent of the route taken
quizzes.e: Hess's law: the enthalpy change for a reaction is independent of the route taken, as long as the start and end conditions are the same (conservation of energy).

quizzes.q: Give one reason why calorimetry values are less exothermic than data-book values.
quizzes.e: Heat is lost to the surroundings (and the apparatus), combustion may be incomplete, and some fuel may evaporate, so the measured temperature rise is too small.

quizzes.q: Bond breaking is
quizzes.e: Breaking a bond needs energy to overcome the attraction between the atoms, so it is endothermic. Making bonds releases energy (exothermic).

quizzes.q: Burning 0.082 mol of fuel heats 94 g of water by 6.9 K (c = 4.18). Find ΔcH (kJ mol⁻¹, 3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: q = mcΔT = 94 × 4.18 × 6.9 = 2711 J = 2.71 kJ. ΔcH = −q ÷ n = −2.71 ÷ 0.082 = −33.1 kJ mol⁻¹ (negative because heat is released).

quizzes.q: Burning 0.066 mol of fuel heats 80 g of water by 2.7 K (c = 4.18). Find ΔcH (kJ mol⁻¹, 3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: q = mcΔT = 80 × 4.18 × 2.7 = 903 J = 0.903 kJ. ΔcH = −q ÷ n = −0.903 ÷ 0.066 = −13.7 kJ mol⁻¹ (negative because heat is released).

quizzes.q: Burning 0.072 mol of fuel heats 65 g of water by 7.5 K (c = 4.18). Find ΔcH (kJ mol⁻¹, 3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: q = mcΔT = 65 × 4.18 × 7.5 = 2038 J = 2.04 kJ. ΔcH = −q ÷ n = −2.04 ÷ 0.072 = −28.3 kJ mol⁻¹ (negative because heat is released).

quizzes.q: Burning 0.03 mol of fuel heats 83 g of water by 2.2 K (c = 4.18). Find ΔcH (kJ mol⁻¹, 3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: q = mcΔT = 83 × 4.18 × 2.2 = 763 J = 0.763 kJ. ΔcH = −q ÷ n = −0.763 ÷ 0.03 = −25.4 kJ mol⁻¹ (negative because heat is released).

quizzes.q: 25 cm³ of 2.0 mol dm⁻³ HCl + 25 cm³ of 2.0 mol dm⁻³ NaOH; ΔT = 11.0 K. Find ΔneutH (kJ mol⁻¹, 3 s.f.). Assume total mass 50 g, c = 4.18.
50 cm³ of 1.0 mol dm⁻³ HCl + 50 cm³ of 1.0 mol dm⁻³ NaOH; ΔT = 4.3 K. Find ΔneutH (kJ mol⁻¹, 3 s.f.). Assume total mass 100 g, c = 4.18.
50 cm³ of 1.0 mol dm⁻³ HCl + 50 cm³ of 1.0 mol dm⁻³ NaOH; ΔT = 6.7 K. Find ΔneutH (kJ mol⁻¹, 3 s.f.). Assume total mass 100 g, c = 4.18.
Why extrapolate a temperature–time graph back to the time of mixing?
quizzes.a: To correct for heat loss and find the maximum temperature change
quizzes.e: The mixture loses heat while the reaction happens. Extrapolating the cooling line back to the time of mixing gives the temperature change there would have been with no heat loss.

quizzes.q: ΔcH(C) = −394, ΔcH(H₂) = −286, ΔcH(CH₄) = −890 kJ mol⁻¹. ΔfH(CH₄) is
quizzes.e: C + 2H₂ → CH₄. Using combustion data: ΔfH = ΣΔcH(reactants) − ΔcH(product) = (−394 + 2 × −286) − (−890) = −76 kJ mol⁻¹.

quizzes.q: Use mean bond enthalpies (C–H 413, O=O 498, C=O 805, O–H 464 kJ mol⁻¹) to find ΔH for CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O.
quizzes.e: ΔH = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds made) = 2648 − 3466 = −818 kJ mol⁻¹.

quizzes.q: Use mean bond enthalpies (H–H 436, Cl–Cl 243, H–Cl 432 kJ mol⁻¹) to find ΔH for H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl.
quizzes.e: ΔH = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds made) = 679 − 864 = −185 kJ mol⁻¹.

quizzes.q: Use mean bond enthalpies (C=C 612, H–H 436, C–H 413, C–C 347 kJ mol⁻¹) to find ΔH for C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆.
quizzes.e: ΔH = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds made) = 2700 − 2825 = −125 kJ mol⁻¹.

quizzes.q: Use mean bond enthalpies (N≡N 945, H–H 436, N–H 391 kJ mol⁻¹) to find ΔH for N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃.
quizzes.e: ΔH = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds made) = 2253 − 2346 = −93 kJ mol⁻¹.

quizzes.q: Use mean bond enthalpies (C–H 413, Cl–Cl 243, C–Cl 346, H–Cl 432 kJ mol⁻¹) to find ΔH for CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl.
quizzes.e: ΔH = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds made) = 1895 − 2017 = −122 kJ mol⁻¹.

quizzes.q: Use mean bond enthalpies (H–H 436, O=O 498, O–H 464 kJ mol⁻¹) to find ΔH for 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.
quizzes.e: ΔH = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds made) = 1370 − 1856 = −486 kJ mol⁻¹.

quizzes.q: ΔfH values (C₂H₆(g) -85, CO₂(g) -394, H₂O(l) -286 kJ mol⁻¹; elements = 0). Find ΔH for C₂H₆ + 3½O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O.
quizzes.e: ΔH = ΣΔfH(products) − ΣΔfH(reactants) = (−1646) − (−85) = −1561 kJ mol⁻¹. O₂ is an element, so its ΔfH is 0.

quizzes.q: ΔfH values (C₂H₅OH(l) -277, CO₂(g) -394, H₂O(l) -286 kJ mol⁻¹; elements = 0). Find ΔH for C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O.
quizzes.e: ΔH = ΣΔfH(products) − ΣΔfH(reactants) = (−1646) − (−277) = −1369 kJ mol⁻¹. O₂ is an element, so its ΔfH is 0.

quizzes.q: ΔfH values (C₃H₈(g) -104, CO₂(g) -394, H₂O(l) -286 kJ mol⁻¹; elements = 0). Find ΔH for C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O.
quizzes.e: ΔH = ΣΔfH(products) − ΣΔfH(reactants) = (−2326) − (−104) = −2222 kJ mol⁻¹. O₂ is an element, so its ΔfH is 0.

quizzes.q: ΔfH values (CaCO₃(s) -1207, CaO(s) -635, CO₂(g) -394 kJ mol⁻¹; elements = 0). Find ΔH for CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂.
quizzes.e: ΔH = ΣΔfH(products) − ΣΔfH(reactants) = (−1029) − (−1207) = 178 kJ mol⁻¹. O₂ is an element, so its ΔfH is 0.

quizzes.q: A catalyst increases rate by
quizzes.a: providing a route with lower activation energy
quizzes.e: A catalyst provides an alternative route with a lower activation energy, so a larger fraction of collisions have energy ≥ Ea. It is not used up.

quizzes.q: Why does a small temperature rise greatly increase rate?
quizzes.e: A small temperature rise shifts the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution, so many more particles have energy at least Ea. This effect is much bigger than the small rise in collision frequency.

quizzes.q: At higher temperature, the Maxwell–Boltzmann peak
quizzes.e: At a higher temperature more molecules have high energies. The peak moves to the right and gets lower, but the area under the curve (the number of molecules) stays the same.

quizzes.q: The area under a Maxwell–Boltzmann curve is
quizzes.e: The area under the curve is the total number of molecules. It stays constant when temperature changes, as long as no molecules are added.

quizzes.q: Order the effect of increasing concentration
quizzes.e: At higher concentration there are more particles in the same volume, so collisions are more frequent. The same fraction have energy ≥ Ea, so there are more successful collisions per second.

quizzes.q: For a reaction to occur, particles must collide with
quizzes.a: energy at least Ea and correct orientation
quizzes.e: Collision theory: particles must collide with at least the activation energy and with the correct orientation for the bonds to break.

quizzes.q: Activation energy is
quizzes.a: the minimum energy needed for a reaction to occur
quizzes.e: Activation energy Eₐ is the minimum energy colliding particles need to react.

quizzes.q: State one way to increase the rate of a reaction.
quizzes.e: Raising the temperature, concentration (or gas pressure) or surface area, or adding a catalyst, all increase the number of successful collisions per second.

quizzes.q: 20 cm³ of gas is collected in 70 s. Mean rate (cm³ s⁻¹, 3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: Mean rate = volume of gas ÷ time = 20 ÷ 70 = 0.286 cm³ s⁻¹.

quizzes.q: 38 cm³ of gas is collected in 40 s. Mean rate (cm³ s⁻¹, 3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: Mean rate = volume of gas ÷ time = 38 ÷ 40 = 0.95 cm³ s⁻¹.

quizzes.q: Increasing surface area increases rate because
quizzes.a: more particles are exposed so collisions are more frequent
quizzes.e: Breaking a solid into smaller pieces exposes more particles at the surface, so collisions with the other reactant are more frequent.

quizzes.q: The rate of reaction is
quizzes.a: the change in concentration per unit time
quizzes.e: The rate of reaction is the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time, measured in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.

quizzes.q: The most probable energy on a Maxwell–Boltzmann curve is
quizzes.e: The peak (mode) of the curve is the most probable energy; the mean is slightly to its right.

quizzes.q: A Maxwell–Boltzmann curve does not touch the energy axis at high energy because
quizzes.e: There is no maximum energy: a few molecules always have very high energy, so the curve approaches the axis but never reaches it.

quizzes.q: How does a catalyst affect the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution?
quizzes.e: The Maxwell–Boltzmann curve itself is unchanged, but the catalyst lowers Ea, so a larger fraction of the particles (area under the curve) has energy ≥ Ea.

quizzes.q: A heterogeneous catalyst is
quizzes.a: in a different phase from the reactants
quizzes.e: A heterogeneous catalyst is in a different phase from the reactants, e.g. solid iron in the Haber process with gaseous N₂ and H₂.

quizzes.q: Increasing gas pressure increases rate because
quizzes.a: particles are closer, so collisions are more frequent
quizzes.e: Higher pressure puts the same number of gas particles into a smaller volume (higher concentration), so collisions are more frequent.

quizzes.q: How does the distribution change at the higher temperature T₂?
quizzes.a: The peak moves to higher energy and becomes lower
w: The peak moves to lower energy and becomes higher
The area under the curve increases
quizzes.e: The number of molecules is unchanged, so the area stays the same.

quizzes.q: [A] falls from 1.85 to 0.67 mol dm⁻³ in 87 s. Mean rate (× 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹, 3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: Mean rate = change in concentration ÷ time = (1.85 − 0.67) ÷ 87 = 0.0136 mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ = 13.6 × 10⁻³.

quizzes.q: [A] falls from 1.54 to 1.12 mol dm⁻³ in 189 s. Mean rate (× 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹, 3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: Mean rate = change in concentration ÷ time = (1.54 − 1.12) ÷ 189 = 0.00222 mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ = 2.22 × 10⁻³.

quizzes.q: [A] falls from 1.3 to 0.82 mol dm⁻³ in 116 s. Mean rate (× 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹, 3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: Mean rate = change in concentration ÷ time = (1.3 − 0.82) ÷ 116 = 0.00414 mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ = 4.14 × 10⁻³.

quizzes.q: The rate at a particular time can be found from
quizzes.a: the gradient of a tangent to the concentration–time curve
quizzes.e: The instantaneous rate at any time is the gradient of a tangent drawn to the concentration–time curve at that time.

quizzes.q: Why is rate often measured using 1/time for a fixed amount of change?
quizzes.e: For a fixed amount of reaction (e.g. a set amount of precipitate), rate ∝ 1/time, so 1/t can be used as a measure of the rate.

quizzes.q: A 10 °C rise roughly doubles rate mainly because
quizzes.a: the proportion of particles with energy ≥ Ea roughly doubles
quizzes.e: The fraction of collisions with energy ≥ Ea roughly doubles for a 10 °C rise. The collision frequency rises only by a few per cent.

quizzes.q: Which method follows a reaction producing CO₂ from marble chips?
quizzes.a: measure gas volume or loss of mass over time
quizzes.e: Collect the CO₂ in a gas syringe or measure the loss of mass on a balance at regular intervals (a continuous monitoring method).

quizzes.q: A catalyst is not used up because
quizzes.a: it is regenerated at the end of the reaction
quizzes.e: A catalyst takes part in the reaction (e.g. by forming an intermediate) but is regenerated at the end, so it is not used up.

quizzes.q: Explain why the iodine clock reaction gives a sudden colour change.
quizzes.e: Iodine reacts with thiosulfate until it is used up; then iodine builds up and turns starch blue-black.

quizzes.q: Enzymes lose activity at high temperature because
quizzes.e: Enzymes are proteins. High temperatures break the bonds holding their tertiary structure, so the active site changes shape (denatures) and the substrate no longer fits.

quizzes.q: Which change does NOT increase collision frequency?
quizzes.e: A catalyst does not change how often particles collide; it lowers Ea instead, so more of the collisions are successful.

quizzes.q: 69 cm³ of gas is collected in 15 s. Mean rate (cm³ s⁻¹, 3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: Mean rate = volume of gas ÷ time = 69 ÷ 15 = 4.6 cm³ s⁻¹.

quizzes.q: [A] falls from 1.6 to 0.91 mol dm⁻³ in 164 s. Mean rate (× 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹, 3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: Mean rate = change in concentration ÷ time = (1.6 − 0.91) ÷ 164 = 0.00421 mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ = 4.21 × 10⁻³.

topics.title: 3.1.6 Chemical equilibria, Le Chatelier’s principle and Kc

quizzes.q: Raising pressure on N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ shifts equilibrium
quizzes.e: There are 4 mol of gas on the left and 2 mol on the right. Le Chatelier: increasing pressure moves the equilibrium to the side with fewer gas moles, i.e. to the right.

quizzes.q: A catalyst
quizzes.a: speeds up reaching equilibrium without moving it
quizzes.e: A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster but its position and Kc do not change.
Kc = [HI]² ÷ ([H₂][I₂]) = 0.8² ÷ (0.1 × 0.1) = 0.64 ÷ 0.01 = 64. There are no units because the powers cancel.

quizzes.q: What is the only factor that changes Kc?
quizzes.e: Kc changes only with temperature. Changing concentration or pressure moves the position of equilibrium but Kc stays the same; a catalyst has no effect.

quizzes.q: Define dynamic equilibrium.
quizzes.e: In a dynamic equilibrium (in a closed system) the forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate, so the concentrations of reactants and products stay constant.

quizzes.q: Le Chatelier's principle: a system at equilibrium responds to a change by
quizzes.e: Le Chatelier's principle: if a factor affecting an equilibrium changes, the position of equilibrium shifts to oppose the change.

quizzes.q: Raising temperature for an exothermic forward reaction shifts equilibrium
quizzes.e: Raising the temperature favours the endothermic direction to absorb the heat. If the forward reaction is exothermic, the equilibrium moves left.

quizzes.q: At dynamic equilibrium, the concentrations of reactants and products
quizzes.e: At dynamic equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal, so the concentrations stay constant (but they are not usually equal to each other).

quizzes.q: Equilibrium can only be reached in
quizzes.e: Equilibrium can only be reached in a closed system, where no reactants or products can escape.

quizzes.q: What does the symbol ⇌ show?
quizzes.e: The ⇌ symbol shows a reversible reaction: it can go forwards and backwards.

quizzes.q: For N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, a compromise temperature (~450 °C) is used because
quizzes.a: lower T gives more yield but too slow a rate
quizzes.e: The forward reaction is exothermic, so a low temperature gives a higher yield, but the rate would be too slow. About 450 °C is a compromise between yield and rate.

quizzes.q: Units of Kc for 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ are
quizzes.e: Kc = [SO₃]² ÷ ([SO₂]²[O₂]). Units: (mol dm⁻³)² ÷ (mol dm⁻³)³ = (mol dm⁻³)⁻¹ = mol⁻¹ dm³.

quizzes.q: Why does adding more reactant not change Kc?
quizzes.e: Kc is only changed by temperature. Adding reactant makes the position shift right until the ratio of concentrations equals Kc again.

quizzes.q: For an endothermic forward reaction, increasing temperature makes Kc
quizzes.e: For an endothermic forward reaction, a rise in temperature shifts the equilibrium right, so more products form and Kc increases.

quizzes.q: Removing product from an equilibrium mixture
quizzes.e: Removing product lowers its concentration. The equilibrium shifts right to oppose the change and replace it.

quizzes.q: A + B ⇌ C. At equilibrium [A] = 0.2, [B] = 0.77, [C] = 1.88 mol dm⁻³. Kc (3 s.f.)?
A + B ⇌ C. At equilibrium [A] = 0.16, [B] = 0.39, [C] = 1.17 mol dm⁻³. Kc (3 s.f.)?
A + B ⇌ C. At equilibrium [A] = 0.85, [B] = 0.32, [C] = 0.44 mol dm⁻³. Kc (3 s.f.)?
A + B ⇌ C. At equilibrium [A] = 0.32, [B] = 0.65, [C] = 1.53 mol dm⁻³. Kc (3 s.f.)?
For 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ (exothermic), a low temperature gives
quizzes.a: a higher yield but slower rate
quizzes.e: The forward reaction is exothermic, so a low temperature shifts the equilibrium right (higher yield), but the rate is slower.

quizzes.q: Increasing pressure on H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI
quizzes.e: H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI has 2 mol of gas on each side, so changing pressure does not change the position of equilibrium.

quizzes.q: Why is a high pressure in industry expensive?
quizzes.e: High pressure needs thick-walled pipes and powerful pumps, which cost a lot to build and run, and uses more energy; there are also safety risks.

quizzes.q: In Kc expressions, solids are
quizzes.e: The concentration of a pure solid (or liquid) is constant, so it is left out of a heterogeneous Kc expression.

quizzes.q: ethanoic acid + ethanol ⇌ ethyl ethanoate + water. Adding water
quizzes.e: Water is a product. Adding it shifts the equilibrium left to oppose the change, so less ester is present; Kc is unchanged.

quizzes.q: If Kc is very large, the equilibrium mixture contains
quizzes.e: A very large Kc means the numerator (products) is much bigger than the denominator, so the position of equilibrium lies far to the right.

quizzes.q: 1.3 mol H₂ and 1.3 mol I₂ in 2 dm³ reach equilibrium with 0.82 mol of H₂ reacted (H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI). Find Kc (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: At equilibrium: H₂ = 1.3 − 0.82 = 0.48 mol, I₂ = 1.3 − 0.82 = 0.48 mol, HI = 2 × 0.82 = 1.64 mol. Kc = [HI]² ÷ ([H₂][I₂]); the volumes cancel, so Kc = 1.64² ÷ (0.48 × 0.48) = 11.7.

quizzes.q: 0.8 mol H₂ and 0.5 mol I₂ in 1 dm³ reach equilibrium with 0.36 mol of H₂ reacted (H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI). Find Kc (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: At equilibrium: H₂ = 0.8 − 0.36 = 0.44 mol, I₂ = 0.5 − 0.36 = 0.14 mol, HI = 2 × 0.36 = 0.72 mol. Kc = [HI]² ÷ ([H₂][I₂]); the volumes cancel, so Kc = 0.72² ÷ (0.44 × 0.14) = 8.42.

quizzes.q: 0.5 mol H₂ and 0.7 mol I₂ in 2 dm³ reach equilibrium with 0.27 mol of H₂ reacted (H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI). Find Kc (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: At equilibrium: H₂ = 0.5 − 0.27 = 0.23 mol, I₂ = 0.7 − 0.27 = 0.43 mol, HI = 2 × 0.27 = 0.54 mol. Kc = [HI]² ÷ ([H₂][I₂]); the volumes cancel, so Kc = 0.54² ÷ (0.23 × 0.43) = 2.95.

quizzes.q: 1.4 mol H₂ and 1.7 mol I₂ in 1 dm³ reach equilibrium with 0.45 mol of H₂ reacted (H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI). Find Kc (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: At equilibrium: H₂ = 1.4 − 0.45 = 0.95 mol, I₂ = 1.7 − 0.45 = 1.25 mol, HI = 2 × 0.45 = 0.90 mol. Kc = [HI]² ÷ ([H₂][I₂]); the volumes cancel, so Kc = 0.90² ÷ (0.95 × 1.25) = 0.682.

quizzes.q: 1.8 mol N₂O₄ in 2 dm³: N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂. At equilibrium 0.62 mol N₂O₄ has dissociated. Kc (mol dm⁻³, 3 s.f.)?
2.9 mol N₂O₄ in 1 dm³: N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂. At equilibrium 1.23 mol N₂O₄ has dissociated. Kc (mol dm⁻³, 3 s.f.)?
1.8 mol N₂O₄ in 2 dm³: N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂. At equilibrium 0.53 mol N₂O₄ has dissociated. Kc (mol dm⁻³, 3 s.f.)?
Oxidation state of Mn in MnO₄⁻?
quizzes.e: O is −2. Let Mn = x: x + 4(−2) = −1, so x = +7.

quizzes.q: Oxidation is
quizzes.e: Oxidation is the loss of electrons (OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain). The oxidation state increases.

quizzes.q: 2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂. The oxidising agent is
quizzes.e: Fe³⁺ gains an electron to become Fe²⁺, so it is reduced. The species that is reduced is the oxidising agent; I⁻ is the reducing agent.

quizzes.q: Oxidation state of S in H₂SO₄?
Electrons needed in MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O?
quizzes.e: Mn goes from +7 in MnO₄⁻ to +2 in Mn²⁺, a change of 5, so 5 electrons are gained: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O.

quizzes.q: Oxidation state of N in NO₃⁻?
quizzes.e: The oxidation states in a species add up to its overall charge. Using O = −2 and H = +1 (except in peroxides and metal hydrides), N is +5.

quizzes.q: Oxidation state of Cl in ClO⁻?
quizzes.e: The oxidation states in a species add up to its overall charge. Using O = −2 and H = +1 (except in peroxides and metal hydrides), Cl is +1.

quizzes.q: Oxidation state of Fe in Fe₃O₄ (average)?
quizzes.e: The oxidation states in a species add up to its overall charge. Using O = −2 and H = +1 (except in peroxides and metal hydrides), Fe is +2.67.

quizzes.q: Half equation for Cl₂ → Cl⁻ is
quizzes.e: Chlorine is reduced: each Cl atom gains an electron. Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻ balances both atoms and charge.

quizzes.q: In Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, zinc is
quizzes.e: Zn loses two electrons (0 → +2), so zinc is oxidised. A species that is oxidised is the reducing agent: it gives electrons to Cu²⁺.

quizzes.q: What is a reducing agent?
quizzes.e: A reducing agent is an electron donor. It reduces another species and is itself oxidised.

quizzes.q: Combine the half-equations MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O and Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻ to give the overall redox equation.
quizzes.e: Multiply the iron half-equation by 5 so that the electrons cancel (5 lost, 5 gained), then add the half-equations.

quizzes.q: How do you combine two half-equations into an overall redox equation?
quizzes.e: Multiply one or both half-equations so that the number of electrons lost equals the number gained, add them together, and cancel the electrons (and any species on both sides).

quizzes.e: In disproportionation the same element is oxidised and reduced in one reaction, e.g. in Cl₂ + H₂O → HCl + HClO, Cl goes from 0 to −1 and to +1.

quizzes.q: Across Period 3, atomic radius
quizzes.e: Across Period 3 the nuclear charge increases but the shielding stays about the same, so the outer electrons are pulled closer and the atomic radius decreases.

quizzes.q: Why does atomic radius decrease across a period?
quizzes.e: Across a period, protons are added to the nucleus while electrons enter the same shell, so shielding is similar. The greater attraction pulls the electrons closer.

quizzes.q: Highest melting point in Period 3
quizzes.e: Si is macromolecular (giant covalent), so many strong covalent bonds must be broken to melt it. Mg and Al are metallic; P is simple molecular.

quizzes.q: Chlorine is in which block?
quizzes.e: An element's block is the sub-level that holds its highest-energy electron. Chlorine's outer electrons are in 3p, so it is in the p-block.

quizzes.q: Period 3 elements are in the
quizzes.e: Na and Mg have their outer electrons in 3s (s-block); Al to Ar have them in 3p (p-block).

quizzes.q: Which Period 3 element has the highest melting point?
quizzes.e: Si has a giant covalent (macromolecular) structure, so many strong covalent bonds must be broken to melt it.

quizzes.q: Structure of the element S at room temperature?
quizzes.e: S: simple molecular (S₈). Na–Al metallic; Si giant covalent; P₄, S₈ and Cl₂ simple molecular; Ar monatomic.

quizzes.q: Structure of the element Al at room temperature?
quizzes.e: Al: metallic. Na–Al metallic; Si giant covalent; P₄, S₈ and Cl₂ simple molecular; Ar monatomic.

quizzes.q: Structure of the element Na at room temperature?
quizzes.e: Na: metallic. Na–Al metallic; Si giant covalent; P₄, S₈ and Cl₂ simple molecular; Ar monatomic.

quizzes.q: Structure of the element Mg at room temperature?
quizzes.e: Mg: metallic. Na–Al metallic; Si giant covalent; P₄, S₈ and Cl₂ simple molecular; Ar monatomic.

quizzes.q: Why does the first IE of Al fall below that of Mg?
quizzes.a: Al's outer electron is in a 3p orbital, higher in energy
quizzes.e: Al's outer electron is in a 3p orbital, which is higher in energy than 3s and partly shielded by the 3s electrons, so it is easier to remove.

quizzes.q: Why is the first IE of S lower than P?
quizzes.a: electron pair repulsion in a 3p orbital in S
quizzes.e: S is 3p⁴, so one 3p orbital contains a pair of electrons. Their repulsion makes one easier to remove than P's unpaired 3p³ electrons.

quizzes.q: Why does Mg have a higher melting point than Na?
quizzes.a: Mg²⁺ has a greater charge and more delocalised electrons
quizzes.e: Mg²⁺ has a higher charge than Na⁺, is smaller and gives 2 delocalised electrons per atom, so the metallic bonding is stronger.

quizzes.q: Why is the melting point of S higher than that of P?
quizzes.a: S₈ molecules are larger than P₄, so van der Waals forces are stronger
quizzes.e: S₈ molecules are larger and have more electrons than P₄, so the van der Waals forces between them are stronger.

quizzes.q: Which best explains the melting point of P?
quizzes.a: weak van der Waals between P₄ molecules
w: metallic bonding, 3 delocalised electrons per atom
van der Waals between larger S₈ molecules
weak van der Waals between Cl₂ molecules
quizzes.e: P: weak van der Waals between P₄ molecules. The stronger the bonding that must be overcome, the higher the melting point.

quizzes.q: Which best explains the melting point of Si?
quizzes.a: strong covalent bonds in a giant lattice
w: metallic bonding, 2 delocalised electrons per atom, smaller ion
van der Waals between larger S₈ molecules
weak van der Waals between Cl₂ molecules
quizzes.e: Si: strong covalent bonds in a giant lattice. The stronger the bonding that must be overcome, the higher the melting point.

quizzes.q: Which best explains the melting point of Ar?
quizzes.a: very weak van der Waals between single atoms
w: metallic bonding, 3 delocalised electrons per atom
weak van der Waals between P₄ molecules
weak van der Waals between Cl₂ molecules
quizzes.e: Ar: very weak van der Waals between single atoms. The stronger the bonding that must be overcome, the higher the melting point.

quizzes.q: Which best explains the melting point of Cl?
quizzes.a: weak van der Waals between Cl₂ molecules
w: metallic bonding, 3 delocalised electrons per atom
weak van der Waals between P₄ molecules
van der Waals between larger S₈ molecules
quizzes.e: Cl: weak van der Waals between Cl₂ molecules. The stronger the bonding that must be overcome, the higher the melting point.

quizzes.q: Which best explains the melting point of Mg?
quizzes.a: metallic bonding, 2 delocalised electrons per atom, smaller ion
w: weak van der Waals between Cl₂ molecules
weak van der Waals between P₄ molecules
very weak van der Waals between single atoms
quizzes.e: Mg: metallic bonding, 2 delocalised electrons per atom, smaller ion. The stronger the bonding that must be overcome, the higher the melting point.

quizzes.q: Which best explains the melting point of Na?
quizzes.a: metallic bonding, 1 delocalised electron per atom
w: weak van der Waals between Cl₂ molecules
weak van der Waals between P₄ molecules
metallic bonding, 3 delocalised electrons per atom
quizzes.e: Na: metallic bonding, 1 delocalised electron per atom. The stronger the bonding that must be overcome, the higher the melting point.

quizzes.q: Which best explains the melting point of S?
quizzes.a: van der Waals between larger S₈ molecules
w: very weak van der Waals between single atoms
weak van der Waals between Cl₂ molecules
metallic bonding, 1 delocalised electron per atom
quizzes.e: S: van der Waals between larger S₈ molecules. The stronger the bonding that must be overcome, the higher the melting point.

quizzes.q: Explain the trend in atomic radius across Period 3.
quizzes.e: Across Period 3 the nuclear charge increases while electrons are added to the same shell (similar shielding), so the outer electrons are pulled closer and the radius decreases.

quizzes.q: Explain why the melting point of Si is much higher than that of P.
quizzes.e: Si is giant covalent, so many strong covalent bonds must break. P exists as P₄ molecules, so only weak van der Waals forces between molecules must be overcome.

quizzes.q: Explain why Ar has the lowest melting point in Period 3.
quizzes.e: Argon exists as single atoms (monatomic). The van der Waals forces between them are very weak, so little energy is needed to melt it.

quizzes.q: Explain the general increase in first ionisation energy across Period 3.
quizzes.e: Across Period 3 there are more protons with similar shielding, so the attraction for the outer electron increases and more energy is needed to remove it.

quizzes.q: Which pair shows the two exceptions to the IE trend across Period 3?
quizzes.e: Mg→Al drops because Al's electron is in the higher-energy 3p sub-shell; P→S drops because of the repulsion between paired electrons in a 3p orbital.

quizzes.q: Which element in Period 3 has the largest atomic radius?
quizzes.e: Na has the fewest protons in Period 3 with the same shielding, so its outer electron is least strongly attracted and its atom is largest.

quizzes.q: Explain why Al has a higher melting point than Mg.
quizzes.e: Al³⁺ has a higher charge than Mg²⁺ and gives 3 delocalised electrons per atom, so the metallic bonding is stronger.

quizzes.q: Structure of the element P at room temperature?
quizzes.e: P: simple molecular (P₄). Na–Al metallic; Si giant covalent; P₄, S₈ and Cl₂ simple molecular; Ar monatomic.

quizzes.q: Structure of the element Si at room temperature?
quizzes.e: Si: giant covalent. Na–Al metallic; Si giant covalent; P₄, S₈ and Cl₂ simple molecular; Ar monatomic.

quizzes.q: Which best explains the melting point of Al?
quizzes.a: metallic bonding, 3 delocalised electrons per atom
w: van der Waals between larger S₈ molecules
metallic bonding, 2 delocalised electrons per atom, smaller ion
weak van der Waals between P₄ molecules
quizzes.e: Al: metallic bonding, 3 delocalised electrons per atom. The stronger the bonding that must be overcome, the higher the melting point.

quizzes.q: Down Group 2, solubility of hydroxides
quizzes.e: Down Group 2 the hydroxides become more soluble (Mg(OH)₂ is sparingly soluble, Ba(OH)₂ is quite soluble). Sulfates show the opposite trend.

quizzes.q: Which sulfate is used in barium meals?
quizzes.e: BaSO₄ is insoluble, so it is not absorbed into the blood and is not toxic. It absorbs X-rays, which shows the outline of the gut.

quizzes.q: Why does reactivity increase down Group 2?
quizzes.e: Down Group 2 the outer electrons are in higher shells, further from the nucleus and more shielded, so the ionisation energies decrease and the atoms lose electrons more easily.

quizzes.q: Magnesium + steam gives
quizzes.e: Mg + H₂O(g) → MgO + H₂ with steam. With cold water magnesium reacts only very slowly to give Mg(OH)₂ and H₂.

quizzes.q: Reaction of Ca with water?
quizzes.a: reacts steadily with cold water forming Ca(OH)₂ + H₂
w: very slow with cold water; burns in steam to MgO + H₂
quizzes.e: Ca: reacts steadily with cold water forming Ca(OH)₂ + H₂. Reactivity with water increases down Group 2 because the ionisation energies decrease.

quizzes.q: Reaction of Ba with water?
w: reacts steadily with cold water forming Ca(OH)₂ + H₂
very slow with cold water; burns in steam to MgO + H₂
quizzes.e: Ba: reacts vigorously with cold water. Reactivity with water increases down Group 2 because the ionisation energies decrease.

quizzes.q: Reaction of Sr with water?
w: reacts steadily with cold water forming Ca(OH)₂ + H₂
very slow with cold water; burns in steam to MgO + H₂
quizzes.e: Sr: reacts quickly with cold water. Reactivity with water increases down Group 2 because the ionisation energies decrease.

quizzes.q: Reaction of Mg with water?
quizzes.a: very slow with cold water; burns in steam to MgO + H₂
w: reacts steadily with cold water forming Ca(OH)₂ + H₂
quizzes.e: Mg: very slow with cold water; burns in steam to MgO + H₂. Reactivity with water increases down Group 2 because the ionisation energies decrease.

quizzes.q: A use of Mg(OH)₂?
quizzes.e: A use of Mg(OH)₂: antacid for indigestion. Group 2 compounds are used because of their basic properties or low solubility.

quizzes.q: A use of BaCl₂ (acidified)?
quizzes.e: A use of BaCl₂ (acidified): testing for sulfate ions. Group 2 compounds are used because of their basic properties or low solubility.

quizzes.q: A use of BaSO₄?
quizzes.e: A use of BaSO₄: barium meal for X-rays. Group 2 compounds are used because of their basic properties or low solubility.

quizzes.q: Explain why the melting point of the Group 2 elements generally decreases down the group.
quizzes.e: The elements have metallic bonding. Down the group the ions get larger, with the same 2+ charge, so the attraction between the ions and the delocalised electrons is weaker and less energy is needed to break it.

quizzes.q: Which statement about the hydroxide of Ca is correct?
quizzes.e: Ca: Ca(OH)₂ – slightly soluble. Hydroxide solubility increases down Group 2, from Mg(OH)₂ (least soluble) to Ba(OH)₂.

quizzes.q: Which statement about the hydroxide of Sr is correct?
quizzes.e: Sr: Sr(OH)₂ – fairly soluble. Hydroxide solubility increases down Group 2, from Mg(OH)₂ (least soluble) to Ba(OH)₂.

quizzes.q: Which statement about the hydroxide of Mg is correct?
quizzes.e: Mg: Mg(OH)₂ – least soluble hydroxide. Hydroxide solubility increases down Group 2, from Mg(OH)₂ (least soluble) to Ba(OH)₂.

quizzes.q: Which statement about the hydroxide of Ba is correct?
quizzes.e: Ba: Ba(OH)₂ – most soluble hydroxide. Hydroxide solubility increases down Group 2, from Mg(OH)₂ (least soluble) to Ba(OH)₂.

quizzes.q: Which statement about the sulfate of Mg is correct?
quizzes.e: Mg: MgSO₄ – most soluble sulfate. Sulfate solubility decreases down Group 2, from MgSO₄ (soluble) to BaSO₄ (insoluble).

quizzes.q: Which statement about the sulfate of Sr is correct?
quizzes.e: Sr: SrSO₄ – very sparingly soluble. Sulfate solubility decreases down Group 2, from MgSO₄ (soluble) to BaSO₄ (insoluble).

quizzes.q: Which statement about the sulfate of Ca is correct?
quizzes.e: Ca: CaSO₄ – sparingly soluble. Sulfate solubility decreases down Group 2, from MgSO₄ (soluble) to BaSO₄ (insoluble).

quizzes.q: Which statement about the sulfate of Ba is correct?
quizzes.e: Ba: BaSO₄ – insoluble. Sulfate solubility decreases down Group 2, from MgSO₄ (soluble) to BaSO₄ (insoluble).

quizzes.q: A use of Mg?
quizzes.e: A use of Mg: extracting titanium from TiCl₄. Group 2 compounds are used because of their basic properties or low solubility.

quizzes.q: Explain why the first IE decreases down Group 2.
quizzes.e: Down Group 2 the outer electron is in a higher shell, further from the nucleus and with more shielding, so less energy is needed to remove it.

quizzes.q: Write the equation for Mg burning in steam.
quizzes.e: With steam, magnesium forms magnesium oxide and hydrogen: Mg + H₂O → MgO + H₂ (it burns with a bright white light).

quizzes.q: Which Group 2 compound or element is used for extracting titanium from TiCl₄?
quizzes.e: Mg is used for extracting titanium from TiCl₄.

quizzes.q: Which Group 2 compound or element is used for removing SO₂ from flue gases?
quizzes.e: CaO / CaCO₃ is used for removing SO₂ from flue gases.

quizzes.q: Which Group 2 compound or element is used for testing for sulfate ions?
quizzes.e: BaCl₂ (acidified) is used for testing for sulfate ions.

quizzes.q: Which Group 2 compound or element is used for antacid for indigestion?
quizzes.e: Mg(OH)₂ is used for antacid for indigestion.

quizzes.q: Which Group 2 compound or element is used for neutralising acidic soil?
quizzes.e: Ca(OH)₂ is used for neutralising acidic soil.

quizzes.q: Which Group 2 compound or element is used for barium meal for X-rays?
quizzes.e: BaSO₄ is used for barium meal for X-rays.

quizzes.q: A use of CaO / CaCO₃?
quizzes.e: A use of CaO / CaCO₃: removing SO₂ from flue gases. Group 2 compounds are used because of their basic properties or low solubility.

quizzes.q: A use of Ca(OH)₂?
quizzes.e: A use of Ca(OH)₂: neutralising acidic soil. Group 2 compounds are used because of their basic properties or low solubility.

quizzes.q: Which halide reduces conc. H₂SO₄ to H₂S?
quizzes.e: I⁻ is the strongest reducing agent of the halides (the largest ion loses an electron most easily). It reduces S from +6 in H₂SO₄ to −2 in H₂S.

quizzes.q: Colour of AgBr precipitate
quizzes.e: With acidified AgNO₃: AgCl is white, AgBr is cream and AgI is yellow.

quizzes.q: Why is chlorine added to drinking water?
quizzes.e: Chlorine kills bacteria in drinking water. The health benefit outweighs the small risk from toxic chlorine and chlorinated organic compounds.

quizzes.q: Down Group 7, oxidising ability
quizzes.e: Down Group 7 the atoms get larger and the outer shell is more shielded, so it is harder to attract an electron. Oxidising ability decreases.

quizzes.q: Which silver halide dissolves in dilute ammonia?
quizzes.e: AgCl dissolves in dilute ammonia, AgBr only in concentrated ammonia, and AgI does not dissolve in either.

quizzes.q: Down Group 7, electronegativity
quizzes.e: Down Group 7 the atoms have more shells, so the bonding pair is further from the nucleus and more shielded; electronegativity decreases.

quizzes.q: Colour of chlorine gas?
quizzes.e: Chlorine is a pale green gas; colour darkens down Group 7.

quizzes.q: Bromine at room temperature is a
quizzes.e: Bromine is the only non-metal liquid at room temperature; it gives off orange-brown vapour.

quizzes.q: Result of adding acidified AgNO₃(aq) to a solution of Br⁻?
quizzes.e: Br⁻ gives a cream precipitate. AgCl is white, AgBr cream and AgI yellow; AgF is soluble, so fluoride gives no precipitate.

quizzes.q: Result of adding acidified AgNO₃(aq) to a solution of F⁻?
quizzes.e: F⁻ gives a no precipitate (AgF soluble). AgCl is white, AgBr cream and AgI yellow; AgF is soluble, so fluoride gives no precipitate.

quizzes.q: Result of adding acidified AgNO₃(aq) to a solution of Cl⁻?
quizzes.e: Cl⁻ gives a white precipitate. AgCl is white, AgBr cream and AgI yellow; AgF is soluble, so fluoride gives no precipitate.

quizzes.q: Chlorine reacts with cold dilute NaOH to give
quizzes.e: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O; the NaClO solution is bleach.

quizzes.q: Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HClO. What happens to chlorine?
quizzes.a: it is both oxidised and reduced (disproportionation)
quizzes.e: In Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HClO, chlorine goes from 0 to −1 (reduced) in HCl and to +1 (oxidised) in HClO: disproportionation.

quizzes.q: Why is chlorine added to drinking water despite being toxic?
quizzes.a: it kills bacteria and the benefit outweighs the risk at low concentration
quizzes.e: Chlorine kills disease-causing bacteria; at the low concentrations used, the health benefit outweighs the toxic risk.

quizzes.q: Why does boiling point increase down Group 7?
quizzes.a: more electrons, so stronger van der Waals forces
quizzes.e: Larger molecules have more electrons, so van der Waals forces are stronger and need more energy to overcome.

quizzes.q: Observation for Cl₂(aq) + KBr(aq)?
quizzes.e: A halogen oxidises (displaces) the halide ions of any halogen below it in the group, because oxidising power decreases down Group 7. Br₂ in water is orange; I₂ is brown.

quizzes.q: Observation for Cl₂(aq) + KI(aq)?
quizzes.e: A halogen oxidises (displaces) the halide ions of any halogen below it in the group, because oxidising power decreases down Group 7. Br₂ in water is orange; I₂ is brown.

quizzes.q: Observation for Br₂(aq) + KI(aq)?
quizzes.e: A halogen oxidises (displaces) the halide ions of any halogen below it in the group, because oxidising power decreases down Group 7. Br₂ in water is orange; I₂ is brown.

quizzes.q: Observation for Br₂(aq) + KCl(aq)?
quizzes.e: A halogen oxidises (displaces) the halide ions of any halogen below it in the group, because oxidising power decreases down Group 7. Br₂ in water is orange; I₂ is brown.

quizzes.q: Observation for I₂(aq) + KBr(aq)?
quizzes.e: A halogen oxidises (displaces) the halide ions of any halogen below it in the group, because oxidising power decreases down Group 7. Br₂ in water is orange; I₂ is brown.

quizzes.q: Result of adding acidified AgNO₃(aq) to a solution of I⁻?
quizzes.e: I⁻ gives a yellow precipitate. AgCl is white, AgBr cream and AgI yellow; AgF is soluble, so fluoride gives no precipitate.

quizzes.q: Explain why the reducing power of halide ions increases down the group.
quizzes.e: Down the group the ions are larger, so the outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded. They are lost more easily, so reducing power increases.

quizzes.q: Oxidation state of S in the H₂S formed from NaI + concentrated H₂SO₄?
quizzes.e: I⁻ is a strong reducing agent and reduces sulfur from +6 in H₂SO₄ all the way to −2 in H₂S.

quizzes.q: Half-equation for I⁻ reducing H₂SO₄ to H₂S:
quizzes.e: S goes from +6 to −2, gaining 8 electrons. Balance O with 4H₂O and H with 8H⁺: H₂SO₄ + 8H⁺ + 8e⁻ → H₂S + 4H₂O.

quizzes.q: Why is nitric acid added before silver nitrate in the halide test?
quizzes.e: Nitric acid reacts with carbonate and hydroxide ions, which would otherwise form precipitates with Ag⁺ and give a false positive.

quizzes.q: Which is NOT a reason HCl cannot be oxidised by concentrated H₂SO₄?
quizzes.a: Cl⁻ is a stronger reducing agent than I⁻
w: Cl⁻ is a weak reducing agent
quizzes.e: Cl⁻ is the weakest reducing agent of the three.

quizzes.q: Explain why HCl, not HBr, cannot be oxidised to the halogen by concentrated H₂SO₄.
quizzes.e: Cl⁻ is the weakest reducing agent of the halides because its outer electrons are held tightly, so it cannot reduce concentrated H₂SO₄. Br⁻ can (to SO₂).

quizzes.q: Equation for chlorine with water in sunlight?
quizzes.e: In sunlight the HClO decomposes and chlorine reacts with water to give HCl and oxygen: 2Cl₂ + 2H₂O → 4HCl + O₂.

quizzes.q: Ionic equation for Cl₂ displacing iodide?
quizzes.e: Chlorine is a stronger oxidising agent than iodine, so it oxidises I⁻ to I₂ (brown solution).

quizzes.q: Products when solid sodium halide containing I⁻ reacts with concentrated H₂SO₄?
quizzes.a: HI, I₂ (purple/black), S and H₂S (bad eggs)
quizzes.e: I⁻ gives HI, I₂ (purple/black), S and H₂S (bad eggs). Reducing power of the halide ions increases down the group, so iodide reduces H₂SO₄ furthest (to H₂S).

quizzes.q: Products when solid sodium halide containing Br⁻ reacts with concentrated H₂SO₄?
w: HI, I₂ (purple/black), S and H₂S (bad eggs)
quizzes.e: Br⁻ gives HBr, Br₂ (orange-brown) and SO₂. Reducing power of the halide ions increases down the group, so iodide reduces H₂SO₄ furthest (to H₂S).

quizzes.q: Products when solid sodium halide containing F⁻ reacts with concentrated H₂SO₄?
w: HI, I₂ (purple/black), S and H₂S (bad eggs)
quizzes.e: F⁻ gives HF only (steamy fumes). Reducing power of the halide ions increases down the group, so iodide reduces H₂SO₄ furthest (to H₂S).

quizzes.q: Products when solid sodium halide containing Cl⁻ reacts with concentrated H₂SO₄?
w: HI, I₂ (purple/black), S and H₂S (bad eggs)
quizzes.e: Cl⁻ gives HCl only (steamy fumes). Reducing power of the halide ions increases down the group, so iodide reduces H₂SO₄ furthest (to H₂S).

quizzes.q: A functional group isomer of propanal is
quizzes.e: Propanal (an aldehyde) and propanone (a ketone) are both C₃H₆O but have different functional groups, so they are functional group isomers.

quizzes.q: E/Z isomerism needs
quizzes.a: restricted C=C rotation with two different groups on each carbon
quizzes.e: E/Z isomers need restricted rotation about a C=C double bond, and each carbon of the C=C must have two different groups attached.

quizzes.q: What is a homologous series?
quizzes.e: A homologous series has the same functional group and general formula. Each member differs from the next by CH₂, and they have similar chemical properties.

quizzes.q: How many structural isomers does C₄H₁₀ have?
quizzes.e: C₄H₁₀ has two structural isomers: butane (a chain of 4 carbons) and methylpropane (a chain of 3 with a methyl branch).

quizzes.q: IUPAC name of CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₃
quizzes.e: The longest carbon chain is 3 carbons (propane) with a methyl group on carbon 2. The locant is not needed because there is only one position, so it is methylpropane.

quizzes.q: A homologous series has the same
quizzes.e: Members of a homologous series share a general formula and functional group, and differ by CH₂.

quizzes.q: Structural isomers have the same
quizzes.a: molecular formula but different structural formula
quizzes.e: Structural isomers: same molecular formula, different structural formula (chain, position or functional group isomers).

quizzes.q: Empirical formula of C₆H₁₂?
quizzes.e: Divide C₆H₁₂ by the highest common factor, 6, to get the simplest ratio CH₂.

quizzes.q: In a free-radical mechanism, the unpaired electron on a radical is shown by
quizzes.e: Radicals are drawn with a dot. Curly arrows are not required for radical mechanisms at A level.

quizzes.q: IUPAC name of CH₃COCl?
quizzes.e: CH₃COCl is ethanoyl chloride: the longest carbon chain gives the stem, the functional group gives the suffix or prefix, with the lowest locant.

quizzes.q: IUPAC name of CH₂=CHCH₃?
quizzes.e: CH₂=CHCH₃ is propene: the longest carbon chain gives the stem, the functional group gives the suffix or prefix, with the lowest locant.

quizzes.q: IUPAC name of CH₃CH(OH)CH₃?
quizzes.e: CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ is propan-2-ol: the longest carbon chain gives the stem, the functional group gives the suffix or prefix, with the lowest locant.

quizzes.q: IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂CH₂Br?
quizzes.e: CH₃CH₂CH₂Br is 1-bromopropane: the longest carbon chain gives the stem, the functional group gives the suffix or prefix, with the lowest locant.

quizzes.q: How many structural isomers does C₅H₁₂ have?
quizzes.e: C₅H₁₂ has three: pentane, 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane.

quizzes.q: E/Z isomerism arises because
quizzes.e: The π bond in C=C stops rotation, so if each carbon has two different groups, two different spatial arrangements (E and Z) are possible.

quizzes.q: Which shows E/Z isomerism?
quizzes.e: But-2-ene has two different groups (H and CH₃) on each C=C carbon; the others have two identical groups on one carbon.

quizzes.q: In (E)-1-bromo-1-chloropropene, the higher-priority groups are
quizzes.e: On C1, Br has a higher atomic number than Cl; on C2, CH₃ beats H. E (entgegen) means the two higher-priority groups are on opposite sides.

quizzes.q: CIP priority is decided by
quizzes.a: atomic number of the attached atom
quizzes.e: Cahn–Ingold–Prelog rules: the atom with the higher atomic number directly attached gets the higher priority.

quizzes.q: Which equation is a propagation step in the free-radical chlorination of methane?
quizzes.e: Propagation steps use up one radical and make another. Initiation makes radicals from Cl₂ (UV light); termination joins two radicals.

quizzes.q: In a reaction mechanism, a curly arrow shows
quizzes.a: the movement of a pair of electrons, starting from a bond or a lone pair
w: the movement of a single atom
the movement of a single electron in a radical reaction
quizzes.e: A curly arrow starts at a lone pair or at the middle of a covalent bond (when it breaks) and points to where the electron pair goes.

quizzes.q: Why do chemists use mechanisms to explain the reactions of organic compounds?
quizzes.e: A mechanism shows, step by step, which bonds break and form and how the electron pairs move, so it explains why the products form and lets chemists predict similar reactions.

quizzes.q: Define the term stereoisomer.
quizzes.e: Stereoisomers have the same structural formula but a different arrangement of the atoms in space. E–Z isomers and optical isomers are both types of stereoisomerism.

quizzes.q: But-2-ene shows stereoisomerism (E–Z) because
quizzes.a: rotation about the C=C bond is restricted and each carbon of the C=C has two different groups
w: it has a functional group isomer
quizzes.e: The π bond prevents rotation about C=C. Each double-bond carbon carries H and CH₃, so the groups can be on the same side (Z) or opposite sides (E): these are stereoisomers.

quizzes.q: IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂CHO?
quizzes.e: CH₃CH₂CHO is propanal: the longest carbon chain gives the stem, the functional group gives the suffix or prefix, with the lowest locant.

quizzes.q: IUPAC name of CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃?
quizzes.e: CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃ is 2-methylbutane: the longest carbon chain gives the stem, the functional group gives the suffix or prefix, with the lowest locant.

quizzes.q: IUPAC name of (CH₃)₃COH?
quizzes.e: (CH₃)₃COH is 2-methylpropan-2-ol: the longest carbon chain gives the stem, the functional group gives the suffix or prefix, with the lowest locant.

quizzes.q: Which is a functional group isomer of propanal?
quizzes.e: Propanal (aldehyde) and propanone (ketone) are both C₃H₆O but have different functional groups.

quizzes.q: A compound is 85.7% C and 14.3% H, Mr 56. Molecular formula?
quizzes.e: C : H = 85.7/12 : 14.3/1 = 7.14 : 14.3 = 1 : 2, so the empirical formula is CH₂ (Mr 14). 56 ÷ 14 = 4, so the molecular formula is C₄H₈.

quizzes.q: A hydrocarbon is 82.8% C by mass and has Mr 58. How many C atoms per molecule?
quizzes.e: C : H = 82.8/12 : 17.2/1 = 6.9 : 17.2 = 1 : 2.5, so the empirical formula is C₂H₅ (Mr 29). 58 ÷ 29 = 2, giving C₄H₁₀, with 4 carbon atoms.

quizzes.q: How many structural isomers are alkenes with formula C₄H₈ (ignore E/Z)?
quizzes.e: The C₄H₈ alkenes are but-1-ene, but-2-ene and methylpropene: 3 structural isomers (cyclic isomers are not alkenes).

quizzes.q: Name of CH₃CH(Cl)CH(CH₃)CH₃?
quizzes.e: The longest chain has 4 carbons. Numbering from either end gives positions 2 and 3, so alphabetical order decides: chloro comes first and gets 2. The name is 2-chloro-3-methylbutane.

quizzes.q: Explain why but-2-ene has E/Z isomers but but-1-ene does not.
quizzes.e: In but-1-ene, C1 has two H atoms attached, so swapping sides gives the same molecule. In but-2-ene, each C=C carbon has an H and a CH₃, so E and Z forms exist.

quizzes.q: IUPAC name of HCOOCH₃?
quizzes.e: HCOOCH₃ is methyl methanoate: the longest carbon chain gives the stem, the functional group gives the suffix or prefix, with the lowest locant.

quizzes.q: IUPAC name of CH₃CHBrCH₃?
quizzes.e: CH₃CHBrCH₃ is 2-bromopropane: the longest carbon chain gives the stem, the functional group gives the suffix or prefix, with the lowest locant.

quizzes.q: IUPAC name of CH₃CONH₂?
quizzes.e: CH₃CONH₂ is ethanamide: the longest carbon chain gives the stem, the functional group gives the suffix or prefix, with the lowest locant.

quizzes.q: IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂COOH?
quizzes.e: CH₃CH₂COOH is propanoic acid: the longest carbon chain gives the stem, the functional group gives the suffix or prefix, with the lowest locant.

quizzes.q: Order the free-radical chlorination of methane
quizzes.e: Initiation makes radicals with UV light; the two propagation steps use and regenerate Cl•; termination removes radicals. Further substitution gives CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃ and CCl₄.

quizzes.q: Fractional distillation separates crude oil by
quizzes.e: Crude oil is heated and the vapour rises up a column that is hotter at the bottom. Fractions condense at different heights because they have different boiling points.

quizzes.q: Catalytic converters change CO and NO into
quizzes.e: In a catalytic converter (Pt/Rh on a ceramic honeycomb) 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂, removing toxic CO and NO.

quizzes.q: Why is cracking useful?
quizzes.e: There is more demand for shorter-chain alkanes (such as petrol) than distillation provides. Cracking also makes alkenes, which are used to make polymers.

quizzes.q: CFCs damage ozone through
quizzes.e: UV light breaks the C–Cl bond in CFCs to form Cl• radicals. Cl• catalyses the breakdown of ozone and is regenerated, so one radical destroys many O₃ molecules.

quizzes.q: Alkanes are
quizzes.e: Alkanes contain only single C–C bonds (saturated) and only C and H (hydrocarbons).

quizzes.q: Crude oil is separated by
quizzes.e: Fractions with different boiling points condense at different heights of the column.

quizzes.q: Thermal cracking uses
quizzes.e: Thermal cracking uses high temperature (up to 1000 °C) and high pressure (up to 70 atm), and gives a high proportion of alkenes.

quizzes.q: Catalytic cracking uses
quizzes.a: a zeolite catalyst at slight pressure, ~450 °C
quizzes.e: Catalytic cracking uses a zeolite catalyst at a slight pressure and about 450 °C. It gives motor fuels, aromatic hydrocarbons and branched alkanes.

quizzes.q: Incomplete combustion produces
quizzes.e: With limited oxygen, carbon monoxide and soot (carbon) form instead of CO₂.

quizzes.q: Catalytic converters remove CO and NO by
quizzes.e: In the catalytic converter, CO is oxidised and NO is reduced on a Pt/Rh catalyst: 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂.

quizzes.q: Why does boiling point increase with chain length?
quizzes.a: more surface contact, stronger van der Waals forces
quizzes.e: Longer chains have more surface contact and more electrons, so stronger van der Waals forces between molecules.

quizzes.q: Branched alkanes have lower boiling points because
quizzes.e: Branching stops molecules packing closely, so there is less surface contact and weaker van der Waals forces.

quizzes.q: SO₂ from fuel combustion causes
quizzes.e: SO₂ dissolves in rainwater, forming acidic solutions that damage buildings and ecosystems.

quizzes.q: NOx forms in engines because
quizzes.a: N₂ and O₂ react at high temperatures
quizzes.e: The high temperature in the engine provides the energy for N₂ and O₂ from the air to react.

quizzes.q: Mechanism/type of reaction for methane → chloromethane (Cl₂, UV light)?
quizzes.e: methane → chloromethane with Cl₂, UV light is free-radical substitution. Identify how the functional group changes and what attacks it.

quizzes.q: Moles of O₂ needed to burn 1 mol of an alkane with 8 carbons completely.
quizzes.e: C8H18 gives 8 CO₂ and 9 H₂O. O atoms needed = 2 × 8 + 9 = 25, so O₂ = 12.5 mol.

quizzes.q: Moles of O₂ needed to burn 1 mol of an alkane with 9 carbons completely.
quizzes.e: C9H20 gives 9 CO₂ and 10 H₂O. O atoms needed = 2 × 9 + 10 = 28, so O₂ = 14 mol.

quizzes.q: Molecular formula of the alkane with 12 carbons: how many H atoms?
quizzes.e: Alkanes have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. With n = 12: 2 × 12 + 2 = 26 H atoms.

quizzes.q: Molecular formula of the alkane with 7 carbons: how many H atoms?
quizzes.e: Alkanes have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. With n = 7: 2 × 7 + 2 = 16 H atoms.

quizzes.q: Initiation step for chlorination of methane?
quizzes.e: UV light breaks the Cl–Cl bond by homolytic fission, giving two chlorine radicals: Cl₂ → 2Cl•.

quizzes.q: Which is a propagation step?
quizzes.e: A propagation step uses one radical and makes another: CH₃• + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•. The chain continues.

quizzes.q: Which termination step explains ethane as a by-product?
quizzes.e: Termination: two methyl radicals combine, forming ethane.

quizzes.q: Cl• radicals deplete ozone. Which is correct?
quizzes.a: Cl• + O₃ → ClO• + O₂, then ClO• + O₃ → 2O₂ + Cl•
quizzes.e: Cl• + O₃ → ClO• + O₂, then ClO• + O₃ → 2O₂ + Cl•. Cl• is regenerated, so it acts as a catalyst; overall 2O₃ → 3O₂.

quizzes.q: Balanced cracking: C₁₂H₂₆ → C₈H₁₈ + ?
quizzes.e: Balance the atoms: C 12 − 8 = 4 and H 26 − 18 = 8 remain, which is C₄H₈ = 2C₂H₄.

quizzes.q: C₁₄H₃₀ → C₈H₁₈ + n C₂H₄ + ... How many ethene if only these products form? (n)
quizzes.e: Carbon: 14 − 8 = 6 C left, which makes 3 C₂H₄. Hydrogen check: 30 − 18 = 12 = 3 × 4. So n = 3.

quizzes.q: Volume of CO₂ (dm³, 3 s.f.) from complete combustion of 0.100 mol octane at RTP (24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹).
quizzes.e: C₈H₁₈ + 12½O₂ → 8CO₂ + 9H₂O. 0.100 mol octane gives 0.800 mol CO₂; V = 0.800 × 24.0 = 19.2 dm³.

quizzes.q: Why are CFCs being replaced by HFCs?
quizzes.e: UV light breaks the C–Cl bonds in CFCs to form Cl• radicals that catalyse ozone breakdown. HFCs contain no chlorine, so they do not form Cl•.

quizzes.q: Molecular formula of the alkane with 8 carbons: how many H atoms?
quizzes.e: Alkanes have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. With n = 8: 2 × 8 + 2 = 18 H atoms.

quizzes.q: Reagents/conditions for methane → chloromethane?
quizzes.e: methane → chloromethane: use Cl₂, UV light. The reaction type is free-radical substitution.

quizzes.q: Which bond hydrolyses fastest?
quizzes.e: The C–I bond has the lowest bond enthalpy, so it breaks most easily and iodoalkanes hydrolyse fastest. C–F is strongest and slowest.

quizzes.q: 2-bromopropane with KOH in ethanol, heated, gives mainly
quizzes.e: Hot OH⁻ in ethanol acts as a base and removes H⁺, so elimination of HBr gives propene. In warm aqueous conditions substitution to propan-2-ol is favoured.

quizzes.q: What is a nucleophile?
quizzes.e: A nucleophile is an electron pair donor. It has a lone pair and attacks a δ+ carbon atom, e.g. OH⁻, CN⁻ and NH₃.

quizzes.q: Halogenoalkane + excess NH₃ gives
quizzes.e: NH₃ acts as a nucleophile in a substitution reaction. Excess ammonia (in ethanol, under pressure) gives mainly the primary amine and reduces further substitution.

quizzes.q: Bromoethane + KCN gives
quizzes.e: CN⁻ replaces Br in nucleophilic substitution, adding a carbon: CH₃CH₂Br + CN⁻ → CH₃CH₂CN (propanenitrile) + Br⁻.

quizzes.q: A nucleophile is
quizzes.e: A nucleophile donates a pair of electrons to an electron-deficient atom (e.g. OH⁻, CN⁻, NH₃).

quizzes.q: Which is a nucleophile?
quizzes.e: OH⁻ has a lone pair and a negative charge, so it can donate an electron pair.

quizzes.q: Halogenoalkanes are attacked at the carbon because
quizzes.a: C–X is polar, making C δ+
quizzes.e: Halogens are more electronegative than carbon, so the C–X carbon is δ+ and attracts nucleophiles.

quizzes.q: What does the curly arrow from OH⁻ show?
quizzes.a: A lone pair moving to form a new bond to carbon
w: An electron transferring from carbon to oxygen
quizzes.e: Curly arrows show the movement of a pair of electrons.

quizzes.q: Reagents/conditions for bromoethane → ethanol?
quizzes.e: bromoethane → ethanol: use NaOH(aq), warm. The reaction type is nucleophilic substitution.

quizzes.q: Reagents/conditions for bromoethane → ethene?
quizzes.e: bromoethane → ethene: use KOH in ethanol, hot. The reaction type is elimination.

quizzes.q: Reagents/conditions for bromoethane → propanenitrile?
quizzes.e: bromoethane → propanenitrile: use KCN in aqueous ethanol, reflux. The reaction type is nucleophilic substitution.

quizzes.q: Order of hydrolysis rate (fastest first)?
quizzes.e: Bond enthalpy decreases C–Cl > C–Br > C–I, so C–I breaks most easily and iodoalkanes hydrolyse fastest.

quizzes.q: Rate of hydrolysis depends mainly on
quizzes.e: The C–X bond must break; C–I is the weakest, so iodoalkanes hydrolyse fastest.

quizzes.q: Hydroxide acting as a base (in ethanol) gives
quizzes.e: Hot OH⁻ in ethanol acts as a base: it removes H⁺ from the carbon next to C–X, and X⁻ leaves, forming a C=C (elimination).

quizzes.q: Why use excess ammonia to make a primary amine?
quizzes.e: With excess NH₃, the halogenoalkane is more likely to meet NH₃ than the amine product.

quizzes.q: Elimination of 2-bromobutane can give
quizzes.e: H can be removed from C1 or C3, so but-1-ene and both E- and Z-but-2-ene can form.

quizzes.q: Chlorine radicals from CFCs destroy ozone. In the steps Cl• + O₃ → ClO• + O₂ and ClO• + O₃ → 2O₂ + Cl•, the chlorine radical is
quizzes.a: a catalyst, because it is regenerated
w: a reactant that is used up
quizzes.e: Cl• is re-formed in the second step, so one radical can break down thousands of ozone molecules. The overall reaction is 2O₃ → 3O₂.

quizzes.q: Why were CFCs banned, and what have chemists done since?
quizzes.e: Research by different groups of scientists gave evidence that CFCs destroy the ozone layer, which led to legislation (the Montreal Protocol) banning them. Chemists developed chlorine-free alternatives such as HFCs.

quizzes.q: Mechanism/type of reaction for bromoethane → ethanol (NaOH(aq), warm)?
quizzes.e: bromoethane → ethanol with NaOH(aq), warm is nucleophilic substitution. Identify how the functional group changes and what attacks it.

quizzes.q: Mechanism/type of reaction for bromoethane → ethene (KOH in ethanol, hot)?
quizzes.e: bromoethane → ethene with KOH in ethanol, hot is elimination. Identify how the functional group changes and what attacks it.

quizzes.q: Mechanism/type of reaction for bromoethane → propanenitrile (KCN in aqueous ethanol, reflux)?
quizzes.e: bromoethane → propanenitrile with KCN in aqueous ethanol, reflux is nucleophilic substitution. Identify how the functional group changes and what attacks it.

quizzes.q: Mechanism/type of reaction for bromoethane → ethylamine (excess NH₃ in ethanol, heat under pressure)?
quizzes.e: bromoethane → ethylamine with excess NH₃ in ethanol, heat under pressure is nucleophilic substitution. Identify how the functional group changes and what attacks it.

quizzes.q: In nucleophilic substitution of CH₃CH₂Br by OH⁻, the curly arrows are
quizzes.a: lone pair of OH⁻ to C, and C–Br bond to Br
w: C to OH⁻, Br to C
quizzes.e: One arrow from the OH⁻ lone pair to the δ+ C; one from the C–Br bond to Br, which leaves as Br⁻.

quizzes.q: In elimination with OH⁻, OH⁻ attacks
quizzes.a: an H on the carbon next to the C–Br
quizzes.e: In elimination, OH⁻ acts as a base and removes an H⁺ from the carbon next to the C–Br; the C–H electrons form the C=C and Br⁻ leaves.

quizzes.q: Explain why tertiary halogenoalkanes favour elimination.
quizzes.e: Tertiary halogenoalkanes have bulky alkyl groups around the C–X carbon (steric hindrance), so OH⁻ cannot easily reach it and acts as a base instead.

quizzes.q: Why is hydrolysis with water and AgNO₃ in ethanol used to compare C–X rates?
quizzes.e: As the halogenoalkane is hydrolysed, halide ions are released and form a silver halide precipitate. The time taken for the precipitate to appear compares the rates.

quizzes.q: Which product forms first in AgNO₃/ethanol tests: 1-chloro-, 1-bromo- or 1-iodobutane?
quizzes.e: The C–I bond is weakest, so 1-iodobutane hydrolyses fastest and the yellow AgI precipitate appears first. C–Cl is slowest (white AgCl last).

quizzes.q: Moles of NH₃ needed for 0.25 mol bromoethane → ethylamine (equation uses 2NH₃).
quizzes.e: CH₃CH₂Br + 2NH₃ → CH₃CH₂NH₂ + NH₄Br, so n(NH₃) = 2 × 0.25 = 0.50 mol.

quizzes.q: Nitrile formation is useful because
quizzes.a: it adds a carbon to the chain
quizzes.e: CN⁻ substitution adds one carbon atom, lengthening the carbon chain in a synthesis.

quizzes.q: Mechanism of CN⁻ with 1-bromopropane?
quizzes.e: CN⁻ has a lone pair and attacks the δ+ carbon, replacing Br⁻: nucleophilic substitution, giving butanenitrile.

quizzes.q: Product of 1-bromopropane with KCN?
quizzes.e: CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + CN⁻ → CH₃CH₂CH₂CN + Br⁻. The nitrile has 4 carbons: butanenitrile.

quizzes.q: Reagents/conditions for bromoethane → ethylamine?
quizzes.a: excess NH₃ in ethanol, heat under pressure
quizzes.e: bromoethane → ethylamine: use excess NH₃ in ethanol, heat under pressure. The reaction type is nucleophilic substitution.

quizzes.q: Bromine water with an alkene goes
quizzes.e: Orange bromine water is decolourised as Br₂ adds across the C=C bond (electrophilic addition). This is the test for an alkene.

quizzes.q: Major product of HBr + propene
quizzes.e: H⁺ adds to the end carbon to form the more stable secondary carbocation, which then bonds to Br⁻, giving 2-bromopropane (Markovnikov's rule).

quizzes.q: Why is 2-bromopropane the major product?
quizzes.e: A secondary carbocation is more stable than a primary one because the alkyl groups push electrons towards the positive carbon, so it forms faster and gives the major product.

quizzes.q: Mechanism of alkene + Br₂
quizzes.e: The C=C bond is electron rich and induces a dipole in Br₂. The δ+ Br is attacked by the π electrons, so the mechanism is electrophilic addition.

quizzes.q: The addition polymer of ethene is
quizzes.e: Ethene molecules join by addition polymerisation into poly(ethene). The saturated C–C chain is non-polar and unreactive.

quizzes.q: An electrophile is
quizzes.e: An electrophile accepts a pair of electrons (e.g. H⁺, NO₂⁺, Br₂ with an induced dipole).

quizzes.q: Alkenes are reactive because the C=C has
quizzes.a: a high electron density π bond
quizzes.e: The π bond is a region of high electron density above and below the C–C axis, so it attracts electrophiles.

quizzes.q: Product of propene + H₂ (Ni, 150 °C)?
quizzes.e: Hydrogenation: H₂ adds across the C=C with a nickel catalyst, giving the alkane.

quizzes.q: Reagents/conditions for ethene → bromoethane?
quizzes.e: ethene → bromoethane: use HBr, room temperature. The reaction type is electrophilic addition.

quizzes.q: Reagents/conditions for ethene → 1,2-dibromoethane?
quizzes.e: ethene → 1,2-dibromoethane: use Br₂, room temperature. The reaction type is electrophilic addition.

quizzes.q: Reagents/conditions for ethene → ethyl hydrogensulfate?
quizzes.e: ethene → ethyl hydrogensulfate: use cold concentrated H₂SO₄. The reaction type is electrophilic addition.

quizzes.q: Major product of propene + HBr?
quizzes.e: H⁺ adds to the end carbon, forming the more stable secondary carbocation; Br⁻ then bonds to the middle carbon, giving 2-bromopropane.

quizzes.q: Stability of carbocations:
quizzes.e: Alkyl groups push electron density towards the positive carbon (positive inductive effect), so more alkyl groups make the carbocation more stable.

quizzes.q: In Br₂ + ethene, Br₂ acts as an electrophile because
quizzes.a: the C=C induces a dipole in Br₂
quizzes.e: The high electron density of the C=C repels electrons in Br₂, making the nearer Br δ+.

quizzes.q: Product of ethene + Br₂ in the presence of Cl⁻(aq)?
quizzes.e: After Br⁺ adds, the carbocation can be attacked by Br⁻ or by Cl⁻ from the solution, so some 1-bromo-2-chloroethane forms as well as 1,2-dibromoethane.

quizzes.q: Addition polymers are
quizzes.a: unreactive because of strong C–C and C–H bonds
quizzes.e: Poly(alkenes) are saturated with strong, non-polar C–C and C–H bonds, so they are chemically inert.

quizzes.q: A section of polymer is –CH₂–CH(Cl)–CH₂–CH(Cl)–. The monomer is
quizzes.e: The repeating unit is –CH₂–CHCl–. Put back the C=C between its two carbons to get the monomer, chloroethene.

quizzes.q: Mechanism/type of reaction for ethene → bromoethane (HBr, room temperature)?
quizzes.e: ethene → bromoethane with HBr, room temperature is electrophilic addition. Identify how the functional group changes and what attacks it.

quizzes.q: Mechanism/type of reaction for ethene → 1,2-dibromoethane (Br₂, room temperature)?
quizzes.e: ethene → 1,2-dibromoethane with Br₂, room temperature is electrophilic addition. Identify how the functional group changes and what attacks it.

quizzes.q: Mechanism/type of reaction for ethene → ethyl hydrogensulfate (cold concentrated H₂SO₄)?
quizzes.e: ethene → ethyl hydrogensulfate with cold concentrated H₂SO₄ is electrophilic addition. Identify how the functional group changes and what attacks it.

quizzes.q: How many H atoms in an alkene with 8 carbons and one C=C?
quizzes.e: Alkenes with one C=C have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ, so with n = 8 there are 16 H atoms.

quizzes.q: First step in ethene + HBr mechanism?
quizzes.a: π electrons attack H of HBr, H–Br bond breaks to Br
quizzes.e: The π electrons of C=C attack the δ+ H of HBr, and the H–Br bond breaks heterolytically to Br⁻, forming a carbocation. Br⁻ then attacks the carbocation.

quizzes.q: Explain why 2-bromopropane is the major product of propene + HBr.
quizzes.e: The secondary carbocation is more stable than the primary one because it has two alkyl groups pushing electron density onto the positive carbon, so it forms faster.

quizzes.q: Major product of 2-methylpropene + HBr?
quizzes.e: H⁺ adds to the CH₂ end, forming the very stable tertiary carbocation (CH₃)₃C⁺; Br⁻ then bonds to it, giving 2-bromo-2-methylpropane.

quizzes.q: Repeat unit of poly(propene)?
quizzes.e: Open the C=C: two carbons in the main chain, with the CH₃ as a branch.

quizzes.q: Ethyl hydrogensulfate + water gives
quizzes.e: Ethene + conc. H₂SO₄ gives ethyl hydrogensulfate; adding water hydrolyses it to ethanol and regenerates H₂SO₄, which is a catalyst overall.

quizzes.q: Mass of Br₂ (g, 3 s.f.) that adds to 2.80 g ethene (Mr 28.0; Br₂ 159.8).
quizzes.e: C₂H₄ + Br₂ → C₂H₄Br₂ (1 : 1). n(ethene) = 2.80 ÷ 28.0 = 0.100 mol, so mass of Br₂ = 0.100 × 159.8 = 16.0 g.

quizzes.q: 1.00 g of an alkene CₙH₂ₙ reacts with 2.85 g Br₂ (Mr 159.8). n = ?
quizzes.e: One C=C reacts with one Br₂. n(Br₂) = 2.85 ÷ 159.8 = 0.0178 mol, so Mr(alkene) = 1.00 ÷ 0.0178 ≈ 56. CₙH₂ₙ has Mr = 14n, so n = 4 (C₄H₈).

quizzes.q: Why is bromine water decolourised by alkenes but not alkanes?
quizzes.e: Br₂ adds across the C=C bond of an alkene (electrophilic addition), removing the orange colour. Alkanes have no C=C, so no reaction happens without UV light.

quizzes.q: Plasticisers make PVC more flexible by
quizzes.a: getting between chains and reducing forces between them
quizzes.e: Plasticiser molecules push the chains apart, weakening intermolecular forces so chains slide more easily.

quizzes.q: How many H atoms in an alkene with 7 carbons and one C=C?
quizzes.e: Alkenes with one C=C have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ, so with n = 7 there are 14 H atoms.

quizzes.q: Primary alcohol + excess acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ under reflux gives
quizzes.e: Under reflux with excess oxidising agent, a primary alcohol is oxidised to an aldehyde and then fully to a carboxylic acid. Distilling immediately would stop at the aldehyde.

quizzes.q: Tertiary alcohols with acidified dichromate
quizzes.e: Tertiary alcohols have no hydrogen on the carbon bonded to OH, so they cannot be oxidised by acidified dichromate. The orange colour stays.

quizzes.q: Moles of CO₂ per mole of glucose fermented?
quizzes.e: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂, so 2 mol of CO₂ form per mole of glucose (yeast, 35 °C, anaerobic).

quizzes.q: Colour change when dichromate oxidises an alcohol?
quizzes.e: The orange Cr₂O₇²⁻ ion (Cr +6) is reduced to green Cr³⁺ (+3) as the alcohol is oxidised.

quizzes.q: Alcohol dehydration uses
quizzes.e: Dehydration (elimination of water) needs a concentrated acid catalyst such as H₃PO₄ or H₂SO₄ and heat, giving an alkene.

quizzes.q: Reagents/conditions for ethene → ethanol?
w: excess NH₃ in ethanol, heat under pressure
quizzes.e: ethene → ethanol: use steam, H₃PO₄ catalyst, 300 °C, 6–7 MPa. The reaction type is hydration (electrophilic addition).

quizzes.q: Reagents/conditions for glucose → ethanol?
w: excess NH₃ in ethanol, heat under pressure
quizzes.e: glucose → ethanol: use yeast, 35 °C, anaerobic. The reaction type is fermentation.

quizzes.q: Reagents/conditions for ethanol → ethanal?
quizzes.e: ethanol → ethanal: use acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, distil as formed. The reaction type is oxidation.

quizzes.q: Reagents/conditions for ethanol → ethanoic acid?
quizzes.e: ethanol → ethanoic acid: use excess acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, reflux. The reaction type is oxidation.

quizzes.q: Reagents/conditions for propan-2-ol → propanone?
quizzes.e: propan-2-ol → propanone: use acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, heat. The reaction type is oxidation.

quizzes.q: Why is fermentation kept at about 35 °C?
quizzes.a: fast enough rate without denaturing enzymes
quizzes.e: Higher temperatures would denature the yeast enzymes; lower ones make the reaction too slow.

quizzes.q: Bioethanol is called carbon-neutral because
quizzes.a: CO₂ absorbed in photosynthesis = CO₂ released
quizzes.e: The CO₂ released when bioethanol is burned equals the CO₂ the crops absorbed by photosynthesis. In practice, farming, transport and processing release extra CO₂.

quizzes.q: Why is an aldehyde distilled off as it forms?
quizzes.a: to stop further oxidation to a carboxylic acid
quizzes.e: Distilling the aldehyde off immediately prevents it being oxidised further to a carboxylic acid.

quizzes.q: Mechanism/type of reaction for ethene → ethanol (steam, H₃PO₄ catalyst, 300 °C, 6–7 MPa)?
quizzes.e: ethene → ethanol with steam, H₃PO₄ catalyst, 300 °C, 6–7 MPa is hydration (electrophilic addition). Identify how the functional group changes and what attacks it.

quizzes.q: Mechanism/type of reaction for glucose → ethanol (yeast, 35 °C, anaerobic)?
