quizzes.e: glucose → ethanol with yeast, 35 °C, anaerobic is fermentation. Identify how the functional group changes and what attacks it.

quizzes.q: Mechanism/type of reaction for ethanol → ethanal (acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, distil as formed)?
quizzes.e: ethanol → ethanal with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, distil as formed is oxidation. Identify how the functional group changes and what attacks it.

quizzes.q: Mechanism/type of reaction for ethanol → ethanoic acid (excess acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, reflux)?
quizzes.e: ethanol → ethanoic acid with excess acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, reflux is oxidation. Identify how the functional group changes and what attacks it.

quizzes.q: Mechanism/type of reaction for propan-2-ol → propanone (acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, heat)?
quizzes.e: propan-2-ol → propanone with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, heat is oxidation. Identify how the functional group changes and what attacks it.

quizzes.q: Mechanism/type of reaction for ethanol → ethene (concentrated H₃PO₄, heat)?
quizzes.e: ethanol → ethene with concentrated H₃PO₄, heat is elimination (dehydration). Identify how the functional group changes and what attacks it.

quizzes.q: Mass of ethanol from 6.06 g glucose by fermentation (Mr 180.0 → 2 × 46.0), 3 s.f.?
quizzes.e: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂. n(glucose) = 6.06 ÷ 180.0 = 0.0337 mol, so n(ethanol) = 0.0673 mol and mass = 0.0673 × 46.0 = 3.1 g.

quizzes.q: Mass of ethanol from 9.87 g glucose by fermentation (Mr 180.0 → 2 × 46.0), 3 s.f.?
quizzes.e: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂. n(glucose) = 9.87 ÷ 180.0 = 0.0548 mol, so n(ethanol) = 0.11 mol and mass = 0.11 × 46.0 = 5.04 g.

quizzes.q: Mechanism of acid-catalysed dehydration of alcohols?
quizzes.e: The OH is protonated, water leaves to form a carbocation, then H⁺ is lost from an adjacent carbon to form C=C.

quizzes.q: Dehydration of butan-2-ol can give how many alkenes (including E/Z)?
quizzes.e: H can be removed from C1 or C3: from C1 gives but-1-ene; from C3 gives but-2-ene, which has E and Z isomers. So 3 alkenes.

quizzes.q: Product of butan-2-ol with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇?
quizzes.e: Butan-2-ol is a secondary alcohol, so it is oxidised to a ketone, butanone. Ketones are not oxidised further.

quizzes.q: Fermentation: mass of glucose (g, 3 s.f.) needed for 23.0 g ethanol (Mr 180.0, 46.0).
quizzes.e: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂. n(ethanol) = 23.0 ÷ 46.0 = 0.500 mol, so n(glucose) = 0.250 mol, and mass = 0.250 × 180.0 = 45.0 g.

quizzes.q: Why is reflux used to oxidise a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid?
quizzes.e: Heating under reflux lets volatile substances (the alcohol and aldehyde) evaporate, condense and return to the flask, so the oxidation goes all the way to the carboxylic acid.

quizzes.q: Give one advantage of making ethanol by hydration of ethene over fermentation.
quizzes.e: Hydration of ethene is fast, continuous and gives a purer product with a high atom economy (100%). But ethene comes from crude oil, a non-renewable resource.

quizzes.q: Half-equation for oxidation of ethanol to ethanal:
quizzes.e: Ethanol loses two H atoms: as a half-equation, 2H⁺ and 2e⁻ are released.

quizzes.q: Which alcohol gives a positive Tollens' test after distilling with acidified dichromate?
quizzes.e: Propan-1-ol is a primary alcohol; distilling with acidified dichromate gives the aldehyde propanal, which gives a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent.

quizzes.q: Colour change when a secondary alcohol is warmed with acidified dichromate?
quizzes.e: The secondary alcohol is oxidised to a ketone, and orange Cr₂O₇²⁻ is reduced to green Cr³⁺.

quizzes.q: Reagents/conditions for ethanol → ethene?
quizzes.e: ethanol → ethene: use concentrated H₃PO₄, heat. The reaction type is elimination (dehydration).

quizzes.q: Test for an aldehyde
quizzes.a: Tollens' reagent gives a silver mirror
quizzes.e: Aldehydes reduce Tollens' reagent [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ to silver, giving a silver mirror. Ketones are not oxidised, so they give no mirror.

quizzes.q: Match each bond to its IR range (cm⁻¹)
quizzes.e: Use the data sheet: acid O–H 2500–3000 (very broad), C=O 1680–1750, alcohol O–H 3230–3550 (broad), C–H 2850–3300.

quizzes.q: A broad IR absorption at 2500–3000 cm⁻¹ shows
quizzes.e: A very broad absorption at 2500–3000 cm⁻¹ is the O–H of a carboxylic acid, broadened by hydrogen bonding.

quizzes.q: Integer Mr of C₂H₆O (M⁺ peak)?
quizzes.e: Mr = 2 × 12 + 6 × 1 + 16 = 46. The molecular ion peak M⁺ is at m/z = 46.

quizzes.q: What is the fingerprint region used for?
quizzes.e: The fingerprint region (below 1500 cm⁻¹) is unique to each compound, so comparing it with known spectra identifies the compound; it can also show impurities.

quizzes.q: A positive test for a carboxylic acid?
quizzes.e: carboxylic acid: Na₂CO₃: effervescence (CO₂).

quizzes.q: A positive test for a alkene?
quizzes.e: alkene: bromine water: orange → colourless.

quizzes.q: A positive test for a halogenoalkane?
quizzes.a: warm with NaOH(aq), acidify, AgNO₃: precipitate
quizzes.e: halogenoalkane: warm with NaOH(aq), acidify, AgNO₃: precipitate.

quizzes.q: A positive test for a primary/secondary alcohol?
quizzes.e: primary/secondary alcohol: acidified K₂Cr₂O₇: orange → green.

quizzes.q: A positive test for a aldehyde?
w: warm with NaOH(aq), acidify, AgNO₃: precipitate
quizzes.e: aldehyde: Tollens’ reagent: silver mirror.

quizzes.q: 2,4-DNPH: orange precipitate indicates a
quizzes.e: 2,4-DNPH: orange precipitate is the positive test for a aldehyde or ketone.

quizzes.q: acidified K₂Cr₂O₇: orange → green indicates a
quizzes.e: acidified K₂Cr₂O₇: orange → green is the positive test for a primary/secondary alcohol.

quizzes.q: Tollens’ reagent: silver mirror indicates a
quizzes.e: Tollens’ reagent: silver mirror is the positive test for a aldehyde.

quizzes.q: Na₂CO₃: effervescence (CO₂) indicates a
quizzes.e: Na₂CO₃: effervescence (CO₂) is the positive test for a carboxylic acid.

quizzes.q: bromine water: orange → colourless indicates a
quizzes.e: bromine water: orange → colourless is the positive test for a alkene.

quizzes.q: warm with NaOH(aq), acidify, AgNO₃: precipitate indicates a
quizzes.e: warm with NaOH(aq), acidify, AgNO₃: precipitate is the positive test for a halogenoalkane.

quizzes.q: IR absorption range for C≡N?
quizzes.e: From the data sheet, C≡N absorbs at 2220–2260 cm⁻¹. Use these ranges to identify functional groups in an IR spectrum.

quizzes.q: IR absorption range for O–H (alcohols)?
quizzes.e: From the data sheet, O–H (alcohols) absorbs at 3230–3550 cm⁻¹ (broad). Use these ranges to identify functional groups in an IR spectrum.

quizzes.q: IR absorption range for C=C?
quizzes.e: From the data sheet, C=C absorbs at 1620–1680 cm⁻¹. Use these ranges to identify functional groups in an IR spectrum.

quizzes.q: IR absorption range for C–H?
quizzes.e: From the data sheet, C–H absorbs at 2850–3300 cm⁻¹. Use these ranges to identify functional groups in an IR spectrum.

quizzes.q: Peaks at 1720 cm⁻¹ and 2500–3000 cm⁻¹ (broad). Compound type?
quizzes.e: 1720 cm⁻¹ is C=O; the very broad 2500–3000 cm⁻¹ band is the O–H of a carboxylic acid.

quizzes.q: A peak at 1700 cm⁻¹ and no broad O–H. Possible compound?
quizzes.e: C=O is present but there is no O–H, so it is a ketone or aldehyde, not an acid or alcohol.

quizzes.q: Fingerprint region is used to
quizzes.a: identify a compound by matching a known spectrum
quizzes.e: The fingerprint region (below 1500 cm⁻¹) is unique to each compound. Matching it with a database spectrum identifies the compound.

quizzes.q: Why do CO₂, H₂O and CH₄ contribute to global warming?
quizzes.e: The bonds in CO₂, H₂O and CH₄ absorb infrared radiation emitted by the Earth, so they trap heat in the atmosphere.

quizzes.q: Compound X gives a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent and has an IR peak at about 1730 cm⁻¹. What type of compound is X?
quizzes.e: Only aldehydes give a silver mirror; the IR peak confirms C=O.

quizzes.q: High-resolution MS gives M⁺ = 44.0262. Which formula fits? (C 12.0000, H 1.0078, O 15.9949)
A positive test for a aldehyde or ketone?
quizzes.e: aldehyde or ketone: 2,4-DNPH: orange precipitate.

quizzes.q: IR absorption range for C=O?
quizzes.e: From the data sheet, C=O absorbs at 1680–1750 cm⁻¹. Use these ranges to identify functional groups in an IR spectrum.

quizzes.q: IR absorption range for O–H (acids)?
quizzes.e: From the data sheet, O–H (acids) absorbs at 2500–3000 cm⁻¹ (very broad). Use these ranges to identify functional groups in an IR spectrum.

quizzes.q: IR absorption range for N–H?
quizzes.e: From the data sheet, N–H absorbs at 3300–3500 cm⁻¹. Use these ranges to identify functional groups in an IR spectrum.

quizzes.q: ΔH = +50 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔS = +200 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Minimum T for feasibility?
quizzes.e: Feasible when ΔG = ΔH − TΔS ≤ 0. Convert ΔS to kJ: 0.200 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. T = ΔH ÷ ΔS = 50 ÷ 0.200 = 250 K.

quizzes.q: Lattice enthalpy is more exothermic for ions that are
quizzes.e: Smaller ions get closer together and higher charges attract more strongly, so the electrostatic attraction in the lattice is stronger and the lattice enthalpy is more exothermic.

quizzes.q: When is a reaction feasible?
quizzes.e: A reaction is feasible when ΔG = ΔH − TΔS is zero or negative.

quizzes.q: Entropy increases when
quizzes.a: a gas is produced from a solid
quizzes.e: Gases have much more disorder (more ways of arranging particles and energy) than solids, so forming a gas from a solid increases entropy.

quizzes.q: The first electron affinity of oxygen is
w: larger than the second in magnitude and positive
quizzes.e: O(g) + e⁻ → O⁻(g) releases energy because the nucleus attracts the electron. The second electron affinity is endothermic because the electron is repelled by O⁻.

quizzes.q: Entropy is a measure of
quizzes.e: Entropy S measures disorder: the number of ways particles and their energy can be arranged.

quizzes.q: Which has the highest entropy?
quizzes.e: Gas particles move freely and randomly, with many more ways of arranging the particles and their energy, so gases have the highest entropy.

quizzes.q: Enthalpy of hydration is
quizzes.a: the enthalpy change when 1 mol of gaseous ions dissolves in water
quizzes.e: ΔhydH is the enthalpy change when 1 mol of gaseous ions dissolves in water to form aqueous ions. It is exothermic because the ions attract water molecules.

quizzes.q: ΔsolH =
quizzes.a: lattice dissociation enthalpy + sum of hydration enthalpies
quizzes.e: By Hess's law, ΔsolH = ΔLH (lattice dissociation, endothermic) + ΣΔhydH of the ions (exothermic).

quizzes.q: A reaction with ΔH > 0 and ΔS < 0 is
quizzes.e: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. With ΔH positive and ΔS negative, −TΔS is positive, so ΔG is positive at every temperature and the reaction is never feasible.

quizzes.q: Why do perfect ionic model lattice enthalpies differ from Born–Haber values?
quizzes.e: The perfect ionic model treats ions as perfect spheres. In reality the cation can polarise the anion, giving some covalent character, so the Born–Haber value is more exothermic.

quizzes.q: A reaction with ΔH < 0 and ΔS > 0 is
quizzes.e: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. With ΔH negative and ΔS positive, −TΔS is negative too, so ΔG is negative at every temperature.

quizzes.q: ΔH = 143 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔS = 123 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Temperature at which ΔG = 0 (3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: ΔG = 0 when T = ΔH ÷ ΔS. Convert ΔH to J: 143000 J mol⁻¹. T = 143000 ÷ 123 = 1160 K.

quizzes.q: ΔH = 104 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔS = 298 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Temperature at which ΔG = 0 (3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: ΔG = 0 when T = ΔH ÷ ΔS. Convert ΔH to J: 104000 J mol⁻¹. T = 104000 ÷ 298 = 349 K.

quizzes.q: ΔH = -189 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔS = -26 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Temperature at which ΔG = 0 (3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: ΔG = 0 when T = ΔH ÷ ΔS. Convert ΔH to J: −189000 J mol⁻¹. T = −189000 ÷ −26 = 7270 K.

quizzes.q: ΔH = 45 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔS = 91 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Temperature at which ΔG = 0 (3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: ΔG = 0 when T = ΔH ÷ ΔS. Convert ΔH to J: 45000 J mol⁻¹. T = 45000 ÷ 91 = 495 K.

quizzes.q: ΔH = -98 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔS = -124 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, T = 833 K. Find ΔG (kJ mol⁻¹, 3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Convert ΔS to kJ: −0.124 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS = −98 − 833 × (−0.124) = 5.29 kJ mol⁻¹.

quizzes.q: ΔH = -16 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔS = -56 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, T = 579 K. Find ΔG (kJ mol⁻¹, 3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Convert ΔS to kJ: −0.056 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS = −16 − 579 × (−0.056) = 16.4 kJ mol⁻¹.

quizzes.q: ΔH = 47 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔS = -153 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, T = 678 K. Find ΔG (kJ mol⁻¹, 3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Convert ΔS to kJ: −0.153 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS = 47 − 678 × (−0.153) = 151 kJ mol⁻¹.

quizzes.q: ΔH = 157 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔS = 191 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, T = 968 K. Find ΔG (kJ mol⁻¹, 3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Convert ΔS to kJ: 0.191 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS = 157 − 968 × (0.191) = −27.9 kJ mol⁻¹.

quizzes.q: Why might a feasible reaction (ΔG < 0) not happen?
quizzes.e: ΔG tells us whether a reaction is thermodynamically feasible, not how fast it goes. A high activation energy can make it too slow to observe (kinetically inert).

quizzes.q: The second electron affinity of oxygen is endothermic because
quizzes.a: an electron is added to a negative ion, which repels it
quizzes.e: O⁻(g) + e⁻ → O²⁻(g): the electron is added to a negative ion, so energy is needed to overcome the repulsion. It is endothermic.

quizzes.q: Lattice enthalpy of MgO is more exothermic than NaCl because
quizzes.a: Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ have higher charges and are smaller
quizzes.e: Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ have double the charges of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ and are smaller, so the electrostatic attraction in the lattice is much stronger.

quizzes.q: A graph of ΔG against T has gradient
quizzes.e: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS has the form y = c + mx, with y = ΔG and x = T, so the gradient is −ΔS and the intercept is ΔH.

quizzes.q: Use the cycle to calculate the enthalpy of lattice formation of NaCl.
quizzes.e: By Hess's law, ΔfH = atomisation of Na + atomisation of ½Cl₂ + IE(Na) + EA(Cl) + lattice formation. So lattice formation = −411 − (107 + 122 + 496 − 349) = −787 kJ mol⁻¹.

quizzes.q: Born–Haber for NaCl: Na at +107, Cl at +122, IE1 Na +496, EA Cl -349, ΔfH NaCl -411 kJ mol⁻¹. Find the lattice enthalpy of formation.
quizzes.e: By Hess's law, ΔfH = atomisations + IE + EA + lattice formation. So lattice formation = −411 − (107 + 122 + 496 + (−349)) = −787 kJ mol⁻¹.

quizzes.q: Born–Haber for KCl: K at +89, Cl at +122, IE1 K +419, EA Cl -349, ΔfH KCl -437 kJ mol⁻¹. Find the lattice enthalpy of formation.
quizzes.e: By Hess's law, ΔfH = atomisations + IE + EA + lattice formation. So lattice formation = −437 − (89 + 122 + 419 + (−349)) = −718 kJ mol⁻¹.

quizzes.q: Born–Haber for NaBr: Na at +107, Br at +112, IE1 Na +496, EA Br -325, ΔfH NaBr -361 kJ mol⁻¹. Find the lattice enthalpy of formation.
quizzes.e: By Hess's law, ΔfH = atomisations + IE + EA + lattice formation. So lattice formation = −361 − (107 + 112 + 496 + (−325)) = −751 kJ mol⁻¹.

quizzes.q: S° values (N₂ 192, H₂ 131, NH₃ 193 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹). Find ΔS for N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃.
quizzes.e: ΔS = ΣS(products) − ΣS(reactants) = 386 − 585 = −199 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Multiply each S by its coefficient.

quizzes.q: S° values (CH₄ 186, O₂ 205, CO₂ 214, H₂O(l) 70 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹). Find ΔS for CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O(l).
quizzes.e: ΔS = ΣS(products) − ΣS(reactants) = 354 − 596 = −242 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Multiply each S by its coefficient.

quizzes.q: S° values (C(s) 5.7, O₂ 205, CO₂ 214 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹). Find ΔS for C(s) + O₂ → CO₂.
quizzes.e: ΔS = ΣS(products) − ΣS(reactants) = 214 − 210.7 = 3.3 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Multiply each S by its coefficient.

quizzes.q: rate = k[A]²[B]. Overall order?
quizzes.e: The overall order is the sum of the individual orders: 2 (for A) + 1 (for B) = 3.

quizzes.q: Second order in A. [A] doubles. Rate increases by a factor of
quizzes.e: rate ∝ [A]², so doubling [A] multiplies the rate by 2² = 4.

quizzes.q: Units of k for a first-order reaction
quizzes.e: For rate = k[A], k = rate ÷ [A] = (mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹) ÷ (mol dm⁻³) = s⁻¹.

quizzes.q: What is the rate-determining step?
quizzes.e: The rate-determining step is the slowest step in the mechanism. Species in the rate equation appear in (or before) this step.

quizzes.q: Plotting ln k against 1/T gives a gradient of
quizzes.e: The Arrhenius equation in log form is ln k = ln A − Ea/(RT). A graph of ln k against 1/T is a straight line of gradient −Ea/R and intercept ln A.

quizzes.q: Overall order is
quizzes.a: the sum of the orders for each reactant
quizzes.e: The overall order is the sum of the powers in the rate equation, e.g. rate = k[A]ᵐ[B]ⁿ has overall order m + n.

quizzes.q: rate = k[A]^2[B]^0, k = 2.35, [A] = 0.85, [B] = 0.84 (consistent units). Rate (3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: rate = 2.35 × 0.85^2 × 0.84^0 = 1.7 mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. Anything to the power 0 is 1.

quizzes.q: rate = k[A]^2[B]^0, k = 2.41, [A] = 0.75, [B] = 0.87 (consistent units). Rate (3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: rate = 2.41 × 0.75^2 × 0.87^0 = 1.36 mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. Anything to the power 0 is 1.

quizzes.q: rate = k[A]^1[B]^2, k = 4.41, [A] = 0.14, [B] = 0.92 (consistent units). Rate (3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: rate = 4.41 × 0.14^1 × 0.92^2 = 0.523 mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. Anything to the power 0 is 1.

quizzes.q: For a zero-order reactant, a concentration–time graph is
quizzes.a: a straight line with negative gradient
quizzes.e: For zero order the rate does not depend on concentration, so the concentration falls at a constant rate: a straight line with a negative gradient.

quizzes.q: For a first-order reaction, half-life is
quizzes.e: A first-order reaction has a constant half-life, t½ = ln 2 ÷ k, whatever the starting concentration.

quizzes.q: Why can't the rate equation be found from the balanced equation?
quizzes.e: The rate equation depends on the mechanism (the rate-determining step), not on the overall stoichiometry, so it must be found by experiment.

quizzes.q: A rate–concentration graph that is a straight line through the origin shows
quizzes.e: A straight line through the origin means rate ∝ [A], which is first order with respect to A.

quizzes.q: Which is a continuous monitoring method for following the rate of a reaction that produces a gas?
quizzes.a: collecting the gas in a gas syringe and reading the volume every 30 s
w: measuring the time for a cross to disappear once
measuring initial rates in separate experiments
titrating one sample at the end
quizzes.e: Continuous monitoring follows one reaction mixture over time; a concentration–time (or volume–time) graph is then drawn and its gradients give the rate.

quizzes.q: When [A] is multiplied by 2 (all else constant), the rate is multiplied by 1. What is the order with respect to A?
quizzes.e: Rate factor = (concentration factor)^order. 2^0 = 1, so the order with respect to A is 0.

quizzes.q: When [A] is multiplied by 3 (all else constant), the rate is multiplied by 1. What is the order with respect to A?
quizzes.e: Rate factor = (concentration factor)^order. 3^0 = 1, so the order with respect to A is 0.

quizzes.q: When [A] is multiplied by 2 (all else constant), the rate is multiplied by 2. What is the order with respect to A?
quizzes.e: Rate factor = (concentration factor)^order. 2^1 = 2, so the order with respect to A is 1.

quizzes.q: Units of k for an overall first-order reaction?
quizzes.e: k = rate ÷ [concentration]^order. Rate is in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹, so each extra order adds mol⁻¹ dm³ to the units.

quizzes.q: Units of k for an overall third-order reaction?
quizzes.e: k = rate ÷ [concentration]^order. Rate is in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹, so each extra order adds mol⁻¹ dm³ to the units.

quizzes.q: Units of k for an overall zero-order reaction?
quizzes.e: k = rate ÷ [concentration]^order. Rate is in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹, so each extra order adds mol⁻¹ dm³ to the units.

quizzes.q: Units of k for an overall second-order reaction?
quizzes.e: k = rate ÷ [concentration]^order. Rate is in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹, so each extra order adds mol⁻¹ dm³ to the units.

quizzes.q: If rate = k[A][B], the slow step involves
quizzes.e: Species that appear in the rate equation are involved in or before the rate-determining step, so the slow step involves one A and one B.

quizzes.q: How can you find order using the initial rates method?
quizzes.e: Change the initial concentration of one reactant at a time, keeping the others constant, and compare the initial rates: if doubling it doubles the rate, it is first order.

quizzes.q: Increasing temperature increases k because
quizzes.e: At a higher temperature more molecules have energy ≥ Ea, so k increases (k = Ae^(−Ea/RT)).

quizzes.q: A ln k vs 1/T graph has intercept
quizzes.e: ln k = ln A − (Ea/R)(1/T). A graph of ln k against 1/T has intercept ln A and gradient −Ea/R.

quizzes.q: rate = k[A]^1[B]^2. When [A] = 0.10 and [B] = 0.20 mol dm⁻³, rate = 0.0255 mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. Find k (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: k = rate/([A]^1[B]^2); overall order 3, so the units are mol⁻² dm⁶ s⁻¹.

quizzes.q: rate = k[A]^1[B]^1. When [A] = 0.10 and [B] = 0.20 mol dm⁻³, rate = 0.0322 mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. Find k (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: k = rate/([A]^1[B]^1); overall order 2, so the units are mol⁻¹ dm³ s⁻¹.

quizzes.q: rate = k[A]^1[B]^1. When [A] = 0.10 and [B] = 0.20 mol dm⁻³, rate = 0.0346 mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. Find k (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: k = rate/([A]^1[B]^1); overall order 2, so the units are mol⁻¹ dm³ s⁻¹.

quizzes.q: rate = k[A]^1[B]^2. When [A] = 0.10 and [B] = 0.20 mol dm⁻³, rate = 0.0288 mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. Find k (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: k = rate/([A]^1[B]^2); overall order 3, so the units are mol⁻² dm⁶ s⁻¹.

quizzes.q: k increases by a factor of 4.73 from 298 K to 320 K. Find Ea (kJ mol⁻¹, 3 s.f.).
k increases by a factor of 4.73 from 300 K to 320 K. Find Ea (kJ mol⁻¹, 3 s.f.).
k increases by a factor of 57.9 from 300 K to 340 K. Find Ea (kJ mol⁻¹, 3 s.f.).

topics.title: 3.1.10 Equilibrium constant Kp for homogeneous systems

quizzes.q: Total pressure 200 kPa, mole fraction of N₂ 0.25. Partial pressure of N₂?
quizzes.e: Partial pressure = mole fraction × total pressure = 0.25 × 200 = 50 kPa.

quizzes.q: Kp expressions use
quizzes.e: Kp uses the partial pressures of the gases only. Solids and liquids are left out because they do not have a partial pressure.

quizzes.q: 2NO₂ ⇌ N₂O₄: pNO₂ = 50 kPa, pN₂O₄ = 25 kPa. Kp?
quizzes.e: Kp = p(N₂O₄) ÷ p(NO₂)² = 25 ÷ 50² = 0.01. The units are kPa ÷ kPa² = kPa⁻¹.

quizzes.q: What is a mole fraction?
quizzes.e: Mole fraction of a gas = moles of that gas ÷ total moles of gas in the mixture. The mole fractions add up to 1.

quizzes.q: Total pressure equals
quizzes.a: the sum of the partial pressures
quizzes.e: Dalton's law: the total pressure of a gas mixture equals the sum of the partial pressures of the gases in it.

quizzes.q: Sum of mole fractions in a mixture is
quizzes.e: Each mole fraction is moles of one gas ÷ total moles, so the mole fractions of all the gases add up to 1.

quizzes.q: What does Kp depend on?
quizzes.e: Kp, like Kc, depends only on temperature. Pressure and concentration changes shift the position, not the constant.

quizzes.q: Mole fraction 0.33, total pressure 657 kPa. Partial pressure (3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: Partial pressure = mole fraction × total pressure = 0.33 × 657 = 217 kPa.

quizzes.q: Mole fraction 0.29, total pressure 381 kPa. Partial pressure (3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: Partial pressure = mole fraction × total pressure = 0.29 × 381 = 110 kPa.

quizzes.q: Mole fraction 0.15, total pressure 542 kPa. Partial pressure (3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: Partial pressure = mole fraction × total pressure = 0.15 × 542 = 81.3 kPa.

quizzes.q: For N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, units of Kp are
quizzes.e: Kp = p(NH₃)² ÷ (p(N₂) × p(H₂)³). Units: kPa² ÷ kPa⁴ = kPa⁻².

quizzes.q: Increasing total pressure for N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂
quizzes.e: Higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles: the left (1 mol N₂O₄ vs 2 mol NO₂). Kp depends only on temperature, so it is unchanged.

quizzes.q: A mixture has 0.4 mol N₂, 1.8 mol H₂ and 1.8 mol NH₃. Mole fraction of NH₃ (3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: Mole fraction = moles of NH₃ ÷ total moles = 1.8 ÷ (0.4 + 1.8 + 1.8) = 0.45.

quizzes.q: A mixture has 0.4 mol N₂, 1.9 mol H₂ and 0.9 mol NH₃. Mole fraction of NH₃ (3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: Mole fraction = moles of NH₃ ÷ total moles = 0.9 ÷ (0.4 + 1.9 + 0.9) = 0.281.

quizzes.q: A mixture has 1.6 mol N₂, 1.6 mol H₂ and 0.7 mol NH₃. Mole fraction of NH₃ (3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: Mole fraction = moles of NH₃ ÷ total moles = 0.7 ÷ (1.6 + 1.6 + 0.7) = 0.179.

quizzes.q: A mixture has 1.4 mol N₂, 1.4 mol H₂ and 1.7 mol NH₃. Mole fraction of NH₃ (3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: Mole fraction = moles of NH₃ ÷ total moles = 1.7 ÷ (1.4 + 1.4 + 1.7) = 0.378.

quizzes.q: N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂. p(N₂O₄) = 87 kPa, p(NO₂) = 47 kPa. Kp (kPa, 3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: Kp = p(NO₂)² ÷ p(N₂O₄) = 47² ÷ 87 = 25.4 kPa.

quizzes.q: N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂. p(N₂O₄) = 106 kPa, p(NO₂) = 192 kPa. Kp (kPa, 3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: Kp = p(NO₂)² ÷ p(N₂O₄) = 192² ÷ 106 = 348 kPa.

quizzes.q: N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂. p(N₂O₄) = 164 kPa, p(NO₂) = 157 kPa. Kp (kPa, 3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: Kp = p(NO₂)² ÷ p(N₂O₄) = 157² ÷ 164 = 150 kPa.

quizzes.q: Why are solids not included in Kp?
quizzes.e: Kp uses partial pressures, and only gases have partial pressures, so solids (and liquids) are left out.

quizzes.q: For an exothermic reaction, raising temperature makes Kp
quizzes.e: For an exothermic forward reaction, a higher temperature shifts the equilibrium left (endothermic direction), so Kp decreases.

quizzes.q: A catalyst's effect on Kp is
quizzes.e: A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally, so it has no effect on Kp or the position of equilibrium.

quizzes.q: For CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g), Kp =
quizzes.e: CaCO₃ and CaO are solids, so they are left out: Kp = p(CO₂).

quizzes.q: 1.0 mol N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂; at equilibrium 0.46 mol N₂O₄ has dissociated and total pressure is 441 kPa. Find Kp (kPa, 3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Moles: N₂O₄ = 1.0 − 0.46 = 0.54, NO₂ = 2 × 0.46 = 0.92, total = 1.46. Partial pressures: N₂O₄ 163 kPa, NO₂ 278 kPa. Kp = 278² ÷ 163 = 473 kPa.

quizzes.q: 1.0 mol N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂; at equilibrium 0.45 mol N₂O₄ has dissociated and total pressure is 280 kPa. Find Kp (kPa, 3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Moles: N₂O₄ = 1.0 − 0.45 = 0.55, NO₂ = 2 × 0.45 = 0.90, total = 1.45. Partial pressures: N₂O₄ 106 kPa, NO₂ 174 kPa. Kp = 174² ÷ 106 = 284 kPa.

quizzes.q: 1.0 mol N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂; at equilibrium 0.23 mol N₂O₄ has dissociated and total pressure is 250 kPa. Find Kp (kPa, 3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Moles: N₂O₄ = 1.0 − 0.23 = 0.77, NO₂ = 2 × 0.23 = 0.46, total = 1.23. Partial pressures: N₂O₄ 157 kPa, NO₂ 93.5 kPa. Kp = 93.5² ÷ 157 = 55.9 kPa.

quizzes.q: 1.0 mol N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂; at equilibrium 0.54 mol N₂O₄ has dissociated and total pressure is 389 kPa. Find Kp (kPa, 3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Moles: N₂O₄ = 1.0 − 0.54 = 0.46, NO₂ = 2 × 0.54 = 1.08, total = 1.54. Partial pressures: N₂O₄ 116 kPa, NO₂ 273 kPa. Kp = 273² ÷ 116 = 640 kPa.

quizzes.q: H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI at 480 kPa: mole fractions H₂ 0.24, I₂ 0.33, HI 0.43. Kp (3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: Each partial pressure is (mole fraction) × P. Kp = (x_HI P)² ÷ (x_H₂ P × x_I₂ P) = 0.43² ÷ (0.24 × 0.33) = 2.33. P cancels and Kp has no units.

quizzes.q: H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI at 423 kPa: mole fractions H₂ 0.23, I₂ 0.27, HI 0.5. Kp (3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: Each partial pressure is (mole fraction) × P. Kp = (x_HI P)² ÷ (x_H₂ P × x_I₂ P) = 0.5² ÷ (0.23 × 0.27) = 4.03. P cancels and Kp has no units.

quizzes.q: H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI at 435 kPa: mole fractions H₂ 0.29, I₂ 0.22, HI 0.49. Kp (3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: Each partial pressure is (mole fraction) × P. Kp = (x_HI P)² ÷ (x_H₂ P × x_I₂ P) = 0.49² ÷ (0.29 × 0.22) = 3.76. P cancels and Kp has no units.

quizzes.q: E°: Zn²⁺/Zn −0.76 V, Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34 V. E°cell?
quizzes.e: E°cell = E°(right, positive) − E°(left, negative) = +0.34 − (−0.76) = 1.10 V.

quizzes.q: In a cell, the more negative electrode
quizzes.e: The electrode with the more negative E° releases electrons: it is oxidised and is the negative terminal (anode). Electrons flow from it through the wire.

quizzes.q: What does a salt bridge do?
quizzes.e: The salt bridge (e.g. filter paper soaked in KNO₃) lets ions move between the half-cells to complete the circuit and balance the charge, without the solutions mixing.

quizzes.q: Standard hydrogen electrode conditions
quizzes.a: 1.00 mol dm⁻³ H⁺, 100 kPa H₂, 298 K, Pt electrode
quizzes.e: The SHE uses 1.00 mol dm⁻³ H⁺, H₂ gas at 100 kPa, 298 K and a platinum electrode. Its E° is defined as 0.00 V.

quizzes.q: A hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell produces
quizzes.e: Overall: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. The only product is water, but the hydrogen must be made and stored, which needs energy.

quizzes.q: The standard electrode potential of the SHE is
quizzes.e: The standard hydrogen electrode is the reference electrode; its standard electrode potential is defined as 0.00 V.

quizzes.q: In a cell, electrons flow through the wire from
quizzes.a: the negative electrode to the positive electrode
quizzes.e: Oxidation at the negative electrode releases electrons, which flow through the external wire to the positive electrode, where reduction occurs.

quizzes.q: In the cell shown, which electrode is the negative electrode?
quizzes.e: Zn is more easily oxidised (more negative E°); electrons leave it.

quizzes.q: E° Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ = +0.77 V and Ni²⁺/Ni = -0.25 V. Find E°cell (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: E°cell = E°(more positive) − E°(more negative) = +0.77 − (−0.25) = 1.02 V.

quizzes.q: E° Cu²⁺/Cu = +0.34 V and Fe²⁺/Fe = -0.44 V. Find E°cell (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: E°cell = E°(more positive) − E°(more negative) = +0.34 − (−0.44) = 0.78 V.

quizzes.q: In conventional cell notation, the left-hand side is
quizzes.e: Conventional notation puts the oxidation half-cell (the negative electrode) on the left, e.g. Zn ∣ Zn²⁺ ∥ Cu²⁺ ∣ Cu.

quizzes.q: A platinum electrode is used when
quizzes.a: the half-cell has no solid metal (e.g. Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺)
quizzes.e: If neither species in the half-cell is a solid metal (e.g. Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺), an inert platinum electrode conducts the electrons without reacting.

quizzes.q: Why is a salt bridge not made of copper wire?
quizzes.e: A salt bridge must let ions move to balance the charge. A copper wire would conduct electrons and would set up its own half-cells with the solutions.

quizzes.q: Lithium cells are rechargeable because
quizzes.a: the reactions can be reversed by applying a current
quizzes.e: In rechargeable cells such as lithium-ion cells, the reactions can be reversed by applying an external current, which regenerates the reactants.

quizzes.q: Use Eᶿ values to predict the direction of the reaction between Cu²⁺(aq) and Zn(s). Eᶿ(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V, Eᶿ(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V.
quizzes.a: Zn reduces Cu²⁺: Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu is feasible
w: Cu reduces Zn²⁺: Cu + Zn²⁺ → Cu²⁺ + Zn is feasible
quizzes.e: The more negative electrode (Zn) loses electrons and the more positive species (Cu²⁺) gains them. Ecell = +0.34 − (−0.76) = +1.10 V, which is positive, so the reaction in this direction is feasible.

quizzes.q: E° MnO₄⁻/Mn²⁺ = +1.51 V and Cu²⁺/Cu = +0.34 V. Find E°cell (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: E°cell = E°(more positive) − E°(more negative) = +1.51 − (+0.34) = 1.17 V.

quizzes.q: E° I₂/I⁻ = +0.54 V and Ni²⁺/Ni = -0.25 V. Find E°cell (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: E°cell = E°(more positive) − E°(more negative) = +0.54 − (−0.25) = 0.79 V.

quizzes.q: E° MnO₄⁻/Mn²⁺ = +1.51 V and Mg²⁺/Mg = -2.37 V. Find E°cell (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: E°cell = E°(more positive) − E°(more negative) = +1.51 − (−2.37) = 3.88 V.

quizzes.q: E° Cu²⁺/Cu = +0.34 V and MnO₄⁻/Mn²⁺ = +1.51 V. Find E°cell (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: E°cell = E°(more positive) − E°(more negative) = +1.51 − (+0.34) = 1.17 V.

quizzes.q: Cell from Cu²⁺/Cu (+0.34 V) and Zn²⁺/Zn (-0.76 V): which half-cell is the negative electrode?
quizzes.e: Zn²⁺/Zn has the more negative E° (−0.76 V), so it releases electrons more readily: it is oxidised and is the negative electrode.

quizzes.q: Cell from Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ (+0.77 V) and MnO₄⁻/Mn²⁺ (+1.51 V): which half-cell is the negative electrode?
quizzes.e: Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ has the more negative E° (+0.77 V), so it releases electrons more readily: it is oxidised and is the negative electrode.

quizzes.q: Cell from Mg²⁺/Mg (-2.37 V) and Ag⁺/Ag (+0.80 V): which half-cell is the negative electrode?
quizzes.e: Mg²⁺/Mg has the more negative E° (−2.37 V), so it releases electrons more readily: it is oxidised and is the negative electrode.

quizzes.q: Cell from Ni²⁺/Ni (-0.25 V) and MnO₄⁻/Mn²⁺ (+1.51 V): which half-cell is the negative electrode?
quizzes.e: Ni²⁺/Ni has the more negative E° (−0.25 V), so it releases electrons more readily: it is oxidised and is the negative electrode.

quizzes.q: A fuel cell differs from a battery because
quizzes.e: In a fuel cell the reactants (e.g. H₂ and O₂) are supplied continuously, so it does not need recharging; a battery stores a fixed amount of reactants.

quizzes.q: Give one disadvantage of hydrogen fuel cells.
quizzes.e: Hydrogen is flammable and hard to store, and it is often made using energy from fossil fuels, so fuel cells are not carbon-neutral.

quizzes.q: Changing concentrations from 1 mol dm⁻³ changes
quizzes.e: Changing the concentration from 1 mol dm⁻³ shifts the half-cell equilibrium (Le Chatelier), so the electrode potential is no longer the standard value.

quizzes.q: E°cell positive means the reaction
quizzes.e: A positive E°cell means ΔG is negative, so the reaction is feasible as written (although it may still be slow).

quizzes.q: Which is the strongest oxidising agent: Pb²⁺ (E° -0.13 V) or Ni²⁺ (E° -0.25 V)?
quizzes.e: The more positive E° (−0.13 V) means Pb²⁺ is more easily reduced (it gains electrons more readily), so it is the stronger oxidising agent.

quizzes.q: Which is the strongest oxidising agent: Cl₂ (E° +1.36 V) or Fe³⁺ (E° +0.77 V)?
quizzes.e: The more positive E° (+1.36 V) means Cl₂ is more easily reduced (it gains electrons more readily), so it is the stronger oxidising agent.

quizzes.q: Which is the strongest oxidising agent: MnO₄⁻ (E° +1.51 V) or Fe²⁺ (E° -0.44 V)?
quizzes.e: The more positive E° (+1.51 V) means MnO₄⁻ is more easily reduced (it gains electrons more readily), so it is the stronger oxidising agent.

quizzes.q: Which is the strongest oxidising agent: Pb²⁺ (E° -0.13 V) or Fe³⁺ (E° +0.77 V)?
quizzes.e: The more positive E° (+0.77 V) means Fe³⁺ is more easily reduced (it gains electrons more readily), so it is the stronger oxidising agent.

quizzes.q: E° Mg²⁺/Mg = -2.37 V and Ni²⁺/Ni = -0.25 V. Find E°cell (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: E°cell = E°(more positive) − E°(more negative) = −0.25 − (−2.37) = 2.12 V.

quizzes.q: E° Ni²⁺/Ni = -0.25 V and Cl₂/Cl⁻ = +1.36 V. Find E°cell (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: E°cell = E°(more positive) − E°(more negative) = +1.36 − (−0.25) = 1.61 V.

quizzes.q: pH of 0.010 mol dm⁻³ HCl?
quizzes.e: HCl is a strong acid, so [H⁺] = 0.010 mol dm⁻³. pH = −log₁₀(0.010) = 2.

quizzes.q: pH of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ NaOH at 298 K (Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴)?
Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵, 0.10 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid. pH (3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: For a weak acid [H⁺] ≈ √(Ka × c) = √(1.8 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.10) = 1.34 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³, so pH = 2.87.

quizzes.q: A buffer
quizzes.a: resists pH change when small amounts of acid or base are added
quizzes.e: A buffer (e.g. a weak acid and its salt) resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added. The large reservoirs of HA and A⁻ remove added H⁺ or OH⁻.

quizzes.q: Define a Brønsted–Lowry acid.
quizzes.e: A Brønsted–Lowry acid is a proton (H⁺) donor. A base is a proton acceptor.

quizzes.q: A strong acid
quizzes.e: A strong acid fully dissociates in water, e.g. HCl → H⁺ + Cl⁻.

quizzes.q: Kw at 298 K is
quizzes.e: Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol² dm⁻⁶ at 298 K.

quizzes.q: In the Brønsted–Lowry theory, a base is
w: a substance that releases OH⁻ only
quizzes.e: An acid donates H⁺ (a proton) and a base accepts it.

quizzes.q: pH of 0.1 mol dm⁻³ HCl (3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: HCl is a strong acid, so [H⁺] = 0.1 mol dm⁻³. pH = −log₁₀(0.1) = 1.

quizzes.q: pH of 0.05 mol dm⁻³ HCl (3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: HCl is a strong acid, so [H⁺] = 0.05 mol dm⁻³. pH = −log₁₀(0.05) = 1.3.

quizzes.q: pH of 0.02 mol dm⁻³ HCl (3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: HCl is a strong acid, so [H⁺] = 0.02 mol dm⁻³. pH = −log₁₀(0.02) = 1.7.

quizzes.q: [H⁺] for pH 8.08 (× 10⁻ⁿ notation: give the number, e.g. 3.2e-5)?
[H⁺] for pH 9.18 (× 10⁻ⁿ notation: give the number, e.g. 3.2e-5)?
Pure water at 50 °C has pH < 7 but is
quizzes.e: The dissociation of water is endothermic, so at 50 °C Kw is larger and [H⁺] is higher, giving pH < 7. But [H⁺] = [OH⁻], so water is still neutral.

quizzes.q: Why is ethanoic acid a weak acid?
quizzes.e: Ethanoic acid only partially dissociates in water: CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺, with the equilibrium well to the left.

quizzes.q: pKa =
quizzes.e: pKa = −log₁₀ Ka. A smaller pKa means a larger Ka, so a stronger acid.

quizzes.q: The best indicator for a weak acid–strong base titration is
quizzes.e: The equivalence point of a weak acid–strong base titration is above pH 7 (about 8–9), so phenolphthalein (range 8.3–10) changes colour at the right point.

quizzes.q: From the weak acid curve, where do you read pH = pKₐ?
quizzes.a: at half the equivalence volume (12.5 cm³)
quizzes.e: At half-neutralisation [HA] = [A⁻], so pH = pKₐ.

quizzes.q: pH of 0.1 mol dm⁻³ NaOH at 298 K (Kw = 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴, 3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: NaOH is a strong base, so [OH⁻] = 0.1. [H⁺] = Kw ÷ [OH⁻] = 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ ÷ 0.1 = 1 × 10⁻¹³. pH = −log(1 × 10⁻¹³) = 13.

quizzes.q: pH of 0.05 mol dm⁻³ NaOH at 298 K (Kw = 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴, 3 s.f.)?
quizzes.e: NaOH is a strong base, so [OH⁻] = 0.05. [H⁺] = Kw ÷ [OH⁻] = 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ ÷ 0.05 = 2 × 10⁻¹³. pH = −log(2 × 10⁻¹³) = 12.7.

quizzes.q: Weak acid, Ka = 1.80 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³, c = 0.5 mol dm⁻³. pH (3 s.f.)?
Weak acid, Ka = 1.35 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³, c = 0.05 mol dm⁻³. pH (3 s.f.)?
Weak acid, Ka = 1.80 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³, c = 0.05 mol dm⁻³. pH (3 s.f.)?
At half-neutralisation of a weak acid, pH =
quizzes.e: At half-neutralisation [HA] = [A⁻], so Ka = [H⁺] and pH = pKa.

quizzes.q: How does an ethanoic acid/ethanoate buffer resist added acid?
quizzes.e: The buffer has a large reservoir of CH₃COO⁻. Added H⁺ reacts with it: CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺ → CH₃COOH, so [H⁺] and the pH stay almost constant.

quizzes.q: Diluting a strong acid by a factor of 10 changes the pH by
quizzes.e: For a strong acid [H⁺] falls by a factor of 10, and −log of (x/10) is 1 more than −log x, so the pH rises by 1.

quizzes.q: Blood is buffered mainly by
quizzes.e: Blood is buffered mainly by carbonic acid and hydrogencarbonate ions: H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻, keeping its pH near 7.4.

quizzes.q: Kw = 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol² dm⁻⁶ at 298 K but 5.48 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol² dm⁻⁶ at 323 K. Pure water at 323 K is
w: acidic, because the pH is below 7
quizzes.e: The dissociation of water is endothermic, so Kw increases with temperature. In pure water [H⁺] = [OH⁻] always, so it is neutral, but pH = −log√(5.48 × 10⁻¹⁴) = 6.63.

topics.title: 3.2.4 Properties of Period 3 elements and their oxides

quizzes.q: Na₂O in water gives
quizzes.e: Na₂O is a basic ionic oxide. Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH, a strong alkali with pH about 14.

quizzes.q: SO₂ in water gives
quizzes.e: SO₂ is an acidic covalent oxide. SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃, a weak acid with pH about 3.

quizzes.q: Al₂O₃ is
quizzes.e: Al₂O₃ is amphoteric: it reacts with acids (forming Al³⁺ salts) and with bases (forming aluminate ions). It is insoluble in water.

quizzes.q: Why does MgO have a higher melting point than Na₂O?
quizzes.e: Both are ionic, but Mg²⁺ has a higher charge than Na⁺ and is smaller, so the attraction between the ions in MgO is stronger and more energy is needed to melt it.

quizzes.q: Sodium reacts with cold water to give
quizzes.e: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂. Sodium fizzes vigorously on the water surface and forms a strongly alkaline solution.

quizzes.q: Colour of the flame when Na burns?
quizzes.e: Sodium burns with a yellow-orange flame, forming white Na₂O.

quizzes.q: Mg burns in oxygen with a
quizzes.e: Magnesium burns with a brilliant white flame, forming white MgO.

quizzes.q: Sulfur burns in oxygen with a
quizzes.e: Sulfur burns with a blue flame, forming SO₂.

quizzes.q: Formula of the oxide formed when P burns in excess oxygen (most common Period 3 oxide)?
quizzes.e: P forms P₄O₁₀. Period 3: Na₂O, MgO, Al₂O₃, SiO₂, P₄O₁₀, SO₂.

quizzes.q: Formula of the oxide formed when Al burns in excess oxygen (most common Period 3 oxide)?
quizzes.e: Al forms Al₂O₃. Period 3: Na₂O, MgO, Al₂O₃, SiO₂, P₄O₁₀, SO₂.

quizzes.q: Formula of the oxide formed when Na burns in excess oxygen (most common Period 3 oxide)?
quizzes.e: Na forms Na₂O. Period 3: Na₂O, MgO, Al₂O₃, SiO₂, P₄O₁₀, SO₂.

quizzes.q: Formula of the oxide formed when S burns in excess oxygen (most common Period 3 oxide)?
quizzes.e: S forms SO₂. Period 3: Na₂O, MgO, Al₂O₃, SiO₂, P₄O₁₀, SO₂.

quizzes.q: Formula of the oxide formed when Mg burns in excess oxygen (most common Period 3 oxide)?
quizzes.e: Mg forms MgO. Period 3: Na₂O, MgO, Al₂O₃, SiO₂, P₄O₁₀, SO₂.

quizzes.q: Formula of the oxide formed when Si burns in excess oxygen (most common Period 3 oxide)?
quizzes.e: Si forms SiO₂. Period 3: Na₂O, MgO, Al₂O₃, SiO₂, P₄O₁₀, SO₂.

quizzes.q: Equation for SO₂ reacting with water:
quizzes.e: SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃ (sulfurous acid), a weak acid that gives a pH of about 2–3.

quizzes.q: Equation for P₄O₁₀ reacting with water:
quizzes.e: P₄O₁₀ + 6H₂O → 4H₃PO₄ (phosphoric(V) acid). Check: P 4 = 4, H 12 = 12, O 16 = 16.

quizzes.q: Why is SiO₂ insoluble in water?
quizzes.e: Many strong covalent bonds in the giant lattice would have to be broken; water cannot do this.

quizzes.q: Al₂O₃ reacts with NaOH(aq) to form
quizzes.e: Al₂O₃ is amphoteric. As an acid it reacts with NaOH and water to form the aluminate NaAl(OH)₄: Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH + 3H₂O → 2NaAl(OH)₄.

quizzes.q: pH of the solution when Al₂O₃ is added to water?
quizzes.e: Al₂O₃ gives pH 7 (insoluble). Ionic oxides react with water to give alkaline solutions, non-metal oxides give acidic solutions, and Al₂O₃ and SiO₂ are insoluble.

quizzes.q: pH of the solution when Na₂O is added to water?
quizzes.e: Na₂O gives pH about 14. Ionic oxides react with water to give alkaline solutions, non-metal oxides give acidic solutions, and Al₂O₃ and SiO₂ are insoluble.

quizzes.q: pH of the solution when P₄O₁₀ is added to water?
quizzes.e: P₄O₁₀ gives pH about 0–1. Ionic oxides react with water to give alkaline solutions, non-metal oxides give acidic solutions, and Al₂O₃ and SiO₂ are insoluble.

quizzes.q: pH of the solution when SiO₂ is added to water?
quizzes.e: SiO₂ gives pH 7 (insoluble). Ionic oxides react with water to give alkaline solutions, non-metal oxides give acidic solutions, and Al₂O₃ and SiO₂ are insoluble.

quizzes.q: pH of the solution when MgO is added to water?
quizzes.e: MgO gives pH about 9. Ionic oxides react with water to give alkaline solutions, non-metal oxides give acidic solutions, and Al₂O₃ and SiO₂ are insoluble.

quizzes.q: pH of the solution when SO₂ is added to water?
quizzes.e: SO₂ gives pH about 2–3. Ionic oxides react with water to give alkaline solutions, non-metal oxides give acidic solutions, and Al₂O₃ and SiO₂ are insoluble.

quizzes.q: Equation for SiO₂ reacting with NaOH:
quizzes.e: SiO₂ is an acidic oxide. It reacts with hot concentrated NaOH to form sodium silicate: SiO₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂SiO₃ + H₂O.

quizzes.q: Equation for MgO reacting with HCl:
quizzes.e: MgO is a basic oxide, so it neutralises acids to form a salt and water: MgO + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂O.

quizzes.q: Equation for Al₂O₃ reacting with H₂SO₄:
quizzes.e: Amphoteric Al₂O₃ reacts as a base with acids: Al₂O₃ + 3H₂SO₄ → Al₂(SO₄)₃ + 3H₂O (balance Al, S and O).

quizzes.q: Explain why Na₂O has a higher melting point than P₄O₁₀.
quizzes.e: Na₂O is a giant ionic lattice with strong electrostatic attractions. P₄O₁₀ is molecular, with weak intermolecular forces, so less energy is needed to melt it.

quizzes.q: Explain why MgO has a higher melting point than Na₂O.
quizzes.e: Mg²⁺ has a higher charge and is smaller than Na⁺, so the ionic attraction in MgO is stronger.

quizzes.q: P₄O₁₀ is neutralised by NaOH. Product?
quizzes.e: P₄O₁₀ is acidic, so NaOH neutralises it to form the salt sodium phosphate and water: P₄O₁₀ + 12NaOH → 4Na₃PO₄ + 6H₂O.

quizzes.q: How many moles of NaOH neutralise 1 mol P₄O₁₀ fully?
quizzes.e: P₄O₁₀ + 12NaOH → 4Na₃PO₄ + 6H₂O. Each P₄O₁₀ forms 4 H₃PO₄, each needing 3 NaOH: 4 × 3 = 12 mol.

quizzes.q: How many moles of NaOH neutralise 0.050 mol SO₃ completely?
quizzes.e: SO₃ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + H₂O, so n(NaOH) = 2 × 0.050 = 0.10 mol.

quizzes.q: Why does the pH of the solution formed by Al₂O₃ in water stay at 7?
quizzes.e: Al₂O₃ is insoluble in water, so it does not form an acidic or alkaline solution and the pH stays at 7.

quizzes.q: Oxidation state of P in P₄O₁₀?
quizzes.e: O is −2, so 10 O give −20. 4 P must total +20, so each P is +5.

quizzes.q: Match each ion to its colour in solution
quizzes.e: The colour depends on the metal, its oxidation state, the ligand and the coordination number, because each of these changes the d-orbital energy gap ΔE.

quizzes.q: Why are transition metal complexes coloured?
quizzes.e: Ligands split the d orbitals into two energy levels. Electrons absorb visible light of energy ΔE to move up; the colour seen is the complementary colour of the light not absorbed.

quizzes.q: Shape of [CuCl₄]²⁻
quizzes.e: Cl⁻ ligands are large, so only four fit around Cu²⁺. Four bonding pairs with no lone pairs give a tetrahedral shape (109.5°).

quizzes.q: Shape of cisplatin
quizzes.e: Cisplatin, Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂, is a square planar Pt(II) complex with the two Cl⁻ ligands on the same side (cis).

quizzes.q: Coordination number in [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺?
quizzes.e: The coordination number is the number of co-ordinate (dative) bonds to the central metal ion. Six NH₃ ligands give 6.

quizzes.q: EDTA⁴⁻ is a
quizzes.e: EDTA⁴⁻ has six lone pairs (2 N and 4 O) that form six co-ordinate bonds to one metal ion, so it is hexadentate.

quizzes.q: Shape of [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺?
quizzes.e: [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ is linear. Small ligands (H₂O, NH₃) give 6-coordinate octahedral complexes; large Cl⁻ gives tetrahedral; Ag⁺ forms linear complexes and Pt(II) forms square planar ones.

quizzes.q: Shape of [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺?
quizzes.e: [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺ is octahedral. Small ligands (H₂O, NH₃) give 6-coordinate octahedral complexes; large Cl⁻ gives tetrahedral; Ag⁺ forms linear complexes and Pt(II) forms square planar ones.

quizzes.q: Shape of [CuCl₄]²⁻?
quizzes.e: [CuCl₄]²⁻ is tetrahedral. Small ligands (H₂O, NH₃) give 6-coordinate octahedral complexes; large Cl⁻ gives tetrahedral; Ag⁺ forms linear complexes and Pt(II) forms square planar ones.

quizzes.q: Shape of [CoCl₄]²⁻?
quizzes.e: [CoCl₄]²⁻ is tetrahedral. Small ligands (H₂O, NH₃) give 6-coordinate octahedral complexes; large Cl⁻ gives tetrahedral; Ag⁺ forms linear complexes and Pt(II) forms square planar ones.

quizzes.q: Shape of [Co(NH₃)₆]²⁺?
quizzes.e: [Co(NH₃)₆]²⁺ is octahedral. Small ligands (H₂O, NH₃) give 6-coordinate octahedral complexes; large Cl⁻ gives tetrahedral; Ag⁺ forms linear complexes and Pt(II) forms square planar ones.

quizzes.q: Shape of [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺?
quizzes.e: [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ is octahedral. Small ligands (H₂O, NH₃) give 6-coordinate octahedral complexes; large Cl⁻ gives tetrahedral; Ag⁺ forms linear complexes and Pt(II) forms square planar ones.

quizzes.q: A transition metal forms at least one stable ion with
quizzes.e: A transition metal forms at least one stable ion with an incomplete d sub-shell. Zn only forms Zn²⁺ (3d¹⁰), so it is not a transition metal.

quizzes.q: Electron configuration of the Cu²⁺ ion?
quizzes.e: Cu is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹; ions lose the 4s electrons first, then 3d, giving [Ar] 3d⁹.

quizzes.q: Explain why carbon monoxide is toxic.
quizzes.e: CO forms a stronger co-ordinate bond to the Fe(II) in haemoglobin than oxygen does, so it replaces the oxygen and the blood can no longer transport O₂.

quizzes.q: Tollens' reagent distinguishes aldehydes from ketones because the aldehyde
quizzes.a: reduces [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ to metallic silver, forming a silver mirror
quizzes.e: The aldehyde is oxidised to a carboxylic acid (carboxylate), and Ag⁺ is reduced to Ag. Ketones are not oxidised, so there is no change.

quizzes.q: Colour of [Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺?
quizzes.e: [Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺ is pale violet (yellow in solution). Colour depends on the metal, its oxidation state, the ligands and the co-ordination number.

quizzes.q: Colour of [CuCl₄]²⁻?
quizzes.e: [CuCl₄]²⁻ is yellow. Colour depends on the metal, its oxidation state, the ligands and the co-ordination number.

quizzes.q: Colour of [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺?
quizzes.e: [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ is blue. Colour depends on the metal, its oxidation state, the ligands and the co-ordination number.

quizzes.q: Colour of [Co(NH₃)₆]²⁺?
quizzes.e: [Co(NH₃)₆]²⁺ is pale brown (straw). Colour depends on the metal, its oxidation state, the ligands and the co-ordination number.

quizzes.q: Colour of [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺?
quizzes.e: [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺ is deep blue. Colour depends on the metal, its oxidation state, the ligands and the co-ordination number.

quizzes.q: Colour of [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺?
quizzes.e: [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ is colourless. Colour depends on the metal, its oxidation state, the ligands and the co-ordination number.

quizzes.q: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6Fe²⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 6Fe³⁺ + 7H₂O. Moles of Fe²⁺ per mol dichromate?
quizzes.e: Each Cr goes from +6 to +3, so one Cr₂O₇²⁻ accepts 6e⁻; each Fe²⁺ gives 1e⁻, so 6 Fe²⁺ are needed.

quizzes.q: 25.0 cm³ of Fe²⁺(aq) needs 22.40 cm³ of 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ KMnO₄. Find [Fe²⁺] (mol dm⁻³, 3 s.f.).
An iron tablet needs 15.00 cm³ of 0.0100 mol dm⁻³ KMnO₄. Mass of Fe (mg, 3 s.f., Ar 55.8).
Why does [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 4Cl⁻ change the coordination number?
quizzes.a: Cl⁻ is larger than H₂O, so fewer fit
quizzes.e: Cl⁻ ligands are larger than H₂O, so only four fit round Cu²⁺: octahedral (6) → tetrahedral (4).

quizzes.q: The chelate effect: [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 3en → [Cu(en)₃]²⁺ + 6H₂O is favourable because
quizzes.e: One [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ and three en (4 particles) form one complex and six H₂O (7 particles), so entropy increases. ΔH is about zero, so ΔG is negative.

quizzes.q: Which homogeneous catalysis step is correct for S₂O₈²⁻ + I⁻ with Fe²⁺?
quizzes.e: First Fe²⁺ reduces S₂O₈²⁻: S₂O₈²⁻ + 2Fe²⁺ → 2SO₄²⁻ + 2Fe³⁺. Then 2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂, regenerating the catalyst. Each step is between oppositely charged ions.

quizzes.q: Why is the reaction between S₂O₈²⁻ and I⁻ slow without a catalyst?
quizzes.e: S₂O₈²⁻ and I⁻ are both negative ions, so they repel each other and the activation energy is high.

quizzes.q: In the Contact process V₂O₅ acts as a
quizzes.e: V₂O₅ is a solid catalyst for gaseous reactants (heterogeneous). SO₂ + V₂O₅ → SO₃ + V₂O₄, then V₂O₄ + ½O₂ → V₂O₅, using variable oxidation states.

quizzes.q: Why does a transition metal complex appear coloured?
quizzes.e: Ligands split the d orbitals. Electrons absorb certain frequencies of visible light (ΔE = hν) to jump up; the remaining frequencies are transmitted or reflected and give the colour.

quizzes.q: Cisplatin works by
quizzes.e: Cisplatin binds to nitrogen atoms on guanine in DNA, which stops the DNA replicating so the cancer cells cannot divide.

quizzes.q: A complex absorbs light of wavelength 482 nm. Find ΔE (× 10⁻¹⁹ J, 3 s.f.; h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴, c = 3.00 × 10⁸).
A complex absorbs light of wavelength 620 nm. Find ΔE (× 10⁻¹⁹ J, 3 s.f.; h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴, c = 3.00 × 10⁸).
A complex absorbs light of wavelength 559 nm. Find ΔE (× 10⁻¹⁹ J, 3 s.f.; h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴, c = 3.00 × 10⁸).
Colorimetry: absorbance 1.14, calibration gives A = 20c (c in mol dm⁻³). Find c (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Absorbance is proportional to concentration: c = A ÷ 20 = 1.14 ÷ 20 = 0.057 mol dm⁻³.

quizzes.q: Colorimetry: absorbance 0.73, calibration gives A = 50c (c in mol dm⁻³). Find c (3 s.f.).
quizzes.e: Absorbance is proportional to concentration: c = A ÷ 50 = 0.73 ÷ 50 = 0.0146 mol dm⁻³.

topics.title: 3.2.6 Reactions of ions in aqueous solution

quizzes.q: Cu²⁺(aq) + NaOH(aq) gives
quizzes.e: Cu²⁺ forms a blue precipitate of [Cu(H₂O)₄(OH)₂] with NaOH. It does not dissolve in excess NaOH.

quizzes.q: Fe³⁺(aq) + NaOH(aq) gives
quizzes.e: Fe³⁺ forms an orange-brown precipitate of [Fe(H₂O)₃(OH)₃] with NaOH. Fe²⁺ would give a green precipitate.

quizzes.q: [Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺ is more acidic than [Fe(H₂O)₆]²⁺ because
quizzes.a: Fe³⁺ has a higher charge density
quizzes.e: Fe³⁺ is smaller and more highly charged than Fe²⁺, so it has a higher charge density. It polarises the O–H bonds in its water ligands more, so H⁺ is released more easily.

quizzes.q: What forms when excess NH₃ is added to Cu(OH)₂?
quizzes.e: Excess ammonia replaces four ligands: [Cu(H₂O)₄(OH)₂] + 4NH₃ → [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺ + 2OH⁻ + 2H₂O, a deep blue solution.

quizzes.q: Al(OH)₃ dissolves in excess NaOH because it is
quizzes.e: Al(OH)₃ is amphoteric: it reacts with excess OH⁻ to form the soluble aluminate ion [Al(OH)₄]⁻, so the white precipitate dissolves.

quizzes.q: Observation when a few drops of NaOH(aq) are added to Cu²⁺(aq)?
quizzes.e: Cu²⁺ gives a blue precipitate: OH⁻ removes H⁺ from the water ligands, forming a neutral metal hydroxide precipitate.

quizzes.q: Observation when a few drops of NaOH(aq) are added to Fe³⁺(aq)?
quizzes.e: Fe³⁺ gives a orange-brown precipitate: OH⁻ removes H⁺ from the water ligands, forming a neutral metal hydroxide precipitate.

quizzes.q: Observation when a few drops of NaOH(aq) are added to Al³⁺(aq)?
quizzes.e: Al³⁺ gives a white precipitate: OH⁻ removes H⁺ from the water ligands, forming a neutral metal hydroxide precipitate.

quizzes.q: Observation when a few drops of NaOH(aq) are added to Fe²⁺(aq)?
quizzes.e: Fe²⁺ gives a green precipitate: OH⁻ removes H⁺ from the water ligands, forming a neutral metal hydroxide precipitate.

quizzes.q: Equation for [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 2OH⁻:
quizzes.e: OH⁻ removes H⁺ from two water ligands, giving the neutral blue precipitate Cu(H₂O)₄(OH)₂.

quizzes.q: Why is [Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺ more acidic than [Fe(H₂O)₆]²⁺?
quizzes.a: Fe³⁺ has a higher charge density, polarising O–H bonds more
quizzes.e: Fe³⁺ is smaller and more highly charged, so it polarises the O–H bonds in its water ligands more and releases H⁺ more readily.

quizzes.q: Equation for hydrolysis of [Al(H₂O)₆]³⁺:
quizzes.e: The 3+ ion polarises a water ligand, which loses H⁺ to a water molecule, forming H₃O⁺ (so the solution is acidic).

quizzes.q: Observation with excess NaOH(aq) for Fe²⁺(aq)?
quizzes.e: Fe²⁺ with excess NaOH: green precipitate (no change). Only amphoteric Al(OH)₃ dissolves in excess, forming [Al(OH)₄]⁻.

quizzes.q: Observation with excess NaOH(aq) for Fe³⁺(aq)?
quizzes.e: Fe³⁺ with excess NaOH: orange-brown precipitate (no change). Only amphoteric Al(OH)₃ dissolves in excess, forming [Al(OH)₄]⁻.

quizzes.q: Observation with excess NaOH(aq) for Al³⁺(aq)?
quizzes.e: Al³⁺ with excess NaOH: colourless solution. Only amphoteric Al(OH)₃ dissolves in excess, forming [Al(OH)₄]⁻.

quizzes.q: Observation with excess NaOH(aq) for Cu²⁺(aq)?
quizzes.e: Cu²⁺ with excess NaOH: blue precipitate (no change). Only amphoteric Al(OH)₃ dissolves in excess, forming [Al(OH)₄]⁻.

quizzes.q: Observation with excess NH₃(aq) for Cu²⁺(aq)?
quizzes.e: Cu²⁺ with excess NH₃: deep blue solution. NH₃ acts as a base first; only Cu²⁺ then undergoes ligand substitution, giving deep blue [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺.

quizzes.q: Observation with excess NH₃(aq) for Fe³⁺(aq)?
quizzes.e: Fe³⁺ with excess NH₃: orange-brown precipitate (no change). NH₃ acts as a base first; only Cu²⁺ then undergoes ligand substitution, giving deep blue [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺.

quizzes.q: Observation with excess NH₃(aq) for Fe²⁺(aq)?

quizzes.q: Blue solution gives a blue precipitate with NH₃, which dissolves in excess to a deep blue solution. Ion?

quizzes.q: Observation with Na₂CO₃(aq) for Fe²⁺(aq)?

quizzes.q: Observation with Na₂CO₃(aq) for Cu²⁺(aq)?

quizzes.q: Observation with Na₂CO₃(aq) for Fe³⁺(aq)?

quizzes.q: Which drug example shows why single enantiomers matter?
quizzes.e: Thalidomide was sold as a racemic mixture: one enantiomer treated morning sickness, but the other caused birth defects. This shows why single enantiomers matter in drugs.

quizzes.q: Number of chiral centres in CH₃CH(OH)CH(Cl)CH₃?
quizzes.e: C2 carries H, OH, CH₃ and CH(Cl)CH₃; C3 carries H, Cl, CH₃ and CH(OH)CH₃. Both have four different groups, so there are 2 chiral centres.

quizzes.q: Maximum number of stereoisomers for a molecule with 2 chiral centres?
quizzes.e: Each chiral centre can have two configurations, so the maximum is 2ⁿ = 2² = 4.

quizzes.q: Which product of nucleophilic addition to a ketone is NOT chiral?
quizzes.e: Propanone + HCN gives (CH₃)₂C(OH)CN. Its central carbon has two identical CH₃ groups, so it is not a chiral centre and the product is not chiral.

quizzes.q: Explain why the product of HCN + butanone is optically inactive.
quizzes.e: The C=O in butanone is planar, so CN⁻ attacks equally from either side, giving equal amounts of the two enantiomers (a racemic mixture) whose rotations cancel.

quizzes.q: Why might a drug company make a single enantiomer?
quizzes.e: Often only one enantiomer has the right shape to fit the target receptor; the other may be inactive or cause harmful side effects. A single enantiomer gives a safer, more effective drug.

quizzes.q: Which formula represents an optically active amino acid?
quizzes.e: In alanine, H₂NCH(CH₃)COOH, the central carbon has H, NH₂, CH₃ and COOH: four different groups, so it is chiral. Glycine has two H atoms on that carbon.

quizzes.q: How do enantiomers react with achiral reagents?
quizzes.e: Enantiomers have the same chemical properties and react identically with achiral reagents. They differ only with plane-polarised light and with other chiral molecules.

quizzes.q: Which compound has an enantiomer?
quizzes.e: C2 of 2-chlorobutane carries H, Cl, CH₃ and C₂H₅: four different groups.

quizzes.q: Which reaction of an alkene gives a racemic product?
quizzes.e: H⁺ adds to but-1-ene to give a planar secondary carbocation. Br⁻ attacks it equally from either side, so 2-bromobutane forms as a racemic mixture.

quizzes.q: Number of chiral centres in glucose's open-chain form (CHO(CHOH)₄CH₂OH)?
quizzes.e: In open-chain glucose, C2, C3, C4 and C5 each carry four different groups, so there are 4 chiral centres. C1 (CHO) and C6 (CH₂OH) are not chiral.

quizzes.q: Why is KCN used instead of HCN?
quizzes.e: HCN is a highly toxic gas, so acidified KCN is used to make it in situ. KCN itself is still toxic and must be handled carefully.

quizzes.e: The hydride ion H⁻ from NaBH₄ attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon, then the O⁻ is protonated. This is nucleophilic addition.

quizzes.q: Why is benzene more stable than expected?

quizzes.e: Benzene has six carbons and six hydrogens in a ring.

quizzes.q: The shape around each C in benzene is

quizzes.q: Benzene mainly undergoes
quizzes.e: Electrophilic substitution keeps the stable delocalised ring of π electrons intact; addition would destroy it.

quizzes.q: Electrophile in nitration?

quizzes.q: Why is the nitration temperature kept below about 55 °C?
