quizzes.q: Nitrobenzene is used to make
quizzes.e: Nitrobenzene is reduced to phenylamine for dyes; polynitro compounds such as TNT are explosives.

quizzes.q: Why does benzene resist addition reactions?
quizzes.e: Addition would break the delocalised ring and lose its extra stability; substitution keeps it.

quizzes.q: Mechanism/type of reaction for benzene → nitrobenzene (concentrated HNO₃ + concentrated H₂SO₄, 50 °C)?
quizzes.e: benzene → nitrobenzene with concentrated HNO₃ + concentrated H₂SO₄, 50 °C is electrophilic substitution. Identify how the functional group changes and what attacks it.

quizzes.q: Mechanism/type of reaction for benzene → phenylethanone (CH₃COCl, AlCl₃ catalyst)?
quizzes.e: benzene → phenylethanone with CH₃COCl, AlCl₃ catalyst is electrophilic substitution (Friedel–Crafts acylation). Identify how the functional group changes and what attacks it.

quizzes.q: Reagents/conditions for benzene → phenylethanone?
quizzes.e: benzene → phenylethanone: use CH₃COCl, AlCl₃ catalyst. The reaction type is electrophilic substitution (Friedel–Crafts acylation).

quizzes.q: Reagents/conditions for benzene → nitrobenzene?
quizzes.e: benzene → nitrobenzene: use concentrated HNO₃ + concentrated H₂SO₄, 50 °C. The reaction type is electrophilic substitution.

quizzes.q: Catalyst in Friedel–Crafts acylation?
quizzes.e: AlCl₃ is a halogen carrier: it generates the acylium ion RCO⁺.

quizzes.q: Explain the evidence that benzene is more stable than the Kekulé structure suggests.
quizzes.e: Hydrogenating benzene releases −208 kJ mol⁻¹, not the −360 kJ mol⁻¹ expected for three C=C (3 × −120). It is 152 kJ mol⁻¹ more stable because of delocalisation.

quizzes.q: Expected ΔH for hydrogenating a 'cyclohexatriene' if cyclohexene is −120 kJ mol⁻¹ (kJ mol⁻¹).
quizzes.e: One C=C releases −120 kJ mol⁻¹, so three would release 3 × (−120) = −360 kJ mol⁻¹.

quizzes.q: Delocalisation energy (kJ mol⁻¹) if benzene's actual ΔH hydrogenation is −208 and the expected is −360.
quizzes.e: Delocalisation energy = expected − actual = 360 − 208 = 152 kJ mol⁻¹ more stable.

quizzes.q: First mechanism step in nitration of benzene:
quizzes.e: The delocalised π electrons attack NO₂⁺, forming an unstable intermediate.

quizzes.q: Final step in electrophilic substitution:
quizzes.a: C–H bond electrons return to the ring, H⁺ is lost
quizzes.e: The electrons in the C–H bond return to the ring, restoring the delocalised π system, and H⁺ is lost.

quizzes.q: The intermediate in electrophilic substitution has
quizzes.a: a broken delocalised ring with + charge
quizzes.e: Part of the delocalised ring is broken; the positive charge is spread over the remaining five carbons.

quizzes.q: Regenerating the AlCl₃ catalyst:
quizzes.e: H⁺ lost from the ring reacts with AlCl₄⁻, regenerating the catalyst and forming HCl.

quizzes.q: Theoretical mass of nitrobenzene (g, 3 s.f., Mr 123.0) from 7.80 g benzene (Mr 78.0).
quizzes.e: 1 : 1 ratio. n(benzene) = 7.80 ÷ 78.0 = 0.100 mol, so mass of nitrobenzene = 0.100 × 123.0 = 12.3 g.

quizzes.q: Why is a C=C in cyclohexene more reactive towards Br₂ than benzene?
quizzes.e: The C=C in cyclohexene has a localised, high electron density that can polarise Br₂. In benzene the π electrons are spread out (delocalised), so the electron density is too low.

quizzes.q: Product of benzene + CH₃CH₂COCl / AlCl₃?
quizzes.e: Friedel–Crafts acylation adds the CH₃CH₂CO group to the ring: C₆H₅COCH₂CH₃.

quizzes.q: Name of C₆H₅COCH₃?
quizzes.e: A ketone with a phenyl group and a methyl group: phenylethanone.

quizzes.q: Strongest base
quizzes.e: The ethyl group pushes electrons onto N (positive inductive effect), so its lone pair is more available to accept a proton. Phenylamine's lone pair is delocalised.

quizzes.q: Why is phenylamine a weaker base than ammonia?
quizzes.e: The N lone pair overlaps with the delocalised π system of the ring, so it is less available to accept a proton.

quizzes.q: Nitrobenzene is reduced to phenylamine using
quizzes.e: Nitrobenzene is reduced with tin and concentrated HCl (heat under reflux), then NaOH is added to release the free amine.

quizzes.q: Amines are nucleophiles because they have
quizzes.e: The nitrogen atom has a lone pair that it can donate to a δ+ carbon, so amines are nucleophiles (and bases).

quizzes.q: Amines act as bases because
quizzes.a: N has a lone pair that accepts H⁺
quizzes.e: The lone pair on nitrogen accepts a proton (Brønsted–Lowry base).

quizzes.q: Primary amine general formula?
quizzes.e: One alkyl or aryl group on the nitrogen: RNH₂.

quizzes.q: Product of ethylamine + HCl?
quizzes.e: The amine accepts H⁺ from HCl, forming the salt CH₃CH₂NH₃⁺Cl⁻.

quizzes.q: Quaternary ammonium salts are used in
quizzes.e: The positive head and long chain make them cationic surfactants (fabric softeners, hair conditioners).

quizzes.q: Reagents/conditions for nitrobenzene → phenylamine?
quizzes.e: nitrobenzene → phenylamine: use Sn + concentrated HCl, then NaOH. The reaction type is reduction.

quizzes.q: Reagents/conditions for propanenitrile → propylamine?
quizzes.e: propanenitrile → propylamine: use LiAlH₄ or H₂/Ni. The reaction type is reduction.

quizzes.q: Order of base strength (strongest first)?
quizzes.e: Alkyl groups push electron density onto N (more available lone pair); a benzene ring delocalises it.

quizzes.q: Why is ethylamine a stronger base than ammonia?
quizzes.a: the ethyl group donates electrons, raising N's electron density
quizzes.e: The ethyl group has a positive inductive effect: it pushes electron density onto the nitrogen, so its lone pair is more available to accept H⁺.

quizzes.q: Reducing agent to convert nitrobenzene to phenylamine?
quizzes.e: Tin and concentrated HCl reduce the NO₂ group; NaOH then releases the free amine.

quizzes.q: Why is the amine from bromoethane + NH₃ often impure?
quizzes.a: further substitution gives secondary and tertiary amines
quizzes.e: The amine product is itself a nucleophile, so it reacts with more halogenoalkane.

quizzes.q: Nitrile reduction to an amine gives
quizzes.e: Reducing a nitrile (LiAlH₄ or H₂/Ni) gives only the primary amine, with no further substitution.

quizzes.q: Mechanism/type of reaction for nitrobenzene → phenylamine (Sn + concentrated HCl, then NaOH)?
quizzes.e: nitrobenzene → phenylamine with Sn + concentrated HCl, then NaOH is reduction. Identify how the functional group changes and what attacks it.

quizzes.q: Mechanism/type of reaction for propanenitrile → propylamine (LiAlH₄ or H₂/Ni)?
quizzes.e: propanenitrile → propylamine with LiAlH₄ or H₂/Ni is reduction. Identify how the functional group changes and what attacks it.

quizzes.q: Mechanism/type of reaction for ethylamine → N-ethylethanamide (ethanoyl chloride)?
quizzes.e: ethylamine → N-ethylethanamide with ethanoyl chloride is nucleophilic addition–elimination. Identify how the functional group changes and what attacks it.

quizzes.q: Reagents/conditions for ethylamine → N-ethylethanamide?
quizzes.e: ethylamine → N-ethylethanamide: use ethanoyl chloride. The reaction type is nucleophilic addition–elimination.

quizzes.q: Product of excess bromoethane with ammonia eventually?
quizzes.e: With excess halogenoalkane, substitution continues all the way to the quaternary salt (C₂H₅)₄N⁺Br⁻.

quizzes.q: Mechanism for ethylamine + bromoethane?
quizzes.e: The amine's lone pair attacks the δ+ C of the halogenoalkane, displacing Br⁻.

quizzes.q: Mechanism for ethylamine + ethanoyl chloride?
quizzes.e: The amine adds to the C=O, then Cl⁻ is eliminated: nucleophilic addition–elimination.

quizzes.q: Product of methylamine + ethanoyl chloride?
quizzes.e: Methylamine attacks ethanoyl chloride, giving the N-substituted amide CH₃CONHCH₃ and HCl.

quizzes.q: Mass of phenylamine (g, 3 s.f., Mr 93.0) from 24.6 g nitrobenzene (Mr 123.0) at 60% yield.
quizzes.e: 1 : 1 ratio. n(nitrobenzene) = 24.6 ÷ 123.0 = 0.200 mol; theoretical mass = 0.200 × 93.0 = 18.6 g; at 60% yield, 0.60 × 18.6 = 11.2 g.

quizzes.q: Equation for nitrobenzene reduction:
quizzes.e: Six [H] remove both O atoms as 2H₂O and add 2H to N.

quizzes.q: Why is NaOH added after Sn/HCl when making phenylamine?
quizzes.e: In acid, the product forms as the phenylammonium salt, C₆H₅NH₃⁺. Adding NaOH removes H⁺ and releases the free amine, C₆H₅NH₂.

quizzes.q: Explain why primary aliphatic amines are stronger bases than ammonia.
quizzes.e: Alkyl groups push electron density onto the nitrogen (positive inductive effect), so its lone pair is more available to accept a proton than in ammonia.

quizzes.q: Name of (CH₃)₂NH?
quizzes.e: Two methyl groups on the nitrogen make (CH₃)₂NH a secondary amine called dimethylamine.

quizzes.q: How many moles of HCl react with 1 mol ethane-1,2-diamine?
quizzes.e: Ethane-1,2-diamine has two NH₂ groups. Each accepts one H⁺, so 2 mol HCl react with 1 mol of the diamine.

quizzes.q: Which reagents make propylamine without further substitution?
quizzes.a: bromoethane + KCN, then reduce with LiAlH₄
quizzes.e: Bromoethane + KCN gives propanenitrile, CH₃CH₂CN (adding a carbon). Reducing it with LiAlH₄ gives only propylamine, CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂, with no further substitution.

quizzes.q: Polyesters form by
quizzes.e: A dicarboxylic acid and a diol join with the loss of a small molecule (water) for each ester link, so this is condensation polymerisation.

quizzes.q: Kevlar is a
quizzes.e: Kevlar is made from benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid (or its acyl chloride) and benzene-1,4-diamine, so it is an aromatic polyamide.

quizzes.q: Why are polyesters biodegradable but poly(alkenes) not?
quizzes.e: Ester links are polar, so they can be hydrolysed by acids, bases and enzymes. Poly(alkenes) have non-polar C–C and C–H bonds, so they are unreactive.

quizzes.q: A dicarboxylic acid + diamine forming nylon eliminates
quizzes.e: Each amide link forms with the loss of H₂O. If a diacyl chloride is used instead of the diacid, HCl is eliminated.

quizzes.q: Condensation polymerisation releases
quizzes.a: a small molecule such as water or HCl
quizzes.e: Each link formed releases a small molecule, usually H₂O (or HCl from an acyl chloride).

quizzes.q: Polyesters are formed from
quizzes.a: a diol and a dicarboxylic acid
quizzes.e: The OH of the diol reacts with COOH, forming ester links and water.

quizzes.q: Polyamides are formed from
quizzes.a: a diamine and a dicarboxylic acid (or diacyl chloride)
quizzes.e: The NH₂ reacts with COOH (or COCl), forming amide links and water (or HCl).

quizzes.q: Polymer made from chloroethene?
quizzes.e: chloroethene gives PVC by addition polymerisation.

quizzes.q: Polymer made from ethane-1,2-diol + benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid?
quizzes.e: ethane-1,2-diol + benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid gives Terylene (PET, a polyester) by condensation polymerisation.

quizzes.q: Polymer made from ethene?
quizzes.e: ethene gives poly(ethene) by addition polymerisation.

quizzes.q: Polymer made from propene?
quizzes.e: propene gives poly(propene) by addition polymerisation.

quizzes.q: Why are polyesters biodegradable?
quizzes.a: their polar ester links can be hydrolysed
quizzes.e: The polar C–O ester link can be attacked by nucleophiles and hydrolysed by water, acids or alkalis.

quizzes.q: Kevlar is strong because of
quizzes.e: The flat, rigid chains line up, and many N–H···O=C hydrogen bonds form between neighbouring chains.

quizzes.q: Poly(alkenes) are difficult to dispose of because they
quizzes.e: Strong non-polar C–C and C–H bonds mean they are not hydrolysed or broken down by microbes.

quizzes.q: An advantage of recycling polymers?
quizzes.a: reduces landfill and saves crude oil
quizzes.e: Recycling saves raw materials and energy, and reduces landfill; sorting and collecting are the drawbacks.

quizzes.q: Type of polymerisation for ethene → poly(ethene)?
quizzes.e: ethene → poly(ethene) is addition polymerisation. Addition polymers form from C=C monomers with no other product; condensation polymers lose a small molecule (H₂O or HCl) at each link.

quizzes.q: Type of polymerisation for propene → poly(propene)?
quizzes.e: propene → poly(propene) is addition polymerisation. Addition polymers form from C=C monomers with no other product; condensation polymers lose a small molecule (H₂O or HCl) at each link.

quizzes.q: Type of polymerisation for chloroethene → PVC?
quizzes.e: chloroethene → PVC is addition polymerisation. Addition polymers form from C=C monomers with no other product; condensation polymers lose a small molecule (H₂O or HCl) at each link.

quizzes.q: Type of polymerisation for ethane-1,2-diol + benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid → Terylene (PET, a polyester)?
quizzes.e: ethane-1,2-diol + benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid → Terylene (PET, a polyester) is condensation polymerisation. Addition polymers form from C=C monomers with no other product; condensation polymers lose a small molecule (H₂O or HCl) at each link.

quizzes.q: Type of polymerisation for hexane-1,6-diamine + hexanedioic acid → nylon-6,6 (a polyamide)?
quizzes.e: hexane-1,6-diamine + hexanedioic acid → nylon-6,6 (a polyamide) is condensation polymerisation. Addition polymers form from C=C monomers with no other product; condensation polymers lose a small molecule (H₂O or HCl) at each link.

quizzes.q: Type of polymerisation for benzene-1,4-diamine + benzene-1,4-dicarbonyl chloride → Kevlar (a polyamide)?
quizzes.e: benzene-1,4-diamine + benzene-1,4-dicarbonyl chloride → Kevlar (a polyamide) is condensation polymerisation. Addition polymers form from C=C monomers with no other product; condensation polymers lose a small molecule (H₂O or HCl) at each link.

quizzes.q: Type of polymerisation for 2-hydroxypropanoic acid → poly(lactic acid) (a polyester)?
quizzes.e: 2-hydroxypropanoic acid → poly(lactic acid) (a polyester) is condensation polymerisation. Addition polymers form from C=C monomers with no other product; condensation polymers lose a small molecule (H₂O or HCl) at each link.

quizzes.q: Repeat unit of nylon-6,6 contains
quizzes.e: Hexane-1,6-diamine and hexanedioic acid joined by amide links; 6 + 6 carbons.

quizzes.q: Molecules of water lost when 50 diol + 50 diacid monomers form one chain.
quizzes.e: Each new link releases one water molecule. A single chain of 100 monomers has 99 links, so 99 water molecules are lost.

quizzes.q: Hydrolysis of a polyamide with acid gives
quizzes.a: a dicarboxylic acid and a diammonium salt
quizzes.e: Acid hydrolysis breaks the amide links; the amine groups are protonated, forming an ammonium salt.

quizzes.q: Hydrolysis of a polyester with NaOH gives
quizzes.a: a diol and a dicarboxylate salt
quizzes.e: NaOH hydrolysis breaks the ester links; the acid is deprotonated to its carboxylate salt.

quizzes.q: Explain why nylon has a higher melting point than poly(ethene).
quizzes.e: Nylon chains form hydrogen bonds between N–H and C=O groups on neighbouring chains. Poly(ethene) has only weak van der Waals forces between chains.

quizzes.q: Monomers of PET (Terylene)?
quizzes.e: PET is a polyester from a diol and an aromatic dicarboxylic acid.

quizzes.q: Why is incinerating waste polymers controversial?
quizzes.e: Burning polymers releases CO₂ (a greenhouse gas) and can release toxic gases such as HCl from PVC, which must be removed. It does recover energy.

quizzes.q: Polymer made from hexane-1,6-diamine + hexanedioic acid?
quizzes.e: hexane-1,6-diamine + hexanedioic acid gives nylon-6,6 (a polyamide) by condensation polymerisation.

quizzes.q: Polymer made from benzene-1,4-diamine + benzene-1,4-dicarbonyl chloride?
quizzes.e: benzene-1,4-diamine + benzene-1,4-dicarbonyl chloride gives Kevlar (a polyamide) by condensation polymerisation.

quizzes.q: Polymer made from 2-hydroxypropanoic acid?
quizzes.e: 2-hydroxypropanoic acid gives poly(lactic acid) (a polyester) by condensation polymerisation.

quizzes.q: At its isoelectric point an amino acid exists as a
quizzes.e: At its isoelectric point an amino acid exists as a zwitterion, H₃N⁺–CHR–COO⁻, with no overall charge.

quizzes.q: DNA strands are held together by
quizzes.e: The two strands are held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases: two between A and T, and three between C and G.

quizzes.q: How does cisplatin act as an anticancer drug?
quizzes.e: Cisplatin binds to N atoms on guanine bases in DNA, stopping the DNA replicating, so cancer cells cannot divide. It also harms healthy cells.

quizzes.q: DNA base pairing is
quizzes.e: In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine and cytosine with guanine. In RNA, uracil replaces thymine.

quizzes.q: Primary protein structure is
quizzes.e: The primary structure is the sequence of amino acids. Secondary structure is the α-helix or β-pleated sheet, held by hydrogen bonds.

quizzes.q: R group of lysine?
quizzes.e: Amino acids have the general formula H₂NCH(R)COOH. In lysine, R = (CH₂)₄NH₂.

quizzes.q: R group of alanine?
quizzes.e: Amino acids have the general formula H₂NCH(R)COOH. In alanine, R = CH₃.

quizzes.q: R group of cysteine?
quizzes.e: Amino acids have the general formula H₂NCH(R)COOH. In cysteine, R = CH₂SH.

quizzes.q: R group of serine?
quizzes.e: Amino acids have the general formula H₂NCH(R)COOH. In serine, R = CH₂OH.

quizzes.q: R group of aspartic acid?
quizzes.e: Amino acids have the general formula H₂NCH(R)COOH. In aspartic acid, R = CH₂COOH.

quizzes.q: R group of glycine?
quizzes.e: Amino acids have the general formula H₂NCH(R)COOH. In glycine, R = H.

quizzes.q: Primary structure of a protein is
quizzes.e: The primary structure is the order of amino acids in the polypeptide chain.

quizzes.q: Secondary structure is held by
quizzes.e: α-helices and β-pleated sheets are held by hydrogen bonds between N–H and C=O groups.

quizzes.q: Tertiary structure includes
quizzes.a: disulfide bridges, ionic bonds and H-bonds
w: only H-bonds between C=O and N–H in a helix
quizzes.e: Tertiary structure is the 3D folding, held by S–S bridges, ionic bonds and hydrogen bonds between R groups.

quizzes.q: DNA bases pair as
quizzes.e: Complementary base pairing: adenine–thymine (2 H-bonds) and cytosine–guanine (3 H-bonds).

quizzes.q: An enzyme's active site is
quizzes.e: Only a substrate with the right shape and orientation (stereospecific) fits the active site.

quizzes.q: The bond formed between two amino acids is a
quizzes.e: The COOH of one amino acid and the NH₂ of the next form an amide (peptide) link, losing H₂O.

quizzes.q: Which base is NOT in DNA?
quizzes.e: DNA contains adenine, thymine, guanine and cytosine. Uracil replaces thymine in RNA.

quizzes.q: Form of an amino acid in strong acid (low pH)?
quizzes.e: Low pH protonates NH₂ to NH₃⁺; high pH deprotonates COOH to COO⁻; at the isoelectric point both are ionised (zwitterion).

quizzes.q: Form of an amino acid at the isoelectric point?
quizzes.e: Low pH protonates NH₂ to NH₃⁺; high pH deprotonates COOH to COO⁻; at the isoelectric point both are ionised (zwitterion).

quizzes.q: Form of an amino acid in strong alkali (high pH)?
quizzes.e: Low pH protonates NH₂ to NH₃⁺; high pH deprotonates COOH to COO⁻; at the isoelectric point both are ionised (zwitterion).

quizzes.q: Number of H-bonds in a C–G base pair?
quizzes.e: C–G pairs form 3 hydrogen bonds; A–T pairs form 2.

quizzes.q: Thin-layer chromatography of amino acids uses which locating agent?
quizzes.e: Ninhydrin turns amino acid spots purple; UV light can also be used on a fluorescent plate.

quizzes.q: An enzyme inhibitor works by
quizzes.a: binding to the active site, blocking the substrate
quizzes.e: A competitive inhibitor has a similar shape to the substrate, binds to the active site and blocks it.

quizzes.q: The DNA backbone consists of
quizzes.e: Each nucleotide's deoxyribose bonds to a phosphate, forming the sugar–phosphate backbone.

quizzes.q: Explain why heating an enzyme stops it working.
quizzes.e: High temperature breaks the hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds and other interactions holding the tertiary structure, so the active site changes shape (denatures) and the substrate no longer fits.

quizzes.q: Products of hydrolysing the dipeptide Gly–Ala with HCl(aq)?
quizzes.e: Acid hydrolysis breaks the peptide link. In acidic solution both amino acids are protonated on the NH₂ group, giving the cations H₃N⁺CH₂COOH and H₃N⁺CH(CH₃)COOH.

quizzes.q: Why do amino acids have high melting points?
quizzes.e: Amino acids exist as zwitterions (H₃N⁺–CHR–COO⁻), so the solid has strong ionic attractions between molecules that need a lot of energy to overcome.

quizzes.q: Cisplatin prevents DNA replication because
quizzes.a: it binds to nitrogen atoms on guanine bases in DNA, so the strands cannot separate and copy
w: it breaks hydrogen bonds between all base pairs
it binds to the cell membrane and stops it dividing
quizzes.e: Cisplatin swaps its two chloride ligands for bonds to nitrogen atoms on guanine. This distorts the DNA and stops it unwinding, so the cancer cell cannot replicate its DNA and divide.

quizzes.q: How many water molecules are released when 3 amino acids join into one chain?
quizzes.e: 3 amino acids in one chain are joined by 2 peptide bonds, and each bond releases one H₂O, so 2 water molecules.

quizzes.q: How many water molecules are released when 4 amino acids join into one chain?
quizzes.e: 4 amino acids in one chain are joined by 3 peptide bonds, and each bond releases one H₂O, so 3 water molecules.

quizzes.q: How many water molecules are released when 5 amino acids join into one chain?
quizzes.e: 5 amino acids in one chain are joined by 4 peptide bonds, and each bond releases one H₂O, so 4 water molecules.

quizzes.q: Order the route from ethene to ethanoic acid
quizzes.e: Step 1: hydration of ethene with steam and H₃PO₄ catalyst gives ethanol. Step 2: reflux with excess acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ oxidises it to ethanoic acid.

quizzes.q: Reagent for bromoethane → ethanol
quizzes.e: Warm aqueous NaOH gives nucleophilic substitution (OH⁻ replaces Br). NaOH in ethanol would favour elimination.

quizzes.q: Conditions for propan-1-ol → propanal
quizzes.e: Use acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ and distil the aldehyde off as it forms, so it is not oxidised further to propanoic acid.

quizzes.q: Why do chemists prefer fewer steps?
quizzes.e: Each step has a yield below 100%, so more steps lower the overall yield, use more chemicals and energy, and create more waste.

quizzes.q: Synthesis step: which reagents convert methane into chloromethane?
w: excess NH₃ in ethanol, heat under pressure
quizzes.e: methane → chloromethane needs Cl₂, UV light (free-radical substitution). The other reagents carry out different conversions.

quizzes.q: Synthesis step: which reagents convert bromoethane into ethanol?
quizzes.e: bromoethane → ethanol needs NaOH(aq), warm (nucleophilic substitution). The other reagents carry out different conversions.

quizzes.q: Synthesis step: which reagents convert bromoethane into ethene?
quizzes.e: bromoethane → ethene needs KOH in ethanol, hot (elimination). The other reagents carry out different conversions.

quizzes.q: Synthesis step: which reagents convert bromoethane into propanenitrile?
quizzes.e: bromoethane → propanenitrile needs KCN in aqueous ethanol, reflux (nucleophilic substitution). The other reagents carry out different conversions.

quizzes.q: Synthesis step: which reagents convert ethene into ethyl hydrogensulfate?
quizzes.e: ethene → ethyl hydrogensulfate needs cold concentrated H₂SO₄ (electrophilic addition). The other reagents carry out different conversions.

quizzes.q: Synthesis step: which reagents convert ethene into ethanol?
quizzes.e: ethene → ethanol needs steam, H₃PO₄ catalyst, 300 °C, 6–7 MPa (hydration (electrophilic addition)). The other reagents carry out different conversions.

quizzes.q: Why do chemists try to design processes that do not need a solvent and that use non-hazardous starting materials?
quizzes.e: Solvents and hazardous chemicals create waste and risks to people and the environment, and cost money to dispose of safely. Avoiding them makes the process safer, cheaper and more sustainable (greener).

quizzes.q: Synthesis step: which reagents convert bromoethane into ethylamine?
quizzes.a: excess NH₃ in ethanol, heat under pressure
quizzes.e: bromoethane → ethylamine needs excess NH₃ in ethanol, heat under pressure (nucleophilic substitution). The other reagents carry out different conversions.

quizzes.q: Synthesis step: which reagents convert ethene into bromoethane?
quizzes.e: ethene → bromoethane needs HBr, room temperature (electrophilic addition). The other reagents carry out different conversions.

quizzes.q: Synthesis step: which reagents convert ethene into 1,2-dibromoethane?
quizzes.e: ethene → 1,2-dibromoethane needs Br₂, room temperature (electrophilic addition). The other reagents carry out different conversions.

quizzes.q: Synthesis step: which reagents convert ethanol into ethanal?
w: excess NH₃ in ethanol, heat under pressure
quizzes.e: ethanol → ethanal needs acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, distil as formed (oxidation). The other reagents carry out different conversions.

quizzes.q: Synthesis step: which reagents convert ethanoyl chloride into N-methylethanamide?
quizzes.e: ethanoyl chloride → N-methylethanamide needs methylamine (nucleophilic addition–elimination). The other reagents carry out different conversions.

quizzes.q: Synthesis step: which reagents convert benzene into nitrobenzene?
w: excess NH₃ in ethanol, heat under pressure
quizzes.e: benzene → nitrobenzene needs concentrated HNO₃ + concentrated H₂SO₄, 50 °C (electrophilic substitution). The other reagents carry out different conversions.

quizzes.q: Synthesis step: which reagents convert benzene into phenylethanone?
quizzes.e: benzene → phenylethanone needs CH₃COCl, AlCl₃ catalyst (electrophilic substitution (Friedel–Crafts acylation)). The other reagents carry out different conversions.

quizzes.q: Synthesis step: which reagents convert propanenitrile into propylamine?

quizzes.q: In GC, retention time is
quizzes.a: the time to pass through the column
quizzes.e: Retention time is the time a component takes to pass through the GC column. Comparing it with known standards identifies the component.

quizzes.q: What does separation in chromatography depend on?
quizzes.e: Components separate by their relative affinity for the stationary phase and the mobile phase: more soluble in the mobile phase means faster movement.

quizzes.q: TLC stationary phase is
quizzes.a: silica or alumina on a plate
quizzes.e: In TLC, the stationary phase is a thin layer of silica (or alumina) on a plate. The mobile phase is the solvent.

quizzes.q: Chromatography separates by
quizzes.a: relative affinity for stationary and mobile phases
quizzes.e: Components that bind more strongly to the stationary phase move more slowly.

quizzes.q: Rf value is
quizzes.a: distance moved by spot ÷ distance moved by solvent
quizzes.e: Rf = distance moved by the spot ÷ distance moved by the solvent front; always between 0 and 1.

quizzes.q: In TLC, the stationary phase is
quizzes.a: silica or alumina on a plate
w: a liquid in a column only
quizzes.e: A thin layer of silica (SiO₂) or alumina (Al₂O₃) on glass, metal or plastic is the stationary phase.

quizzes.q: In gas chromatography, the mobile phase is
quizzes.e: An inert carrier gas such as nitrogen or helium carries the vaporised sample through the column.

quizzes.q: Retention time is
quizzes.e: Each component has a characteristic retention time under the same conditions.

quizzes.q: Why is the start line drawn in pencil?

quizzes.e: Ink would dissolve in the solvent and run up the plate; graphite does not.

quizzes.q: Why must the solvent be below the start line?
quizzes.a: so spots don't dissolve into the solvent
quizzes.e: If the solvent were above the spots, they would dissolve into the solvent pool instead of moving up.

quizzes.q: Why cover the TLC tank with a lid?

quizzes.e: A saturated atmosphere stops the solvent evaporating from the plate, so it rises evenly.

quizzes.q: A spot with high Rf has
quizzes.a: a greater affinity for the mobile phase
w: a greater affinity for the stationary phase
quizzes.e: A high Rf means the spot spends more time in the moving solvent.

quizzes.q: In column chromatography, the mobile phase is
quizzes.e: The solvent (eluent) carries the mixture through the column of stationary phase.
